title: The Life of the Buddha
summary: Ashvaghosha’s court epic of the Buddha’s early life, from his birth to his victory over Mara under the bodhi tree. The Sanskrit survives only this far.
compare: 这部书和别的经最大的不同，是它首先是一首宫廷诗（kāvya）。马鸣处处用双关（śleṣa）：一个词同时指两样东西，比如 ketu 既是「旗帜」又是「彗星」，mokṣa 在同一句里先是「还清债务」、再是「解脱」。英文和中文白话都只能挑一个意思写进正文，另一个放进三语对照注。本站英文尽量保留比喻和排比的节奏，但不押韵；白话更偏向把意思讲明白，常把比喻压平。读者看到一段注特别多，多半就是双关密集的地方。

第二个差别在 dharma。这个词在书里至少有三层：国王和刹帝利该尽的本分、行善得福的功德、以及佛陀要找的那条出路。父王、大臣、频婆娑罗王劝王子回去时说的 dharma，是第一层；王子拒绝时说的，是第三层。整部前半生的张力就在这同一个词上。中文一律写「法」，看不出层次；英文按语境分开：本分写 duty，宗教意义的出路写大写的 Dharma，第 7 章苦行者辩论里的 dharma / adharma 照原词保留。
第三个差别在古译。《佛所行赞》传为北凉昙无谶所译（五世纪），是五言长偈，篇幅完整、一直写到佛陀涅槃，但常常改写：删掉印度神话典故、加上中国读者熟悉的说法（例如把佛诞写成「四月八日」），有些地方甚至把人物关系弄错。梵文只存到第 14 章第 31 颂，后半部只能靠汉译和藏译知道。英文版不放古译，但凡古译和梵文的出入会影响理解的，都写进了注。
compareEn: What sets this book apart from the sutras is that it is first of all a court poem (kāvya). Ashvaghosha puns constantly (śleṣa): one word points to two things at once — ketu is both “banner” and “comet,” and in a single verse mokṣa is first “release from a debt” and then “liberation.” Both the English and the plain Chinese can carry only one sense in the main text; the other goes into the comparison notes. The site’s English tries to keep the poem’s similes and the rhythm of its lists, without rhyme; the plain Chinese leans toward making the meaning clear and often flattens the imagery. Where a verse has unusually many notes, it is usually a place thick with wordplay.

The second difference is dharma. In this book the word has at least three layers: the duty a king and a warrior owe, the merit that good deeds earn, and the way out of suffering the future Buddha is looking for. When his father, the ministers and King Shrenya urge the prince to come home, the dharma they mean is the first; when he refuses, he means the third. The whole tension of his early life sits on this one word. Chinese writes 法 (fǎ, “law, teaching”) every time, so the layers can’t be seen; the English separates them by context, using “duty” for the first, a capitalized “Dharma” for the saving truth, and keeping the bare words dharma / adharma in the ascetics’ debate of Chapter 7.

The third difference is the old Chinese version, 佛所行赞 (Fó suǒ xíng zàn, “Praise of the Buddha’s Deeds”), traditionally credited to Dharmakshema in the 5th century. Written in five-character verse lines, it is complete and runs all the way to the Buddha’s final nirvana, but it often rewrites: it drops Indian mythological allusions, adds things familiar to Chinese readers (dating the birth to 四月八日, sì yuè bā rì, “the eighth day of the fourth month”), and in places even confuses who is related to whom. The Sanskrit survives only up to Chapter 14, verse 31; the second half of the poem is known only from the Chinese and Tibetan translations. The English edition does not print the old Chinese version, but wherever its differences from the Sanskrit matter for understanding, the notes say so.

chapters.title: Chapter 1 · The Birth of the Blessed One (Bhagavatprasūti)

verses.en: (The opening pages of the Sanskrit manuscript are lost; the text picks up at verse 8.) In that splendid grove the queen, seeing that her time to give birth was near, went to a couch hung with a canopy, while thousands of women greeted her with joy.
Then, when Pushya (a lucky lunar mansion) stood favorable, from the side of the queen, purified by her vows, a son was born for the good of the world, without pain and without sickness.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「从身侧」，没说哪一侧；昙无谶译本写明「右脇」，并加上「四月八日」的日期，这是后来佛传的通行说法，梵文这里没有。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only “from her side,” not which side. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version specifies 右脇 (yòu xié, “the right side”) and adds the date 四月八日 (sìyuè bā rì, “eighth day of the fourth month”), details from the later standard legend that are not in the Sanskrit here.

verses.en: As Aurva was born from a thigh, Prithu from a hand, Mandhatri, Indra’s equal, from a head, and Kakshivat from the hollow under the shoulder, so too was his birth.

Coming out of the womb in due course, he shone as if he had dropped from the sky, not born through the birth passage; and since he had cultivated himself through many aeons (kalpas), he was born fully aware, not dazed.
With his radiance and steadiness the child shone like the young sun come down to earth; yet blazing as he was, when people gazed at him he drew their eyes the way the moon does.

cmp.note: bāla 既是「孩子」，也指「初升的（太阳）」。一词双关：这个婴儿就是一轮刚升起的太阳。
cmp.en: Bāla means both “child” and “young, newly risen” (of the sun). The word works double: the infant is himself a rising sun.

verses.en: For with the blazing light of his own body he stole the light of the lamps, as the sun does; and with his lovely color of precious Jambu-river gold he lit up every direction.
Steady, lifting each foot straight up, pressing each one firmly down, striding long, he took seven firm steps, like the seven stars of the Seers (the Great Bear).
“I am born for Awakening, for the good of the world; this is my last coming into being.” So, looking round the four directions with a lion’s bearing, he spoke words that foretold what was to come.
From the sky two streams of water poured down, white as moonbeams, one cool and one warm in their power, and fell on his gentle head to make his body glad at their touch.
He lay on a bed with a splendid canopy, its frame shining with gold and its legs of beryl; and out of reverence the lords of the yakshas stood around it holding golden lotuses in their hands.
Unseen in the sky, the gods bowed their heads before his power, held a white parasol over him, and murmured the highest blessings for his Awakening.

The great serpents, who had served the Buddhas of the past and thirsted for the higher Dharma, fanned him, their eyes bright with devotion, and showered him with mandarava flowers (flowers of heaven).
The gods of the Pure Abodes, pure in nature, rejoiced at the blessing of a Tathagata’s birth even though passion had left them, for the sake of a world sunk in suffering.
At his birth the earth, pinned in place by the king of mountains, shook like a ship struck by the wind; and from a cloudless sky fell a rain scented with sandalwood and full of blue and red lotuses.

Breezes blew, soft to the touch and delightful, letting fall heavenly garments; the sun, still the same sun, shone more brightly than ever; and fire, though no one fanned it, burned with a gentle flame.

In the northeast part of the dwelling a well of clear water appeared of its own accord, and the women of the inner palace, filled with wonder, performed their rites at it as at a sacred bathing place.
Hosts of heavenly beings, seeking the Dharma, filled the grove to see him, and out of sheer eagerness made the trees drop flowers even out of season.
(The manuscript is missing from verse 25 through the first three lines of verse 40; when it resumes, brahmins are reassuring the king.) “…and here are examples of it; hear them from us.”
“The science of kingship that Bhrigu and Angiras, those two seers who founded lineages, did not compose, their sons Shukra and Brihaspati produced in time, good sir.”
“The son of Sarasvati proclaimed again the lost Veda that earlier men had never seen; and Vyasa arranged it in many parts, which Vasishtha, lacking the power, had not done.”
“Valmiki first created verse, which the great seer Chyavana had not composed; and the medicine that Atri did not work out, the seer Atreya taught later.”
“The brahminhood that Kushika failed to win, Gadhin’s son obtained, O king; and Sagara set a shore for the ocean, which the Ikshvakus before him had not bound.”

“Janaka gained the standing of a teacher of brahmins in the practice of yoga, which no one else had gained; and the famous deeds of Shauri (Krishna) were beyond the strength of Shura and his other forebears.”
“So neither age nor lineage is the measure: anyone, anywhere, may rise to the first place in the world. Among kings and seers, sons have done many things their fathers left undone.”
Comforted and cheered in this way by those trusted brahmins, the king let the unwelcome fear go from his mind and rose to still greater joy.
Pleased, he gave wealth with every courtesy to those best of brahmins, thinking, “May he become lord of the earth as they foretold, and go to the forest only when old age has come.”

Then, learning through signs and the power of his austerity of the birth of the one who would put an end to birth, the great seer Asita came to the palace of the lord of the Shakyas, thirsting for the true Dharma.

Blazing with a brahmin’s splendor and the splendor of austerity, he was a knower of Brahman; and the king’s own priest, also a knower of Brahman, showed him into the king’s house with respect and honor.

cmp.note: 两个 brahmavid 一个是主格、一个是宾格：知梵的国王家师，把知梵的阿私陀请进宫。白话译成「知梵者中的知梵者」，把语法读错了。
cmp.en: The two brahmavid forms differ in case: the king’s priest, a knower of Brahman, ushers in Asita, another knower of Brahman. The plain Chinese 知梵者中的知梵者 (“knower of Brahman among knowers of Brahman”) misreads the grammar.

verses.en: He drew near the king’s inner palace, a rush of joy in him at the prince’s birth, and that steady man went in as though it were only a forest, so deep was his austerity and so great his age.
When the sage was seated, the king honored him properly, first with water for his feet and the guest-offering, and addressed him with due ceremony, as Antideva once did Vasishtha.
“I am blessed, and my family is favored, since Your Holiness has come wishing to see me. Command me: what shall I do, kind sir? I am your disciple; you may trust me.”

cmp.note: bhagavat 是对圣者的一般尊称（「尊者」），在这里指阿私陀。白话用「世尊」，读者容易误以为是佛陀。
cmp.en: Bhagavat is a general honorific for a holy man (“Your Holiness”), here addressed to Asita. The plain Chinese uses 世尊 (shìzūn, “World-Honored One”), a title readers normally reserve for the Buddha.

verses.en: So invited by the king with his whole heart, the sage answered as was fitting, his large eyes opened wide with wonder, and spoke words deep and steady.

“This is worthy of you, great-souled as you are, a lover of guests, generous, and devoted to Dharma: that your thoughts toward me should be so warm befits your nature, your family, your learning and your age.”

“This is the very way the royal seers of old, having gained wealth by subtle righteousness, gave it away constantly and as the rules prescribe, so that they were rich in austerity and poor in possessions.”
“But hear the reason for my coming, and be glad: on the path of the sun I heard a heavenly voice saying, ‘A son has been born to you for Awakening.’”
“When I heard those words, I composed my mind and understood it from the signs as well; so I have come, wishing to see this banner of the Shakya clan, raised high like Indra’s banner.”
Hearing these words, the king, his steps unsteady with joy, took the prince from his nurse’s lap and showed him to the man whose wealth was austerity.

Then the great seer looked in wonder at the king’s son: the wheel marked on his soles, the webbing between his fingers and toes, the tuft of hair between his brows, and his private parts drawn into a sheath like an elephant’s.
Seeing him seated on his nurse’s lap, like the son of Agni (Skanda) on the lap of the Goddess, the seer’s eyes filled until tears trembled on his lashes; he sighed and lifted his face toward heaven.
When the king saw Asita’s eyes swimming with tears, he trembled out of love for his son; his voice faltering and his throat choked with weeping, he bowed, joined his palms, and asked:
“His body falls little short of the gods’, his birth was bright and full of wonders, and you have said his future will be the highest. Why, then, steadfast one, do you weep as you look at him?”
“Will the prince live long, holy one? Surely he was not born only for my grief? I have barely gained this handful of water; surely Time is not coming to drink it?”

cmp.note: 「一捧水」不只是比喻珍贵：印度习俗里，儿子要为亡父献上一捧水（祭水）。国王怕的是将来没人给他献水，也就是无后。白话、古译都只取了字面或「甘露」之意。
cmp.en: “A handful of water” is more than an image of something precious: in Indian custom a son offers handfuls of water to his dead father. The king fears there will be no one to make that offering, that is, no heir. The plain Chinese keeps only the literal sense, and Dharmakshema’s Chinese version turns it into 甘露 (gānlù, “sweet dew, nectar”).

verses.en: “Is the treasure-store of my fame safe from running out? Is this mainstay of my family secure? Shall I pass happily to the next world, keeping, even in sleep, one eye unclosed in my son?”
“Surely this young shoot of my family has not sprung up only to wither before it flowers? Tell me quickly, lord, for I have no peace; you know how kinsmen love a son.”
Seeing that the king was shaken by the thought of some misfortune, the sage said, “Let your mind not run to anything else, O king. What I said is beyond doubt.”

“My distress is not over any change that might befall him; I am troubled at being cheated myself. For my time to go has come, and he is born, the one who will know how to end birth, a thing so hard to win.”
“Giving up the kingdom, indifferent to the pleasures of the senses, he will reach the truth by fierce effort, and blaze in the world as a sun made of knowledge to destroy the darkness of delusion.”

“From the ocean of suffering, whose scattered foam is sickness, whose waves are old age and whose fierce current is death, he will carry across, on the great raft of knowledge, a world swept helplessly along.”

“The thirst-tormented world of the living will drink from the supreme river of his Dharma as it flows: its current wisdom, its banks steady moral conduct, its coolness meditation, and its chakravaka birds his vows.”

cmp.note: cakravāka（赤麻鸭）在印度诗里总是成对出现，是河上常见的景物；用它比「誓愿」，是马鸣把整条河一件件对应到修行上。古译把它泛化成「众奇鸟」，并把「禅定」放进「清凉池」。
cmp.en: The chakravaka (ruddy shelduck) is a stock river bird in Indian poetry, always seen in pairs; making it stand for “vows” completes Ashvaghosha’s point-by-point mapping of a river onto practice. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version generalizes it to 众奇鸟 (zhòng qí niǎo, “many rare birds”) and turns meditation into a 清凉池 (qīngliáng chí, “cool pool”).

verses.en: “To those tormented by suffering, hemmed in by the objects of sense, and standing on the wilderness road of the round of rebirth, he will proclaim the path to liberation, as one shows the way to travelers who have lost it.”

“For people in the world who are burning in the fire of passion, whose fuel is the objects of sense, he will bring relief with the rain of Dharma, as a great cloud does with its rain at the end of the hot season.”
“With the supreme, irresistible blow of the true Dharma he will break open the door that keeps creatures from escaping, whose bolt is craving and whose panels are the darkness of delusion.”
“And this king of Dharma, once he is fully awakened, will set free from its bonds a world wrapped in the snares of its own delusion, overwhelmed by suffering and without refuge.”
“So do not grieve for him. The one to be pitied in this world of men is whoever, out of delusion, or love of pleasure, or pride, will not hear his ultimate Dharma.”

“And since I shall miss that blessing, even though I have attained the meditative states, I have failed in my purpose; for not to hear his Dharma, I think, is misfortune, even if one lives in heaven.”

cmp.note: 梵文只说「即使住在天上也算不幸」，意思是天界的福报比不上听法。古译说他死后「必生三难天」，即投生到听不到佛法的长寿天，这是把佛教「八难」的观念加了进去。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only that even living in heaven would be a misfortune, since heavenly bliss is worth less than hearing the Dharma. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says he will be reborn in a 难天 (nàn tiān, “heaven of hardship”), one of the realms where the Dharma cannot be heard, bringing in the Buddhist idea of the unfavorable rebirths.

verses.en: Having heard what it meant, the king, with his friends and his wives, put aside his dismay and rejoiced; for he thought, “Such is this son of mine,” and he counted himself a man of substance too.
Yet the thought “He will go the way of the seers” made his heart a prey to worry. It was not that he did not favor Dharma; rather he saw the danger of his line coming to an end.
Then the sage Asita, having told the truth fixed for the son to the king who was so anxious for him, went back by the path of the winds as he had come, while all gazed at him with deep respect.

Having made up his mind, and having seen his younger sister’s son, that good man, out of compassion, instructed him in many ways, as though he were his own dear son, to listen to the Sage’s words and to follow his teaching.

cmp.note: 梵文没说这个外甥的名字；佛教传说里他叫那罗陀多（Naradatta），后来随佛出家。昙无谶译本没有这一颂。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit does not name this nephew; Buddhist legend calls him Naradatta, who later became the Buddha’s disciple. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has no counterpart for this verse.

verses.en: The king too, delighted at his son’s birth, freed those held in bonds throughout his realm, and had the birth rites performed for his beloved son properly, as befitted his family.
When ten days had passed, his mind devout and filled with the highest joy, he offered worship to the gods for his son’s supreme welfare, with murmured prayers, fire offerings and auspicious rites.
And with his own hand he gave the brahmins, for his son’s thriving, a full hundred thousand cows, young and rich in milk, with sturdy, strong calves and horns covered in gold.
Then, self-controlled, having performed rites of many kinds that gladdened his heart, he joyfully resolved to enter the city at a favorable, fixed and auspicious hour.
Then the queen with her son, after bowing to the gods for good fortune, took her seat in a costly palanquin of elephant ivory, hung with white flowers and lit with jeweled lamps.

The king had his wife, with her child as her protector, enter the city first, followed by the elders; then he himself went in, honored by crowds of citizens, as Indra enters heaven honored by the immortals.

Entering his palace, the Shakya king, as glad as Bhava (Shiva) at the birth of the six-faced god, his face full of joy, kept saying “This! And this!” as he ordered all manner of things to bring prosperity and fame.
So, as the king’s son was born and thrived, the city called Kapila, with all its country, rejoiced, like the city of Kubera, the giver of wealth, crowded with apsarases at the birth of Nalakubara.

From the birth of that son, who would put an end to birth and old age and who had mastered himself, the king grew day by day in wealth, elephants, horses and allies, as a river swells with rushing waters.

cmp.note: ātmaja「自己生的（儿子）」与 ātmajit「战胜自己的人」紧挨着，音近义远，是马鸣惯用的文字游戏；译文只能拆成两层意思。
cmp.en: Ātmaja (“self-born,” i.e. son) and ātmajit (“self-conquering”) stand side by side, alike in sound but far apart in meaning, a typical piece of Ashvaghosha’s wordplay; a translation can only split it into two ideas.

verses.en: For he came upon many treasures then, of riches, of jewels of every kind, and of gold both worked and unworked, more than even his wishes could carry.
Elephants from the Himalaya, fierce in rut, which even lordly elephants like Padma could not have driven into the training ring, came to serve him without any effort.
His city was astir with horses, some branded with various marks and decked with new gold harness, others with long flowing manes, won by force, by friendship, or with money.
And in his kingdom the cows were many, sleek and contented, gentle, clean, with fine milk and tall calves, and they gave milk in plenty.
His enemy became neutral, the neutral became a friend, and a friend became especially firm; he had only these two sides, and no third.

The rain god, too, rained for him at the right time and place, with gentle winds and rumbling clouds, the clouds adorned with earrings of lightning, but without the harm of hailstorms or falling thunderbolts.
The crops sprang up and bore fruit in their season, even where no labor of plowing had been spent; and his herbs grew richer than ever in juice and strength.
Though childbirth is a time that puts the body in danger, like the press of battle, women then gave birth when their time came, safely, easily and free of sickness.
Apart from those under religious vows, no one begged from others, even when their means were wretched; and no noble man, however small his wealth, turned away from anyone who asked.
In his kingdom then, as in the kingdom of Yayati son of Nahusha, there was no one who did not honor his kin, no one who did not give, no one who broke his vows, no liar and no one cruel.
Those who loved Dharma carried out works there, parks, temples, hermitages, wells, water stalls for travelers, lotus pools and groves, as though they saw heaven before their very eyes.
Freed from famine, fear and disease, the people were glad and took their pleasure as if in heaven; husband did not betray wife, nor wife husband.
No one pursued love merely for pleasure, no one hoarded wealth merely for love, no one practiced Dharma merely for wealth, and no one did harm for the sake of Dharma.

cmp.note: 这一颂按印度「人生三目标」排：欲（kāma）、利（artha）、法（dharma），每一项都不被拿来当低一级目标的工具；最后一句暗指以杀生祭祀求法。古译改写成佛教的「四梵行」，原来的结构不见了。
cmp.en: The verse runs through the three aims of life, love (kāma), wealth (artha) and Dharma (dharma), each kept from serving a lower one; the last line glances at killing animals in sacrifice for the sake of religion. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version recasts it in terms of the Buddhist 四梵行 (sì fànxíng, “four sublime states”), and the original pattern disappears.

verses.en: Thieves and enemies had vanished; his own realm was sound and free of foreign armies, safe and well fed, just as in the kingdom of Anaranya long ago.
For at that son’s birth, in that king’s realm, as in the realm of Manu, son of the Sun, joy spread everywhere, evil perished, Dharma blazed up and impurity died down.
Since such prosperity came to the royal house, and every aim was accomplished, the king gave his son the name Sarvarthasiddha, “He Who Accomplishes Every Aim.”
But Queen Maya, seeing her son’s vast power, like that of a divine seer, could not bear the joy it brought her, and so she went to heaven to dwell.

cmp.note: 「去天上住」是对王后去世的委婉说法。白话照字面译，读者可能看不出她是死了；古译直说「命终生天上」。
cmp.en: “Went to heaven to dwell” is a gentle way of saying the queen died. The plain Chinese keeps it literal, so readers may miss that she died; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says it outright: 命终生天上 (mìng zhōng shēng tiānshàng, “her life ended and she was reborn in heaven”).

verses.en: Then the prince, who was like a child of the gods, was raised by his mother’s sister, whose dignity matched his mother’s, as her own son, with no difference in love or feeling.
Then, like the young sun climbing the eastern mountain, like a fire fanned by the wind, like the lord of the stars in the bright fortnight, the prince grew steadily and well.
From the houses of friends they brought him costly sandalwood, strings of gems with healing herbs set inside, and little golden carts drawn by deer.
And ornaments suited to his age, little elephants, deer and horses of gold, carts yoked to little calves, and dolls bright with gold and silver.
Waited on in this way with all kinds of pleasures fit for his years, he was a child, yet not like a child, in steadiness, purity, intelligence and dignity.

When he had properly passed through childhood, and at the right time had undergone the rite that marks the start of study, he mastered in a few days the branches of learning befitting his family, which take others many years.

But the Shakya king, having heard earlier from the great seer Asita that his son’s future aim was the highest good, set about making him attached to pleasures, so that he would not go off to the forests.

Then from a family of steady character he brought for him a virtuous girl, endowed with beauty, modesty and good manners, named Yashodhara, “Bearer of Fame,” wide in fame indeed, like the goddess Shri herself in a woman’s form.
Shining with surpassing beauty, the prince, like Sanatkumara (the ever-young son of Brahma), delighted in her, the Shakya king’s daughter-in-law, as thousand-eyed Indra delights in Shachi.

Thinking, “How can he be kept from seeing anything unpleasant that might disturb his mind?”, the king assigned him a dwelling on the upper floors of the palace, and gave him no chance to walk the ground.

There, in mansions white as autumn clouds, like brightly painted palaces of the gods set down on earth, pleasant to live in through every season, he took his pleasure amid the splendid music of women.
With soft-voiced drums bound in gold, struck by the fingertips of women, and with dances like those of the finest apsarases, that palace shone like Mount Kailasa.
There the women charmed him with soft words, playful gestures, coquettish airs, tipsy games and sweet laughter, with arching brows and sidelong glances.
Held fast by women skilled in the arts of love and untiring in pleasure, he never came down from the palace roof to the ground, just as a man of merit never comes down from his heavenly mansion.
The king, meanwhile, for his son’s welfare and spurred on by what had been foretold, delighted in calm, kept away from evil, practiced self-restraint, and shared his wealth with good men.

He did not cling to sensual pleasure as a weak man does, nor indulge in wrongful passion; with steadfastness he tamed the restless horses of his senses, and by his virtues he won over his kinsmen and citizens.

cmp.note: 这半句写本读法可疑，字面似乎是「对女人／对母亲不起不当的贪恋」。白话取「对女人」；英文只译作「不纵不正当的情欲」，不硬定对象。
cmp.en: The manuscript reading of this half-line is doubtful; literally it seems to say he felt no improper passion toward a woman (or “a mother”). The plain Chinese takes it as “toward women”; the English renders it only as “wrongful passion,” without forcing a definite object.

verses.en: He studied no learning meant to cause others pain, but only the knowledge that brings blessing; and he wished well to all people everywhere just as he did to his own subjects.
For his son’s long life he duly worshiped the shining lunar mansion whose presiding god is Angiras’s son (Brihaspati); he poured offerings into the blazing fire and gave the brahmins gold and cows.

cmp.note: āṅgirasa 是「安吉罗斯的后裔」，即布里哈斯帕提（木星），他主管鬼宿（Puṣya），也就是王子出生时的星宿。白话译成「以安吉罗斯为主神」，少了「后裔」一层。另外这一行 akṛśe kṛśānau…kṛśanaṃ（旺火……火……黄金）是连环谐音。
cmp.en: Āṅgirasa means “descendant of Angiras,” that is Brihaspati (Jupiter), who presides over Pushya, the lunar mansion of the prince’s birth. The plain Chinese 以安吉罗斯为主神 (“with Angiras as presiding god”) drops the “descendant.” The line also chimes akṛśe kṛśānau … kṛśanaṃ (“blazing … fire … gold”), a chain of sound-play.

verses.en: To purify body and mind he bathed in the waters of holy places and in the waters of virtue; and he drank both the Soma the Veda prescribes and the heart’s own joy of peace, which rises from within.
He spoke kindly, yet nothing empty; he spoke truth, yet nothing harsh; for kind words that were false and true words that were harsh he was ashamed to say even to himself.
In matters that came before him, whether to his liking or not, he never let passion or dislike decide; he pursued the blessing of justice cleanly done, and held no sacrifice to be worth as much.
To anyone who came to him full of hope he at once quenched their thirst with the waters of giving; and without battle, with the axe of his good conduct, he split open the swollen pride of his foes.

cmp.note: 「布施之水」双关：印度送礼要倒水立誓为证，水同时又是解渴之物。
cmp.en: “Waters of giving” works two ways: in India a gift was solemnized by pouring water, and water is also what quenches thirst.

verses.en: He disciplined the one and guarded the seven; he gave up the seven and protected the five; he gained the three and understood the three; he knew the two and gave up the two.

cmp.note: 这是一首数字谜，套用印度治国书里的清单，原文不说破。常见的解法：调伏「一」（自身）；守护「七」（王国七要素：君、臣、友、库、土、城、军）；舍弃「七」（七种恶习，如畋猎、赌博、女色、饮酒等）；保护「五」（含义有争议）；得到「三」（法、利、欲）；了解「三」（衰、稳、兴三种国势）；知「二」、舍「二」也有不同解释。这些都是后人的推测。
cmp.en: This is a number riddle built on lists from Indian treatises on statecraft, and the text does not spell them out. A common solution: the one disciplined is himself; the seven guarded are the seven limbs of a kingdom (king, ministers, allies, treasury, territory, fort, army); the seven given up are the seven royal vices (hunting, gambling, women, drink and so on); the five protected are disputed; the three gained are Dharma, wealth and love; the three understood are a state’s decline, stability and growth; the two known and the two given up are explained in various ways. All of these are later guesses.

verses.en: Even offenders who deserved death he convicted but did not have killed, nor did he even look at them in anger; he bound them with gentle words and a fitting penalty, for he saw that simply setting them free was bad policy too.

cmp.note: phala 本义「果、结果」，这里可能指适度的惩处，也可能指给予财物。白话取前者；古译「务施以财物，指授资生路」取后者。
cmp.en: Phala basically means “fruit, result”; here it may mean a measured penalty, or it may mean gifts. The plain Chinese takes the first; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version takes the second: 务施以财物 (wù shī yǐ cáiwù, “made a point of giving them goods”).

verses.en: He practiced the highest vows of the seers; he laid aside long-cherished enmities; he won fame fragrant with virtue; and he shed the dust of passion that stains.

cmp.note: rajas 既是「尘土」，也是「激情、染污」。「去尘」同时就是「去欲」。
cmp.en: Rajas means both “dust” and “passion, defilement,” so shedding dust is at the same time shedding passion.

verses.en: He had no wish to collect any tax that was not customary, no wish to covet another’s property, no wish to speak of his enemies’ wrongs, and no wish to carry anger in his heart.

cmp.note: 末两句的 avivakṣīt「不想说」与 avivākṣīt「不想带着」只差一个长音，是刻意的同音对仗。
cmp.en: In the last two clauses avivakṣīt (“did not wish to speak”) and avivākṣīt (“did not wish to carry”) differ by a single long vowel, a deliberate echo.

verses.en: With the king acting in this way, his servants and citizens behaved likewise, just as the senses of one practicing yoga follow when his mind is calm and clear.
Then in time, to Shuddhodana’s son, by Yashodhara of the lovely breasts, who bore her own fame as her name says, a son was born whose face was like the moon, Rahu’s foe; and he was named Rahula.

cmp.note: 「罗睺（吞日月的魔）的对头」就是月亮，所以说他脸如满月；名字罗睺罗正好跟 Rāhu 同音相扣。同一行 cārupayodharā / yaśodharā / svayaśodharā 也连续押 -dharā。
cmp.en: “Rahu’s rival” is the moon (Rahu being the demon who swallows sun and moon), so the child’s face is moon-like; and the name Rahula plays on Rāhu. The same line chimes -dharā three times: cārupayodharā, yaśodharā, svayaśodharā.

verses.en: Then the king, who had longed for sons and was deeply reassured about the growth of his line, rejoiced at his grandson’s birth just as he had rejoiced at his son’s.
Glad at heart, thinking, “How may my son come to love his son as I love him?”, the king, devoted to his son, performed this rite and that in due season, as one who longs to rise to heaven.
Keeping to the path of the glorious bull-like kings of the first age, he practiced austerities without giving up the white clothes of a householder, and offered sacrifices free of killing.
So that king of meritorious deeds blazed with the splendor of royalty and the splendor of austerity, shining in lineage, conduct and wisdom, like the thousand-rayed sun about to pour out its light.

Secure in his fortune, he honored the hymns of the Self-existent One and recited prayers that his son might stay; and he performed hard austerities, like Ka (Prajapati) at the beginning of time when he wished to bring forth creatures.

cmp.note: 这几个词意思不确定：ārcika 可以是「赞颂诗集」，也可以是「值得礼敬的」。白话理解为礼拜自生者梵天；英文按「礼敬自生者的颂诗」译，两种读法都可能。
cmp.en: The meaning of these words is uncertain: ārcika can mean “a collection of hymn verses” or “worthy of worship.” The plain Chinese takes it as worshiping Brahma, the Self-existent; the English reads “honored the hymns of the Self-existent One.” Either is possible.

verses.en: He laid down the sword and pondered the scriptures; he practiced calm and bore restraints; like a man of self-mastery he indulged in no object of sense, and like a father he watched over all his lands.

cmp.note: śastra「兵器」与 śāstra「经典」只差一个长音。viṣaya 既是「感官对象」又是「领地」：前半说他不沉迷感官对象，后半说他像父亲一样看顾所有领地，同一个词用了两次、两种意思。
cmp.en: Śastra (“weapon”) and śāstra (“scripture”) differ by one long vowel. Viṣaya means both “object of sense” and “territory”: he indulged in no viṣaya, yet watched over every viṣaya like a father, the same word used twice in two senses.

verses.en: He ruled the kingdom for his son’s sake, cherished his son for the family, the family for fame, fame for heaven and heaven for his own sake; and he wished his own life to endure for the sake of Dharma.
So he practiced Dharma in its many forms, as the good have followed it and as scripture establishes it, praying, “Now that my son has seen his own son’s face, how could he go to the forest?”

Kings on earth guard their sons because they want to guard the royal fortune that rests in themselves; but this king, who loved Dharma, guarded his son from Dharma by letting him loose among the pleasures of the senses.

Yet all Bodhisattvas, beings without equal, went to the forest only after they had known the taste of the pleasures of the senses and a son had been born to them. So he too, though he had gathered karma for this and its cause had already taken root, enjoyed pleasure until the time of Awakening came.
Then one day he heard songs that told of the groves outside the city, with their soft lawns, their trees ringing with the calls of male cuckoos, and their lotus ponds set about like jewels.
Hearing how charming the city’s groves were, how dear to the women, he set his mind on going out, like an elephant shut up inside a house.
When the king learned what his son wanted (his son, the very wish of his heart given a name), he ordered an outing fit for his love, for his royal splendor, and for the young man’s age.

cmp.note: 直译是「名叫『儿子』的心愿」:儿子就是国王心愿的化身。白话中文照字面保留了这个说法,英文译成「他心愿的化身、名字叫儿子」。
cmp.en: Literally “of the heart’s wish that bore the name ‘son’”: the boy is the king’s longing made flesh. The plain Chinese keeps the literal phrase; the English unpacks it as “the very wish of his heart given a name.”

verses.en: And he had the crowds of suffering common folk kept off the royal road, thinking, “The prince has a tender heart. He must not be upset.”
So, as gently as could be, they cleared away on every side those missing limbs or with failing senses, the old, the sick and the wretched, and they made the royal road wonderfully beautiful.
When the royal road had been made splendid, the splendid prince, with a well-mannered escort, came down from the palace roof at the proper time and, with leave given, went to the king.
The lord of men, tears in his eyes, kissed his son’s head and gazed at him a long while. With his voice he said, “Go,” but in his heart, out of love, he did not let him go.
Then he mounted a golden chariot yoked to four quiet horses in gold trappings, its shining reins held by a driver who was manly, skilled and honest.
He set out on the road, strewn with nets of bright flowers, hung with garlands, banners fluttering, and his fitting retinue behind him, like the moon entering the sky among the stars.
Slowly, slowly he made his way down the royal road, watched on every side by the townspeople, the road seeming strewn with blue lotus petals: their eyes, opened wide with curiosity.

cmp.note: 「好像撒满了青莲花瓣」:ardha 意为「一半、片」,多指莲瓣,比喻睁大的眼睛;白话中文译成「半开的青莲花」,把「半片」理解成「半开」,略有出入。
cmp.en: “As if with blue-lotus halves”: ardha (“half, piece”) most likely means petals, the classic image for wide eyes. The plain Chinese takes it as 半开 (bàn kāi, “half-opened”) lotuses, which slightly shifts the picture.

verses.en: Some praised him for his gentle nature; others bowed before his radiance; and some, seeing his kindly face, wished him greater fortune and a long life.
Hunchbacks came out of the great houses, and troops of mountain folk and dwarfs, and women from poor cottages, and they bowed like the banners carried in a god’s procession.
Then the women heard from the servants the news, “The prince is going out!” Longing to see him, and given leave by those they had to obey, they went up onto the rooftops.
Hampered by girdle strings slipping loose, eyes bewildered from being woken out of sleep, ornaments thrown on at the news, they crowded round, too curious to keep still.
They scared the flocks of house birds with the clatter of feet on the palace stairs, the jingle of girdles and the ring of anklets, and they scolded one another for pushing ahead.
But some of these lovely women, though eager and in a hurry, were slowed in their going by the weight of their broad, chariot-wide hips and full breasts.

cmp.note: 「臀如车」:把宽大的臀部比作车子,是宫廷诗的惯用夸张;白话中文只说「宽大的臀部」。
cmp.en: Śroṇī-ratha, “hips like chariots,” a stock court-poetry hyperbole for broad hips; the plain Chinese simply says 宽大的臀部 (kuāndà de túnbù, “broad hips”).

verses.en: Another, though she could have gone fast, held back her pace and did not hurry: shy and modest, she was hiding the ornaments she wore only in private.
Pressed together in clusters, their earrings jostled in the crush, their jewelry jingling, there was no quiet at the windows.
The lotus faces of the women, leaning out of the windows with their earrings knocking against each other, shone like lotuses fastened onto the mansions.

cmp.note: 同一个词 paṅkaja(莲花)前后用两次:先是「脸莲」(比喻),再是真正的莲花,是马鸣喜欢的重复修辞。
cmp.en: The same word paṅkaja (“lotus”) appears twice: first as the metaphor “lotus faces,” then as real lotuses, a deliberate echo Ashvaghosha likes.

verses.en: With its mansions crammed with young women, their windows thrown open out of curiosity, the city shone on every side like the sky filled with heavenly palaces full of apsarases.

cmp.note: vimāna 既指人间的多层楼阁,也指天神乘坐或居住的「天宫、飞车」;这里一词两用,把满楼少女比作满天天女。
cmp.en: Vimāna means both a many-storied mansion on earth and the aerial palace of the gods; the one word carries the comparison of the crowded houses to a sky full of apsarases.

verses.en: Because the windows were narrow, the faces of the delighted women, earrings resting against one another’s cheeks, looked like lotuses tied together in bunches.
The women, looking down at the prince on the road, seemed to want to go down to the earth; the men, faces turned upward gazing at him, seemed to want to go up to the sky.
Seeing the king’s son blazing with beauty and splendor, the women whispered, “Lucky is his wife!” They said it with pure hearts, with no other thought.

“They say that this man, with his long, strong arms, Kama of the flowered banner in person to look at, will give up his royal fortune and go to seek the Dharma.” So they felt nothing for him but reverence.

cmp.note: puṣpaketu 字面是「以花为旗者」,爱神迦摩的称号;白话中文作「花箭爱神」,把「花旗」换成了更常见的「花箭」。
cmp.en: Puṣpaketu, “he whose banner is flowers,” an epithet of Kama, the god of love. The plain Chinese renders it 花箭爱神 (huājiàn àishén, “love god of the flower arrows”), swapping the banner for the better-known arrows.

verses.en: Seeing the royal road crowded like this with orderly townspeople in clean, sober dress, the prince, who had never seen such a sight before, was somewhat pleased, and felt almost as if he had been born again.
But the gods of the Pure Abodes (Shuddhadhivasa, the highest heavens), seeing the city as joyful as heaven, created an old man walking along, to stir the king’s son.

cmp.note: 「净居天」诸神,是色界最高的天,住着不再还来的圣者;昙无谶译本说是「净居天王」一位化成老人,梵文是众神一起造出老人。
cmp.en: The Shuddhadhivasa gods, dwellers in the highest form-heavens, home of those who will not be reborn. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has a single 净居天王 (Jìngjūtiān wáng, “king of the Pure Abodes”) turning himself into the old man; the Sanskrit has the gods together creating one.

verses.en: The prince saw the man, crushed by old age and shaped unlike other men, and with his attention caught he fixed his gaze on him without wavering and said to the driver:

“Driver, who is this man coming toward us, with white hair, his hand clutching a stick, eyes hidden under his brows, limbs slack and bent? Is this some change that has come over him, his natural state, or mere chance?”
Asked this, the charioteer told the king’s son the very thing that ought to have been kept from him, seeing no harm in it, for those same gods had clouded his judgment.
“It is called old age, and it has broken this man: it kills beauty, ruins strength, is the source of sorrow and the end of pleasures, the destroyer of memory and the enemy of the senses.
“He too drank milk as a baby, and in time crawled about on the ground; little by little he became a fine young man, and little by little, in the same way, he has come to old age.”
When he had said this, the king’s son was a little shaken, and he said to the driver, “Will this evil come to me too?” And the charioteer answered him:
“Even to you, long-lived sir, this advance of years will come in time without a doubt. So the world knows old age, the ruin of beauty, and yet longs for it all the same.”

cmp.note: 「世人既知道它,又想要它」:想要的是长寿,而长寿就是衰老。白话中文补了「〔长寿〕」;这句话本身是个讽刺的悖论。
cmp.en: “The world both knows it and wants it”: what people want is long life, which means old age. The plain Chinese adds 长寿 (chángshòu, “long life”) in brackets; the Sanskrit leaves the paradox bare.

verses.en: Then that great soul, his mind made pure by the resolve of earlier lives, who had heaped up good deeds through vast ages, heard of old age and shuddered, like a bull hearing a great thunderbolt crash close by.
He drew a long sigh, shook his head, and fixed his eyes on the old man; then, looking at the cheerful crowd, he spoke these words in dismay:
“So old age strikes down memory, beauty and strength alike, without distinction; and yet the world feels no dismay, even when it sees such a thing before its own eyes.”

cmp.note: saṃvega 是本品标题(Saṃvegotpatti)的关键词:因看清无常而生的震动、警醒、厌离。英文用 dismay,白话中文用「惊醒」,昙无谶译本用「厌离」,各取一面。
cmp.en: Saṃvega is the key word of the chapter title (Saṃvegotpatti): the shock and urgency that comes from seeing impermanence clearly. The English uses “dismay”; the plain Chinese has 惊醒 (jīngxǐng, “jolted awake”) and Dharmakshema’s Chinese version 厌离 (yànlí, “weary turning-away”), each catching one side of it.

verses.en: “Things being so, driver, turn the horses back. Go home quickly. How could I enjoy myself in a pleasure garden while the fear of old age is turning over in my mind?”
So at the command of his master’s son the driver turned the chariot round. And the prince, held fast by his thoughts, went back into that same palace, which now seemed empty.
But when he found no peace even there, as he kept turning it over, “old age, old age,” then with the king’s consent he went out once more, in the same way as before.
Then those same gods created another man, his body overrun with disease. Seeing him, the son of Shuddhodana kept his eyes on him and said to the charioteer:
“Belly swollen, body heaving as he gasps for breath, shoulders and arms drooping, limbs thin and pale, crying pitifully ‘Mother!’ as he leans on someone else: who is this man?”

Then the charioteer said to him, “Gentle sir, it is a great affliction called sickness, born of a disturbance of the body’s elements, and it has grown strong; it has made this man, strong as he was, helpless.”

cmp.note: dhātu 指体内的基本成分(如风、胆、痰等体液),prakopa 是「激动、失调」,属古印度医学说法;昙无谶译本换成佛教的「四大俱错乱」(地水火风)。
cmp.en: Dhātu-prakopa, “upset of the bodily elements,” is the language of Indian medicine (wind, bile, phlegm). Dharmakshema’s Chinese version recasts it in Buddhist terms as 四大俱错乱 (sìdà jù cuòluàn, “the four great elements all in disorder”).

verses.en: The king’s son spoke again, looking at the man with compassion: “Is this evil his alone, or is the danger of sickness common to all beings?”
The charioteer replied, “Prince, this evil is shared by all. This is how the world is, racked by diseases, and still, sick and in pain, it goes after pleasure.”
Hearing this, he was downcast and trembled, like the moon reflected on rippling water. And full of pity, he said these words in a rather soft voice:
“People see this calamity of sickness that falls on all beings, and still the world feels at ease. Oh, how vast is human ignorance, that men laugh while they are not free from the fear of disease!
“Driver, turn back from this outing. Let the chariot go to the king’s palace. Ever since I heard of the danger of sickness, my mind, beaten back, seems to shrink from pleasures.”

cmp.note: pratyāhata 是「被击退、被打回」;白话中文作「像被拒绝了一样」,意思稍弱。昙无谶译本用了「如人被打害,卷身待杖至」的比喻,正合这层「挨打缩身」的意思。
cmp.en: Pratyāhata means “struck back, repulsed.” The plain Chinese softens it to 像被拒绝了 (xiàng bèi jùjué le, “as if refused”); Dharmakshema’s Chinese version makes the image explicit: a man who has been beaten, curling up as he waits for the next blow.

verses.en: So he turned back, all his joy turned back too, and went into the palace lost in thought. And when the king saw him come back like this a second time, he made inquiries.

When he heard the reason for the return, he felt that his son had as good as abandoned him. He shouted at the official in charge of clearing the road, but angry as he was, he did not punish him harshly.
And once more he arranged for his son a still richer round of sensual pleasures, praying, “Perhaps, since the senses are fickle, he will become attached and will not leave us.”
But when his son took no delight at all in sounds and the other objects of the senses within the women’s quarters, the king ordered an outing beyond the walls, thinking, “It may change his mood.”
And out of love, knowing his son’s nature and giving no thought to the dangers of passion, he ordered suitable courtesans, skilled in the arts, to be sent there.
Then the king had the royal road specially decorated and inspected, and, changing both the driver and the chariot, he sent the prince out.
As the king’s son went along like this, those same gods fashioned a lifeless man, and only the driver and the prince, no one else, saw him being carried along the road, dead.
Then the king’s son said to the driver, “Who is this being carried by four men, followed by grieving people? He is adorned, and yet they weep for him.”
Then the driver, his mind overpowered by those pure-souled gods of the Pure Abodes, told his master plainly this thing that should not have been told:

“This is someone who has been parted from understanding, senses, breath and every quality; asleep, unconscious, he has become like a bundle of grass or a log. Those dear to him, who loved him and anxiously raised and protected him, are now leaving him behind.”
Hearing the driver’s words, he was somewhat shaken, and said to him, “Is this the law for this man alone, or is this the end that all beings come to?”

cmp.note: dharma 在这里不是「正法」,而是「本性、规律、命定的情形」:这只是他一人的定律吗?白话中文作「命运」。
cmp.en: Dharma here is not the saving Teaching but “law, nature, what is proper to a thing”: is this the rule for him alone? The plain Chinese renders it 命运 (mìngyùn, “fate”).

verses.en: Then the driver told him, “This is the final act for all beings. For high, middling or low, for everyone in the world, destruction is certain.”
Then the king’s son, steady as he was, sank into despair the moment he heard of death. Leaning his shoulder against the end of the chariot pole, he spoke in a deep, resounding voice:
“This is the fixed end of all beings, and yet the world has cast off fear and lives carelessly. I suspect human hearts are hard, to be so at ease while traveling this road.

cmp.note: pramāda 是佛教里很重的词:放逸、疏忽、心不在焉;昙无谶译本正作「放逸」。白话中文的「懵懵懂懂」偏向无知,少了「明知而放纵」的意思。
cmp.en: Pramāda is a heavy Buddhist word: heedlessness, careless indulgence. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has the standard 放逸 (fàngyì, “heedless indulgence”); the plain Chinese 懵懵懂懂 (měngměng dǒngdǒng, “in a daze”) leans toward ignorance and loses the sense of knowing better and indulging anyway.

verses.en: “So, driver, turn our chariot back. This is no time or place for a pleasure ground. Knowing that destruction is coming, how could a thinking man be heedless here, in this hour of danger?”

But even as the king’s son spoke so, the driver did not turn the chariot back. On the king’s orders he drove on instead to the grove called Padmashanda (“Lotus Cluster”), which had been specially made ready.

There he saw that grove, lovely as Nandana, the garden of the gods: auspicious, its young trees in flower, joyful, intoxicated cuckoos flitting about, with pavilions and long ponds bright with lotuses.

Then the king’s son was led, almost by force, into that grove crowded with troops of beautiful women, like a sage new to his vows, fearful of obstacles, led into the palace of the lord of Alaka (Kubera) surrounded by the loveliest apsarases.
Then, from that park outside the city, the women came out to meet the king’s son, their eyes darting with curiosity, as if they were welcoming a bridegroom who had just arrived.
They came up to him, eyes blown wide with wonder, and greeted him with hands folded like lotus buds.
And they stood all around him, their hearts thrown into turmoil by the god of love, as if drinking him in with eyes held motionless and opened wide with delight.
For those women took him for Kama, the god of love, come in bodily form, adorned by his shining marks of greatness as though by ornaments he had been born with.
Some, because of his gentleness and his composure, took him for the moon himself, come down to earth with his rays veiled.

cmp.note: saumya 字面是「属月的、像月的」(出自 soma 月),通常指温和。诗人用这个词作因,自然引出「以为他是月亮」——一语双关,英文 gentleness 与白话「温和」都只译出一半。
cmp.en: Saumya literally means “moon-like” (from soma, the moon) and ordinarily means “gentle.” The poet uses it as the reason the women think he is the moon — a pun that both “gentleness” and the plain Chinese 温和 (wēnhé, “mild”) can carry only halfway.

verses.en: Captivated by his beauty, they yawned, trying to stifle it, and, striking one another with glances, sighed softly.

cmp.note: 「打哈欠」在梵语艳情诗里是相思、情动的固定征象,不是困倦。
cmp.en: Yawning is a stock sign of love-longing in Sanskrit erotic poetry, not of boredom or fatigue.

verses.en: So those women simply gazed at him, with their eyes alone; held in check by his majesty, they neither spoke nor laughed.
Seeing them like this, doing nothing, unnerved by love, Udayin, the wise son of the royal chaplain, spoke these words:

cmp.note: purohita 是王家祭司(家庭祭司),白话作「国师」;昙无谶译本只说「婆罗门子」。
cmp.en: A purohita is the king’s household priest; the plain Chinese calls him 国师 (guóshī, “state preceptor”), while Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says only 婆罗门子 (póluómén zǐ, “a brahmin’s son”).

verses.en: “You are all skilled in every art, adept at catching a lover’s moods, rich in beauty and charm, and each of you has risen to the first rank by her own gifts.
“With these gifts you could grace even the Northern Kurus (a land of bliss in the far north), even the pleasure garden of Kubera, god of wealth — how much more this earth!
“You could shake even seers (rishis) who are free of passion, and captivate even gods who are courted by apsarases (heavenly nymphs).
“With your knowledge of feelings, your coquetry, your wealth of beauty and charm, you could stir passion even in women — how much more in men?
“And yet you, being what you are, behave like this, as though you had lost your way in your own proper field. I am not pleased with this artlessness of yours.
“This sort of conduct would suit new brides, their eyes half closed for shame — or else cowherds’ wives.
“Even granted that he is steadfast, great through the power of his glory, still, the power of women is great too. You must settle on a firm resolve here.
“For long ago the great seer Vyasa, whom even the gods could not overpower, was kicked by a courtesan, a beauty of Kashi.

cmp.note: 「迦尸城的美女」;昙无谶译本把 sundarī(美女)当成人名「孙陀利」。
cmp.en: “A beauty (sundarī) of Kashi”; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version takes sundarī as a personal name, 孙陀利 (Sūntuólì, “Sundari”).

verses.en: “Long ago the monk Manthala Gautama, eager to please Jangha, the chief courtesan, even carried out corpses to earn money for her.

cmp.note: jaṅghā 应是这位名妓的名字(「姜伽」);白话只说「一位名妓」,略去了名字。
cmp.en: Jaṅghā seems to be the courtesan’s name; the plain Chinese says only 一位名妓 (yī wèi míngjì, “a famous courtesan”) and drops it.

verses.en: “The great seer Gautama, a man of long austerities and long life, was won over by a woman of the lowest caste.
“So too Rishyashringa, a sage’s son who knew nothing of women: Shanta (a king’s daughter) caught him with all kinds of wiles and carried him off.
“And the great seer Vishvamitra, though sunk deep in great austerity, was carried away by the apsaras Ghritachi, and took ten years for a single day.
“Women have unsettled seer after seer like these — how much more a tender king’s son in the first flush of youth?
“So, this being the case, set to work with confidence, and see to it that the fortune of the king’s line does not turn its face away from here.

cmp.note: 「王族的福运」;意思是要王子留下继承人。昙无谶译本直说「勿令绝王嗣」。
cmp.en: “The fortune of the line” means, in effect, a royal heir; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says it outright: 勿令绝王嗣 (wù lìng jué wáng sì, “do not let the king’s line of heirs be cut off”).

verses.en: “Any young woman can charm a man of her own kind; but those who capture the hearts of low and high alike — they are women indeed.”
When they heard Udayin’s words, the women, as if stung, rose above themselves in their resolve to capture the prince.
With their brows, their glances, their coquetry, laughter, play and gait, they made alluring advances — yet like women half afraid.
But because of the king’s command, and the prince’s gentleness, they soon cast off their diffidence — with the help of wine, and of love.

cmp.note: mada(醉意)与 madana(爱欲、爱神)音近成对,是诗人惯用的文字游戏。
cmp.en: Mada (intoxication) and madana (love, the love god) are a deliberate sound-pair, a favorite kind of wordplay for the poet.

verses.en: Then, surrounded by the women, the prince roamed the grove like a bull elephant with his herd of females roaming a forest of the Himalaya.

cmp.note: 梵本只写景:公象带着母象群游林。昙无谶译本借这个象喻转而强调太子「心坚固」「不能乱其心」,意思走在了梵本前头。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit is pure scene-painting: a bull elephant roaming with his females. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version turns the simile into a statement that the prince’s mind stayed firm and undisturbed, which the Sanskrit only reaches later (4.54).

verses.en: Ringed by women in that lovely park, he blazed like the sun surrounded by apsarases in Vaibhraja, the pleasure garden of the gods.

cmp.note: Vivasvat 是太阳神;vibhrāja 是天界园林名,字面又有「光辉照耀」之意,与前面「放光」呼应。昙无谶译本把比喻对象换成了帝释天。
cmp.en: Vivasvat is the sun god; Vibhrāja is a heavenly pleasure grove whose name also means “shining,” echoing “he blazed.” Dharmakshema’s Chinese version swaps the sun for Indra, 天帝释 (Tiāndì Shì).

verses.en: There some of the women, pretending to be overcome by wine, touched him with their firm, full, close-set, lovely breasts.
One woman — “the weaker sex,” as they say — her soft arms hanging like tender vines from sloping shoulders, pretended to stumble and held him in an embrace by force.

cmp.note: abalā 字面是「没有力气的」,是「女人」的常用称呼;下文却说她 balāt「用力」抱住他,一字反讽。
cmp.en: Abalā, literally “powerless,” is a common word for “woman”; the verse then has her embrace him balāt, “by force” — a pointed irony.

verses.en: One, with copper-red lips and a mouth smelling of wine, breathed into his ear: “Listen — a secret.”
One, her body still moist with unguent, said as if giving an order, “Draw your devotion here!” — wanting the touch of his hand.

cmp.note: bhakti 一是「心意、敬爱」,二是在身上用香膏描画的花纹。她身上香膏未干,话里双关:「在这儿表表心意」也是「在这儿替我画花纹」,借此让他伸手触碰。白话只译出前一义。
cmp.en: Bhakti means both “devotion” and the decorative lines painted on the skin with unguent. Her unguent is still wet, so “show your devotion here” is also “paint a pattern here” — a pretext for his touch. The plain Chinese keeps only the first sense, 表表你的心意 (biǎobiǎo nǐ de xīnyì, “show your feelings”).

verses.en: Another, letting her blue garment slip again and again on the pretext of drunkenness, her girdle glimpsed beneath, shone like the night lit by flashing lightning.
Some wandered here and there, their golden girdles jingling, showing him their hips veiled in fine muslin.
Others held on to flowering mango boughs and swung from them, displaying breasts like golden jars.
One, lotus-eyed, came from a lotus pond holding a lotus and stood beside the lotus-faced prince like Shri, the goddess of fortune who dwells in the lotus.
One sang a sweet song whose meaning was plain, acting it out, as if to rouse him from his self-possession, her looks saying, “You are being cheated.”
Another veiled her lovely face, drew the bow of her brows, and mimicked his manner, playing at solemnity.

cmp.note: prāvṛtya 是「遮住、蒙上」,即用衣遮脸模仿他庄重的样子;白话译作「把脸一扬」,与梵文不合。
cmp.en: Prāvṛtya means “having covered, veiled” — she covers her face to mimic his gravity. The plain Chinese renders it 把脸一扬 (bǎ liǎn yī yáng, “tossed up her face”), which does not match the Sanskrit.

verses.en: One with full and lovely breasts, laughing till her earrings swung, mocked him aloud: “Come and catch me, sir!”
As he moved away, others likewise bound him with garlands; some caught him with words that were elephant-goads, sweet and taunting.
One, wanting to draw him into a reply, took a spray of mango blossom and, tipsy, asked, “Whose flower is this?”

cmp.note: 芒果花是爱神的五支花箭之一,所以这是个谜语式的挑逗,答案是「爱神的」。
cmp.en: Mango blossom is one of the love god’s five flower-arrows, so the question is a teasing riddle whose answer is “Kama’s.”

verses.en: One, copying a man’s walk and bearing, said to him, “You have been conquered by women — now go and conquer this earth!”
Then one with roving eyes, sniffing a blue lotus, spoke to the king’s son in words a little slurred with wine:
“Look, my lord, at this mango tree heaped with honey-scented blossoms, where a cuckoo sings as though shut in a golden cage.
“Look at this ashoka tree, which only adds to lovers’ sorrow; on it the bees hum as if they were being scorched by fire.

cmp.note: aśoka 字面是「无忧」,却「增长情人的忧」,是名字上的双关;它的红花又像火,所以说蜜蜂像被火烧。
cmp.en: Aśoka literally means “sorrowless,” yet it “increases lovers’ sorrow” — a pun on the name. Its red flowers look like flames, hence the bees seem to be burning.

verses.en: “See this tilaka tree, embraced by a mango bough, like a man in white embraced by a woman whose body is painted yellow.
“See the kurabaka in bloom, glowing like freshly pressed lac — it bows its head as if scolded by the brilliance of women’s nails.
“And look at this young ashoka, covered with new shoots: it stands there as if abashed by the beauty of our hands.
“Look at the long pool, veiled by the sinduvara bushes that grow on its banks, like a young woman lying wrapped in pale linen.
“See the power of women: that chakravaka (a ruddy goose) on the water follows behind its mate like a servant.
“Listen to the call of the cuckoo, singing in its rapture: another cuckoo answers straight back, like an echo.
“Spring has brought intoxication even to the birds — but not to a man who thinks himself wise and keeps pondering what cannot be pondered.”
In this way those young women, their hearts let loose by love, made their approaches to the prince with all these various tactics.
But though he was provoked like this, he kept his senses guarded by steadiness; shaken by the thought “One must die,” he neither rejoiced nor was distressed.
Seeing that they had no footing in what is real, that best of men reflected with a mind at once shaken and steady:
“Do these women not understand that youth is fleeting — that old age will destroy the very beauty they are so drunk with?
“Surely they have never seen sickness flood over anyone, since they are so cheerful and have cast off fear, in a world whose very nature is to fall ill.
“And plainly they know nothing of death, which carries everything away; that is why they play and laugh, at ease and untroubled.
“For what thinking being who knows of old age, sickness and death could stand or sit or lie at ease — let alone laugh?
“And one who sees another old, or sick, or dead, and stays at ease and unshaken, is no different from a thing without a mind.
“For when one tree is stripped of its flowers and its fruit, or falls, or is cut down, the tree beside it does not grieve.”

cmp.note: 梵本只说「另一棵树不会伤心」,让读者自己联想;昙无谶译本写成荒野双树,一棵被砍、另一棵不怕,并点明「此等诸人辈,无心亦如是」。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit simply says the other tree does not grieve and leaves the application to the reader; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version spells it out — two trees in a wild field, one felled, the other unafraid — and adds 无心亦如是 (wú xīn yì rú shì, “they are just as mindless”).

verses.en: Seeing him so intent on meditation, with no longing for the objects of sense, Udayin, who was versed in the science of worldly conduct, spoke to him as a friend:

cmp.note: nītiśāstra 指治国处世之术(政略学),带有讲究手腕与权宜的意味,为下文劝太子「假意顺从」埋了伏笔。
cmp.en: Nītiśāstra is the science of policy and statecraft, the art of handling people expediently — a hint of the tactical advice to “humor them, even with pretense” that follows.

verses.en: “The king gave me to you as a friend, thinking me fit for it; and so, out of that affection, I have something I want to say to you.
“To hold a friend back from harm, to urge him on toward good, and not to desert him in misfortune — these are the three marks of a friend.
“Having pledged my friendship, if I turned my back on a man’s duty and left you to yourself, there would be no friendship in me.

cmp.note: parāṅmukhaḥ 是主格,与「我」同格:是说话人自己若「背弃男子的本分」而不管太子。白话译成「看着你背离人生的目标」,把背离的主体错放到太子身上。昙无谶译本「弃舍丈夫义」与梵文一致。
cmp.en: Parāṅmukhaḥ is nominative and goes with “I”: it is the speaker who would be turning his back on a man’s duty. The plain Chinese reads it as the prince turning from life’s goals, 看着你背离人生的目标 (“watching you turn from life’s aims”), which misplaces the subject; Dharmakshema’s 弃舍丈夫义 (qìshě zhàngfu yì, “abandoning a man’s duty”) agrees with the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “So I speak as a true friend: such ungallantry toward women does not become you, young and handsome as you are.
“It is right to humor women, even with pretense — both to spare them their shyness and for your own pleasure.
“Deference and compliance are what bind a woman’s heart; good qualities are the source of love, and women long to be honored.
“So, my long-eyed friend, even if your heart is turned away, you should humor them with a gallantry that matches your looks.
“Gallantry is the medicine for women; gallantry is the finest ornament. Beauty without gallantry is like a grove without flowers.

cmp.note: dākṣiṇya 本义「右手般的灵巧、体贴」,在情诗里专指对女子殷勤周到的风度(dakṣiṇa nāyaka「殷勤的情人」)。白话作「殷勤」,昙无谶译本作「顺」。
cmp.en: Dākṣiṇya, from dakṣiṇa “right-handed, dexterous,” is the courtly lover’s attentive gallantry. The plain Chinese has 殷勤 (yīnqín, “attentiveness”), Dharmakshema’s Chinese version 顺 (shùn, “compliance”).

verses.en: “But why stop at mere gallantry? Take them to you with real feeling. You have won pleasures that are hard to win — you must not scorn them.
“For even the god Indra, the Sacker of Cities (Purandara), knowing love to be supreme, long ago desired Ahalya, wife of the sage Gautama.
“Agastya courted Rohini, wife of Soma the Moon; and so, tradition says, he won Lopamudra, who resembled her.
“And Brihaspati, of great austerity, begot Bharadvaja on Mamata, daughter of the Maruts and wife of Utathya.
“And the Moon, best of those who offer sacrifice, begot Budha (the planet Mercury), of godlike deeds, on Brihaspati’s queen while she was making an offering.

cmp.note: juhvatī 是「正在献祭的(她)」,与 juhvatāṃ varaḥ「献祭者中最优者(月神)」成文字游戏;白话把它当人名「朱诃蒂」,恐不确(传说中祭主之妻名多罗 Tārā)。budha/vibudha(布陀/天神)也是一对。
cmp.en: Juhvatī means “(she) while offering,” playing on juhvatāṃ varaḥ, “best of offerers” (the Moon); the plain Chinese takes it as a name, 朱诃蒂 (Zhūhēdì), which is probably wrong (Brihaspati’s wife is usually called Tara). Budha / vibudha (“godlike”) is a second pun.

verses.en: “Long ago Parashara, seized by passion, went to the maiden Kali, daughter of a creature born in the water, on the bank of the Yamuna.
“The sage Vasishtha, wanting pleasure, begot a son, Kapinjalada, on Akshamala, a despised outcaste woman.
“And Yayati, the royal seer, even when his youth was spent, took his pleasure with the apsaras Vishvachi in the Chaitraratha grove.
“Pandu the Kaurava, though he knew that union with a woman would end in his death, was carried away by Madri’s beauty and charms and tasted the joy that love brings.
“Karala Janaka, too, carried off a brahmin’s daughter and fell from power for it — yet he did not give up love.
“Great souls like these enjoyed even pleasures that were condemned, for the sake of delight — how much more those that are blameless?
“But you, strong, handsome and young, scorn pleasures that have come to you by right — pleasures to which the whole world clings.”
When he had heard these smooth words, backed by the authority of tradition, the prince replied in a voice like thunder rumbling in a cloud:
“What you say is fitting, and shows your affection for me; but where you misjudge me, I will win you round.
“I do not despise the objects of sense; I know that the world is made of them. But because I see the world as impermanent, my mind finds no delight here.
“If these three — old age, sickness and death — did not exist, I too would take pleasure in the delights of the senses.
“If women’s bodies stayed forever just as they are now, then, faulty as desires are, my mind might well be drawn to them.
“But when old age has drunk up their beauty, so that it is unwelcome even to themselves, then only delusion could find delight in it.
“One whose lot is death, sickness and old age, who sports without a qualm among others made of death, sickness and old age, is no better than the beasts and birds.
“As for what you say — that great souls too were given to desire — that is the very place for dismay, since they too came to their end.

cmp.note: saṃvega 是看清生死无常后的震动、悚然(第三章题名即「生起震动」),带有促人出离的意味,不只是「警醒」。
cmp.en: Saṃvega is the shock or dismay that comes from seeing impermanence clearly — the word in the title of Chapter 3 — and it carries the push toward renunciation, more than mere “alertness,” the plain Chinese 警醒 (jǐngxǐng).

verses.en: “I do not call that greatness where the end is common to all; and clinging to the objects of sense is no mark of self-command, nor of good sense.
“And as for what you say — ‘Humor women, even with pretense’ — I know nothing of falsehood, not even for courtesy’s sake.
“Nor do I care for a compliance that lacks sincerity; if there is no union with the whole heart, then shame on it.
“A heart that has no restraint, that is credulous, attached, blind to faults, and gripped by passion — what is there to be gained in deceiving it?
“And if those gripped by passion deceive one another like this, then surely men are not fit to be looked at by women, nor women by men.
“This being so, you should not try to lure me into ignoble pleasures — me, afflicted by suffering, heir to old age and death.

“Ah, how very steady and strong your mind must be, that you see substance in fleeting pleasures and cling to the objects of sense amid so dreadful a fear, while you watch living beings on the road to death!

cmp.note: 这是反语:表面称赞对方心「坚定强大」,实指其麻木。昙无谶译本「真为大肝胆」同样是反讽。
cmp.en: This is irony: praising Udayin’s mind as “steady and strong” really means it is numb. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version keeps the sarcasm with 真为大肝胆 (zhēn wéi dà gāndǎn, “what tremendous nerve you have”).

verses.en: “But I am timid and deeply anxious; as I ponder the terror of old age, calamity and sickness, I find no peace and no steadiness — how then could I find delight? — seeing the world as if it were ablaze.

“A man who knows beyond doubt that death will come, and still feels passion rising in his heart — his mind, I think, is made of iron, if amid so great a terror he takes his pleasure and does not weep.”
So the prince gave his talk of firm resolve, a talk that struck at the very ground of desire; and the sun, its disc now gentle enough for the eye, sank behind the western mountain.

cmp.note: Asta 是传说中太阳落下处的「西山」(没山),astam iyāya 字面就是「去到西山」,即日落。
cmp.en: Asta is the mythical western mountain behind which the sun sets; astam iyāya, literally “went to Asta,” is the ordinary idiom for sunset.

verses.en: Then the women — their jewels and garlands worn for nothing, their arts, charms and endearments fruitless — forced love back down into their own hearts and returned to the city, their hopes broken.
The king’s son, having seen the splendor of the crowds in the city park gathered in again at evening, pondered the impermanence that runs through everything, and went into his own dwelling.

When the king heard that his son’s mind had turned away from the objects of sense, he did not sleep that night, like an elephant with an arrow lodged in its heart. Then, worn out with counsel, going over many different paths with his ministers, he could see nothing but desire that might restrain his son’s purpose.
So the son of the Shakya king was tempted with pleasures of the senses, even the very finest, yet he found no steadiness and no peace, like a lion struck deep in the heart by a poisoned arrow.
Then one day, longing for calm and wanting to see the woodlands, he set out from the city with the king’s leave, escorted by friends—capable sons of ministers who were full of lively stories.

He mounted Kanthaka, his noble horse, whose bit was new gold hung with little bells and whose fine golden trappings swayed with yak-tail plumes, and rode out like a banner borne aloft—he whose own banner bore the tree and the lotus.

cmp.note: ketu 既是「旗帜」也可指「彗星」，诗人用同一个词作比喻和称号，形成双关；drumābjaketu（以树与莲为旗徽者）这个称号含义不太确定。白话中文只译出「像一面竖起的旗帜」，略去了称号。
cmp.en: Ketu means both “banner” and “comet,” and the poet uses it twice—once for the simile and once in the epithet drumābjaketu, “he whose banner is the tree and lotus,” an epithet whose exact sense is uncertain. The plain Chinese keeps only “like a raised banner” and drops the epithet.

verses.en: Drawn on by love of the forest and the beauty of the land, he rode to the far edge of the woods, and there he saw the earth being ploughed, its furrows rolling like ripples on water.

He saw the ground with its young grass and darbha (sacred grass) torn up by the plough and scattered, strewn with tiny worms, insects and creatures that had been killed; and seeing the earth like that, he grieved deeply, as if his own kin had been slaughtered.
And as he watched the men at the plough, their skin discoloured by wind, sun and dust, and the oxen at the yoke staggering with the strain of hauling, the noblest of men felt the deepest pity.
So he got down from his horse’s back and walked slowly over the ground, overcome with sorrow. Pondering the coming and going of the world’s creatures, he said in his distress, “How wretched this is!”
Wanting to be alone with his thoughts, he held back the friends who followed him and went to the foot of a rose-apple tree (jambu) in a lonely spot, its lovely leaves stirring all around.
There he sat down on clean ground where the grass shone like beryl. Reflecting on the arising and passing away of the world, he took hold of the path that steadies the mind.

At once his mind grew steady, and he was freed from the torments of craving for sense objects and the rest. He entered the first meditation (dhyana)—calm, still accompanied by thought and reflection, and of a kind free from the taints.

cmp.note: anāsrava（无漏）是很强的说法：按一般佛教理论，初禅本身多属「有漏」的世间定。诗人用这个词，暗示王子这次入定已带着出世的性质。白话中文译作「没有烦恼漏失的那一种」，意思对，但英文用 free from the taints 更贴近术语。
cmp.en: Anāsrava, “free from the taints (outflows),” is a strong claim: in ordinary Buddhist theory the first meditation is usually a worldly state still subject to the taints. The poet hints that the prince’s first trance already has a liberating quality. The Chinese renders it 无漏 (wúlòu, “without outflows”).

verses.en: Having reached that concentration of mind which is born of seclusion and full of the highest joy and ease, he looked clearly at the way of the world, and then turned his mind wholly to this thought:

“How pitiful it is that a man, himself helpless and subject to sickness, old age and death, should in his ignorance, blinded by pride, shrink in disgust from another who is worn by age, or sick, or dead!”

cmp.note: 这里应读作 param（别人）+ ajñaḥ（无知），不是 parama-jña（最有智慧）。白话中文「无知地去嫌弃别人」读对了；英文也照此译。
cmp.en: The string is to be read param (“another”) + ajñaḥ (“ignorant”), not parama-jña (“supremely wise”). The plain Chinese reads it correctly as 无知地 (wúzhī de, “ignorantly”), and so does the English.

verses.en: “If I, being just the same myself, were to shrink from another whose nature is the same as mine, it would be neither fitting nor right—for I know this to be the supreme law.”
As he saw truly the flaws of the world—sickness, old age and ruin—the pride within him that sprang from strength, youth and life vanished in an instant.
He felt no elation and no remorse; he fell into no doubt, no sloth or drowsiness; he took no delight in the pleasures of sense, and he neither hated nor scorned anyone else.
So this pure understanding, free of all dust, grew within that great soul. Then a man in the dress of a mendicant came up to him—a man whom no one else could see.
The king’s son asked him, “Tell me, who are you?” and he answered: “Bull among men, I am a shramana (a wandering ascetic). Afraid of birth and death, I have left home for the sake of liberation.”

“In a world whose nature is to perish, I long to be free, and I seek that blessed state which does not perish. I look on my own people and on strangers alike; turned away from sense objects, I am rid of passion and hatred.”

“I stay wherever I happen to be—at the foot of a tree, in an empty shrine, on a mountain or in a forest—and I wander without possessions or expectations, living on whatever alms come my way, for the sake of the highest goal.”
Having said this, he flew up into the sky while the prince looked on; for he was a god who had seen other Buddhas, and had come in that form to awaken the prince’s memory.

cmp.note: smṛti 是「忆念、记起」：天神现身是为了唤起王子的记忆（暗示他前世早已立愿成佛），不只是「提醒」。古译在前面（第16颂处）就点明此人是「净居天化为比丘形」。
cmp.en: Smṛti means “remembrance”: the god appears to awaken the prince’s memory (hinting at a resolve made in past lives), not merely to remind him. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version (already at verse 16) identifies the figure as a god of the Pure Abodes taking a monk’s form.

verses.en: When he had gone up into the sky like a bird, the best of men was thrilled and amazed. Then, having grasped what the Dharma meant, he set his mind on the way of leaving home.

Then he who was like Indra, who had tamed the horses of his senses, mounted his horse, meaning to go back into the city; out of regard for his attendants, he did not go off at once to the forest he longed for.

Intent on putting an end to old age and death, and holding the forest life firmly in his mind, he entered the city again—not out of desire, but as a great elephant comes in from the wild into an enclosure.
A young woman of royal birth saw him entering along the road, and she joined her palms and said, “Happy indeed, and blessed with peace, is the woman whose husband is a man like this, so long-eyed!”
He, whose voice was like a great thundercloud, heard these words and gained the highest calm; for hearing the word “at peace” (nirvrita), he set his mind on the way to final nirvana.

cmp.note: 双关：在少女口中 nirvṛtā 只是「幸福、满足」；但这个词与 nirvāṇa（涅槃，熄灭）同源，王子听成了「熄灭、寂灭」。英文用 at peace 尽量两头兼顾。
cmp.en: A pun: on the girl’s lips nirvṛtā simply means “content, happy,” but the word is related to nirvāṇa, “extinction,” and the prince hears it in that sense. The plain Chinese glosses it as 熄灭 (xīmiè, “extinguished”).

verses.en: Then he went into his dwelling—his body like the peak of a golden mountain, his arms like an elephant’s trunk, his voice like a cloud, his eyes like a bull’s, his face like the moon and his stride like a lion’s—filled with longing for the imperishable Dharma.

With the gait of a king of beasts he went to the king, who sat attended by his councils of ministers, as Sanatkumara (the ever-youthful son of Brahma) in heaven approaches Indra blazing amid the Maruts.

Bowing, with palms joined, he said: “Lord of men, kindly give me your leave. I wish to go forth as a wanderer for the sake of liberation, since this person is bound to be parted from you in any case.”
Hearing his words, the king shook like a tree struck by an elephant. Taking his son’s joined hands, which were like a lotus, he spoke, his throat choked with tears:
“Take back this thought, my son. This is no time for you to turn to the religious life. In the first stage of life, when the mind is unsteady, they say the practice of Dharma is full of pitfalls.”

“When a young man’s senses are hungry for their objects and his resolve is not yet strong enough for the hardships of a vow, his mind wanders away from the forest, above all because he has no experience of solitude.”

“But for me, you who love the Dharma, it is the time for Dharma—to hand the royal fortune over to you, the very emblem of our line. You whose valour is steadfast, your duty lies in valour; to abandon your father would be no duty at all, but its opposite.”

cmp.note: 诗人连用叠词：lakṣmī（王运、荣华）与 lakṣma（标志），vikrama（勇武）两次重复，dharma 与 adharma 对举。意思是：刹帝利的「法」就在勇武治国，不在出家。古译把这层说成「汝应领国事，令我先出家」。
cmp.en: The verse is a chain of word-play: lakṣmī (royal fortune) against lakṣma (emblem), vikrama (valour) repeated, dharma against adharma. The point is that a warrior’s duty lies in valour and rule, not in renunciation. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version puts it bluntly: 汝应领国事，令我先出家 (“you should take up the kingdom and let me leave home first”).

verses.en: “So give up this resolve, and for now devote yourself to the duties of a householder. When a man has enjoyed the pleasures of his youth, then going into the ascetics’ grove is a fine thing.”

Hearing these words of the king, the prince, whose voice was like a kalavinka bird’s (a bird famed for its sweet song), replied: “If you will stand surety for me on four points, Your Majesty, I will not take refuge in the ascetics’ grove.”
“That my life shall not end in death; that sickness shall not steal away this health of mine; that old age shall not overtake my youth; and that misfortune shall not carry off this prosperity.”
When his son had asked for something so hard to grant, the Shakya king said to him: “Give up this notion—it goes too far. An extravagant wish is laughable, and out of all proper order.”

Then he who was weighty as Meru spoke to his weighty father: “If this is not possible, then I should not be held back. When a man is trying to escape from a house on fire, it is not right to seize hold of him.”

cmp.note: guru 一词两用：「像须弥山一样沉重（稳重）」的王子，对他的 guru（父亲、长辈，字面也是「重」）说话。另外上一颂国王说 akrama（不合次序），这里王子接过 krama（次序、办法）一词反驳。
cmp.en: Guru is used twice: the prince, “heavy (steadfast) as Meru,” speaks to his guru—his father, literally “the weighty one.” He also turns the king’s word akrama (“out of order”) from the previous verse back on him with krama (“way, procedure”).

verses.en: “And since parting is certain for everyone in the world, surely it is better to part of one’s own accord, for the sake of Dharma? Otherwise death will tear me away against my will, my purpose unaccomplished and my longing unsatisfied.”
When the lord of the earth heard this resolve of his son, who longed for liberation, he said, “He shall not go,” and once more set guards about him and arranged the choicest pleasures.
The ministers duly counselled him with arguments drawn from the treatises, out of respect and affection, and his father held him back with tears. Then, grieving, he went into his dwelling.
