There the women gazed at him like young does, with restless eyes, their faces kissed by swinging earrings, their breasts trembling with heavy sighs.

For he, gleaming like a golden mountain, maddened the hearts of those lovely women: he captured their ears, their limbs, their eyes and their very selves by his speech, his touch, his form and his virtues.
When the day was over, he climbed to the palace tower, blazing with beauty like the sun—like the rising sun climbing Meru, eager to destroy the darkness with its own light.

He went up and took his seat on a splendid golden throne inlaid with patterns of diamond; around it stood lamp-stands like trees, ablaze with golden light, and the chamber was filled with the smoke of the finest black aloewood.

Then at night the most beautiful women waited on that most excellent man, who was like Indra, with music, as troops of apsarases wait on the son of Kubera, lord of wealth, on a Himalayan peak white as the moon.
Yet even that superb music, which rivalled the music of the gods, gave him no delight and no joy. The good man longed to go forth for the sake of the highest bliss, and so he took no pleasure in it.

Then the gods of the Akanishtha heaven (the highest of the Pure Abodes), foremost in austerity, knowing his resolve, made sleep fall all at once on the throng of women and twisted their limbs into ungainly postures.

cmp.note: Akaniṣṭha（色究竟天）是净居天中最高的一层；古译直接说「净居天子」，所指一致。
cmp.en: Akaniṣṭha is the highest of the Pure Abodes; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version simply says 净居天子 (jìngjū tiānzǐ, “gods of the Pure Abodes”), which points to the same beings.

verses.en: One lay asleep with her cheek propped on an unsteady hand, having let go of her beloved lute, inlaid with gold leaf, which lay in her lap as though she had cast it aside in anger.

Another, a flute still clinging to her hand and her white garment slipping from her breasts, looked as she slept like a river whose lotus is visited by a straight line of bees and whose banks laugh with white foam.
Another slept with her arms—soft as the heart of a fresh lotus, their armlets joined with gleaming gold—wrapped around her drum as if around a lover.
Others, wearing ornaments of new gold and the finest yellow garments, sank down helpless under heavy sleep, like branches of the karnikara tree (a tree with golden flowers) broken by an elephant.
Another, who had fallen asleep leaning against the side of a window, her slender body bent like a bow and her lovely necklace hanging down, looked like a carved figure of a tree-maiden on an archway.

The lotus face of another hung down, the painted leaf-lines on her cheeks pressed by her jewelled earrings, so that it looked like a hundred-petalled lotus on a half-bent stalk, jostled by a duck perched on it.
Others slept just as they sat, their bodies bowed by the weight of their breasts, and they looked lovely, clasping each other in the embrace of arms circled with gold.
One woman slept holding a great seven-stringed lute in her arms as if it were a girlfriend, and she rolled about with its gold strings quivering, her face bright with her tumbled ear-ornaments.
Another young woman slept with her tabor, whose pretty cords had slipped from her arm and shoulder, drawn between her thighs, like a lover she held there, worn out at the end of playful lovemaking.
Others lay with their eyes shut, though they had large eyes and lovely brows, like lotus plants whose buds have closed up when the sun has set.
Another lay with her hair loose and tangled, the ornaments and the hem of her dress slipping from her hips and her necklace scattered, like a statue of a woman knocked over by an elephant.
Others, helpless and stripped of modesty—though steady women by nature and endowed with beauty—lay snoring loudly, distorted, flinging out their arms and yawning.

Others, their ornaments and garlands thrown off, their clothes come untied, lay senseless with eyes open, the whites showing and unmoving; as they lay there they had no beauty at all, and looked like the dead.

Another lay sprawled, her mouth gaping, her body spread out, spittle dribbling from her lips and her private parts exposed, as though reeling with drink; she had no beauty left, only a misshapen body.
So that company of women, lying in all their various ways according to their temperament, family and breeding, looked like a lake whose lotuses have been bent and broken by the wind.
Seeing those young women lying this way and that, distorted, in such unseemly postures—though their bodies were beautiful and their speech was sweet—the king’s son felt disgust.
“So this is the nature of women in the world of the living—impure and repulsive! It is only because he is deceived by clothes and ornaments that a man is drawn by passion to women.”

“If a man would only consider the true nature of women, and how sleep changes them like this, surely he would not let his heedlessness grow. It is because he is struck down by imagining fine qualities that he falls into passion.”
Having seen into the inner truth of things in this way, he felt the urge to leave that very night; and the gods, knowing his mind, caused the palace door to stand open.

cmp.note: antara 意思很宽：「内部、内在本质」「差别」「时机、空隙」都可以。白话中文取「区别」；也可理解为「看清了（女人身体的）内在真相」或「看准了时机」。英文取「内在真相」，但这一处读法并不确定。
cmp.en: Antara has a wide range: “the inside, inner nature,” “difference,” or “opportunity, opening.” The plain Chinese takes it as 区别 (qūbié, “difference”); it may equally mean “seeing the inner truth” or “seeing his chance.” The English takes the first, but the reading is uncertain.

verses.en: Then he came down from the palace roof, despising those young women as they lay asleep; and once down, he went out without hesitation through the first courtyard of the palace.
He woke Chandaka, the swift groom, and said to him: “Bring the horse Kanthaka, quickly! Today I mean to go from here to win the deathless.”

“From the contentment that has arisen in my heart today, and from the way my resolve has taken root in my mind, I feel—though I am alone—as if I had a protector. Surely the goal I long for is close at hand.”
“The young women have cast off their modesty and decorum and lie asleep like this before me, and the door has opened of its own accord: surely the time has come for me to leave this place today.”
Chandaka accepted his master’s command, even though he knew what the king had ordered; as if some other power were urging him on in his mind, he resolved to bring the horse.
So he brought that splendid horse to his master—its mouth filled with a golden bit, its back covered with a light saddle-cloth, a horse endowed with strength, spirit, speed and good breeding.

It was long in the back, the root of the tail and the heels; its coat, tail and ears were short and lay close; its back was low, its belly high, its flanks well shaped; its nostrils, forehead, hips and chest were broad.
The broad-chested prince put his arms around the horse and stroked it with a hand like a lotus, and spoke to it in sweet words, like a warrior about to plunge into the midst of an army.
“Many times, they say, the king has mounted you and routed his enemies in battle. Now, best of horses, do your part so that I too may rightly win the deathless state.”

“Companions are easy to find in battle, or in enjoying the pleasures of the senses, or in making money; but companions are hard to find for a man who has fallen into misfortune, or who turns to the Dharma.”
“And in this world, those who are companions in a deed—whether a foul deed or one undertaken for Dharma—surely share in its fruit too; so my inmost self tells me.”
“So understand that my going forth from here is righteous and for the good of the world. Best of horses, strive with all your speed and strength for your own good and for the world’s good.”

Having instructed the fine horse in its task as one would a friend, the best of men, eager to go to the forest, mounted the white steed—handsome, radiant as fire—like the sun climbing onto an autumn cloud.

cmp.note: sita（白）与 asita（黑）相对：马是白的，王子的光彩像 asitagati（「走过处留下黑迹者」，即火）。白话中文作「光彩照人」，失去了「像火」和黑白相映的字面游戏。
cmp.en: Sita (“white”) is set against asita (“black”): the horse is white, while the prince shines like asitagati, “the one whose path is black”—that is, fire. The plain Chinese says only 光彩照人 (guāngcǎi zhàorén, “dazzling”), losing both the fire image and the black-and-white play.

verses.en: Then the noble horse moved on, avoiding any noise that, fearsome in the dead of night, might wake the household: its jaws made no sound, its neighing was hushed, and it set down its steps as if wary.
Then yakshas, bending low, held up its hooves with the tips of their lotus-like hands, their wrists adorned with gold bracelets, moving timidly, as though scattering lotuses beneath them.
The city gates, shut fast with heavy bars and doors, which even elephants could not easily force, opened of their own accord, without a sound, as the king’s son passed.
Firm in his purpose, he left behind his devoted father, his infant son, the people who loved him, and his unsurpassed fortune, and with no regret he went out from his father’s city.
Then he, whose eyes were long like a spotless lotus, looked back at the city and gave a lion’s roar: “Until I have seen the far shore of birth and death, I will not enter the city named for Kapila.”
Hearing these words of his, the hosts in the retinue of Kubera, lord of wealth, rejoiced; and the companies of gods, glad at heart, wished him success in carrying out his resolve.
Other gods, whose bodies were like fire, knowing how very hard his resolve was to accomplish, cast light upon his frosty road, like moonbeams streaming through a gap in the clouds.

And that horse, like one of Indra’s steeds, galloped on as if urged by something in its mind, and covered a great many leagues (yojanas) while the stars still glittered hard in a sky reddening with dawn.

cmp.note: 梵本说「许多由旬」；古译具体说「已进三由旬」。harituraga 可指因陀罗的马，也可指太阳神的马，白话中文取前者，英文也从之。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says “a great many yojanas”; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version gives a precise figure, 已进三由旬 (“had already gone three yojanas”). Harituraga may mean Indra’s horse or the horses of the sun; the plain Chinese and the English take Indra.

verses.en: Then, a little while after the sun, the eye of the world, had risen, that best of men caught sight of the hermitage of Bhargava (a brahmin seer).

cmp.note: 「世界之眼」是太阳的常用称号；古译「众生眼光出」保留了这一意象。
cmp.en: “The eye of the world” is a stock epithet of the sun; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version keeps the image: 众生眼光出 (zhòngshēng yǎnguāng chū, “the light of beings’ eyes came forth”).

verses.en: The deer there slept without fear and the birds perched at their ease; at the sight of it he felt as if he had already rested, as if he had already won what he had set out for.
To let his wonder settle, and to honor the austerities practiced there, and also to keep his own habit of courtesy, he got down from the horse’s back.

cmp.note: anuvartitā 指顺从、谦让的习性；白话译作「谦恭的礼数」，古译则发挥为「灭除高慢迹」。
cmp.en: anuvartitā is a habit of deference or compliance; the plain Chinese gives “humble courtesy,” while Dharmakshema’s Chinese version expands it into 灭除高慢迹 (mièchú gāomàn jì, “wiping out every trace of pride”).

verses.en: Having dismounted, he stroked the horse, saying, “You have brought me across,” and spoke gladly to Chandaka, bathing him, as it were, with his eyes:

cmp.note: 「渡过了」字面是渡河，也暗指渡过生死之海——这是佛教常用的比喻。
cmp.en: nistīrṇam, “crossed over,” is literally a river crossing, but it also hints at crossing the ocean of birth and death, a common Buddhist image.

verses.en: “By following this steed, swift as Tarkshya (the divine eagle Garuda), my friend, you have shown your devotion to me, and your own courage too.
“Though my heart was wholly set on another purpose, you still held me in yours; such is your love for your master, and such too your strength.
“There are those who are able but have no affection, and those who are devoted but have no ability; one both devoted and able, like you, is hard to find on earth.
“So I am pleased with this noble deed of yours, for your feeling toward me turns its face away even from reward.
“Who does not turn toward a man who has rewards to give? But when fortune turns, even one’s own kin mostly become strangers.

cmp.note: 原文是文字游戏：svajana（自己人）变成 jana（外人、路人）。
cmp.en: There is wordplay here: svajana, “one’s own people,” becomes mere jana, “people,” that is, strangers.

verses.en: “A son is raised for the sake of the family line; a father is served for the sake of his support. The world clings to others out of hope of gain; there is no kinship without a motive.
“Why say more? In short, you have done me a very great kindness. Take the horse and go back; I have reached the place I longed for.”
Having said this, the long-armed prince, wishing to show his gratitude, took off his ornaments and gave them to Chandaka, whose heart was in anguish.
Taking from his crown the shining jewel that did the work of a lamp, he stood speaking these words, like Mount Mandara with the sun upon it.
“Chanda, take this jewel and bow again and again to the king, and tell him this, keeping his trust unshaken, so that his grief may cease:

cmp.note: 字面「不失去信任」，可指车匿应让国王仍保持信心，也可指车匿说话时要坦然无疑；白话取前一义。
cmp.en: Literally “without letting go of trust”: it may mean Chandaka should keep the king’s confidence intact, or that he should speak openly and with assurance; the plain Chinese takes the first sense.

verses.en: “‘I have entered the ascetics’ grove to put an end to birth and death, not out of thirst for heaven, not for want of love, not in anger.

cmp.note: tapovana 字面「苦行之林」，即修行人居住的林中道场；古译作「苦行林」。
cmp.en: tapovana is literally a “grove of austerity,” a forest settlement of ascetics; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version calls it 苦行林 (kǔxíng lín, “forest of austerities”).

verses.en: “‘So you should not grieve for me now that I have gone forth like this. However long a union lasts, in time it will be no more.
“‘Because separation is certain, my mind is set on liberation, thinking: how might there be no more parting from my own people, ever again?
“‘I have gone forth to leave sorrow behind; you should not grieve for me. It is those who cling with passion to pleasures, the very causes of sorrow, who should be grieved for.
“‘And this, they say, was the firm resolve of our forefathers too; so I am not to be mourned as I take the road that has come down to me like an inheritance.

cmp.note: 「如同遗产的」——以继承祖产比喻出家之路；古译读成「今我袭余财，唯法舍非宜」，意思走偏。
cmp.en: “Being like an inheritance”: the road of renunciation is pictured as a family legacy. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version reads it rather differently, as inheriting the remaining wealth while only the Dharma must not be given up.

verses.en: “‘When a man is gone, there are heirs enough to his wealth; but heirs to his Dharma are hard to find on earth, or there are none at all.

cmp.note: viparyaye 字面「在逆转时」，此处指死亡；白话译「死后」是对的。
cmp.en: viparyaye, literally “at the reversal,” here means at death; the plain Chinese correctly gives “after he dies.”

verses.en: “‘And if it should be said, “He went to the forest at the wrong time,” there is no wrong time for Dharma, since life is so unsteady.
“‘Therefore I have resolved that I must seek the highest good this very day; for what trust can one place in life while death stands by as an enemy?’
“With these words and others like them, my friend, you should address the lord of the earth; and do your best so that he does not even remember me.
“You may even speak to the king of my lack of virtues. Through faults, love is given up; and once love is given up, there is no grief.”

cmp.note: nairguṇya 意为「没有美德、一无是处」；白话作「没有好处」稍弱。古译把意思说反了：「汝慎勿惜言，使王念不绝」。
cmp.en: nairguṇya means “lack of good qualities, worthlessness”; the plain Chinese softens it. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version seems to reverse the point, ending with “so that the king’s thoughts of me never cease.”

verses.en: Hearing these words, Chanda, shaken with anguish, joined his palms and replied in a voice knotted with tears:
“Master, at this intention of yours, which brings pain to your kin, my heart sinks like an elephant in the mud of a river.
“Whom would this resolve of yours not bring to tears, even with a heart made of iron, let alone one shaken by love?
“How far apart they are: this tender body, fit to lie on couches in palace towers, and the ground of the ascetics’ grove, bristling with sharp shoots of darbha grass!

cmp.note: vimāna 指高楼宫殿，也指天神的飞行宫殿，暗示王子生活如天人。
cmp.en: vimāna is a palace tower, but also the flying palace of a god, hinting that the prince lived like a celestial.

verses.en: “When I heard your purpose and still brought this horse, master, it was by force: fate alone made me do it.

cmp.note: daiva 可解为「命运」或「天神所为」；第五章中确有天神暗中推动，古译直接说「天神见驱逼」。
cmp.en: daiva can mean “fate” or “the work of the gods”; in Chapter 5 the gods did in fact urge things on, and Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says outright 天神见驱逼 (tiānshén jiàn qūbī, “the gods drove me”).

verses.en: “For how, if I were my own master and knew your purpose, could I have brought out the horse, and with it grief for Kapilavastu?
“So, mighty-armed one, you should not abandon the old king, who loves you and longs for his son, as an unbeliever abandons the true Dharma.

cmp.note: nāstika 指否认来世与业报的人；白话作「不信者」，古译作「邪见」。
cmp.en: A nāstika is one who denies the afterlife and the fruits of deeds; the plain Chinese has “unbeliever,” Dharmakshema’s Chinese version 邪见 (xiéjiàn, “wrong view”).

verses.en: “Nor should you forget the queen, your second mother, worn out with raising you, as an ungrateful man forgets a kindness.
“Nor should you leave the princess, mother of a little son, virtuous, an honor to her family, and devoted to her husband, as a coward leaves the fortune he has won.

cmp.note: klība 字面指无生育能力者、阉人，转指懦弱无能之人；白话作「无能的人」。
cmp.en: klība literally means an impotent man or eunuch, and by extension a weakling or coward; the plain Chinese has “an incompetent person.”

verses.en: “Nor should you leave Yashodhara’s little son, worthy of praise, best of those who uphold fame and Dharma, as a man given to vice throws away the highest fame.

cmp.note: 双关：yāśodhara（耶输陀罗之子）与 yaśo-dharma-bhṛt（持守名声与正法者）音近，诗人借名字作文字游戏。
cmp.en: A pun: yāśodhara, “Yashodhara’s son,” echoes yaśo-dharma-bhṛt, “bearer of fame and Dharma”; the poet plays on the sound of her name.

verses.en: “And even if your mind is made up to leave both kin and kingdom, you should not leave me, my lord; your feet are my only refuge.
“With my heart on fire I cannot go back to the city and leave you in the forest, as Sumantra left Raghava (Rama).

cmp.note: 典出《罗摩衍那》：御者苏曼多罗把被放逐的罗摩送进森林后独自驾车回城。车匿以此自比。
cmp.en: An allusion to the Ramayana: the charioteer Sumantra drove the exiled Rama into the forest and had to return to the city alone. Chandaka sees himself in the same role.

verses.en: “What will the king say to me when I come back to the city without you? And what shall I say to the women of your palace, who are used to seeing you?

cmp.note: 意为「因为（她们）惯于见到（你）」；白话译成「才算合适」，似把 ucita（惯常）误作「合宜」。
cmp.en: This means “because they are accustomed to seeing you”; the plain Chinese renders it “what would be fitting,” apparently taking ucita (“accustomed”) in its other sense of “proper.”

verses.en: “And as for what you said, that I should speak to the king of your lack of virtues: how could I tell of faults you do not have, you who are as faultless as a sage?
“Even if I did say it, with a heart full of shame and a tongue that stuck in my mouth, who could believe it?
“Only a man who would call the moon scorching, or believe it, would speak of your faults, you who know what faults are, or believe in them.
“For one who is always tender-hearted and ever feels compassion, to abandon those who love him is not fitting. Come back; have pity on me.”
Hearing these words of Chanda, overwhelmed by grief, the best of speakers, steady with the utmost firmness, replied:
“Chanda, let go of this anguish over parting from me. Embodied beings born into different states must surely go their different ways.

cmp.note: nānābhāva 意为「各自分开、彼此不同」，既指命运各异，也指终将分离。
cmp.en: nānābhāva means “being apart, being different”: both that beings have different lots and that they must separate.

verses.en: “Even if, out of love, I did not leave my kin of my own accord, death would tear us from one another, whether we would or not.
“The mother who carried me in her womb with great longing and much pain, her labor bore no fruit: where am I now to her, and where is she to me?

cmp.note: 「辛劳落空」暗指摩耶夫人生下太子七天后就去世了，没能抚养他；古译明说「生已即命终，竟不蒙子养」。
cmp.en: “Whose labor bore no fruit” alludes to Queen Maya’s death seven days after his birth, so that she never raised him; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says this outright.

verses.en: “As birds gather in a tree to roost for the night and then fly their separate ways, so the meeting of beings surely ends in parting.
“As clouds come together and then drift apart again, so, I think, do living beings meet and part.
“And since this world goes on, each deceiving the other, it is not right to call anything ‘mine’ in a union that is like a dream.

cmp.note: 「彼此欺骗而去」：众生相聚时仿佛长久，转眼各自离去，好像互相失约。
cmp.en: “Deceiving one another”: beings seem to promise permanence when they meet, then leave, as if each broke faith with the other.

verses.en: “Trees are parted even from the color of their leaves, which was born with them; how much more must one thing be parted from another!
“Since this is so, my friend, do not grieve; go now. But if your love still lingers, go, and then come back to me.
“And tell the people in Kapilavastu who still look to me: ‘Give up your love for him, and hear his resolve:
“‘Either he will soon return, having made an end of birth and death; or else, failing in his aim, his effort spent, he will perish.’”

cmp.note: nirārambha 意为「努力已尽、无所作为」；白话「失去了依靠」不太准确。
cmp.en: nirārambha means “with his effort at an end, no longer striving”; the plain Chinese “having lost his support” is not quite accurate.

verses.en: Hearing his words, Kanthaka, finest of horses, licked his feet with his tongue and shed hot tears.
With his hand, webbed between the fingers, marked with the svastika and with a wheel at the center of the palm, the prince stroked him and spoke to him as to a friend:

cmp.note: 网缦指、卍字、掌中轮相，都是传说中「大人三十二相」里的身体标志。
cmp.en: Webbed fingers, the svastika, and the wheel in the palm are among the bodily marks of a “great man” in Buddhist tradition.

verses.en: “Kanthaka, do not shed tears; you have proved yourself a true horse. Be patient: this labor of yours will soon bear fruit.”

cmp.note: 「会有结果」：后世传说犍陟死后升天并得闻法；古译「恶道苦长息，妙果现于今」把这层意思说得更明。
cmp.en: “Will bear fruit”: later legend says Kanthaka was reborn in heaven and heard the Dharma; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version makes the promise more explicit, speaking of an end to the evil destinies and a wondrous fruit.

verses.en: Then the steadfast one took from Chandaka’s hand the sharp sword, its hilt set with jewels and its blade chased with gold, and drew it from the scabbard like a venomous snake from its hole.
Drawing out the blade, dark as a blue lotus petal, he cut off his ornate crown together with his hair, and flung it, its cloth streaming, into the air, like a goose cast onto a lake.

cmp.note: haṃsa 通常译「天鹅」或「雁」，是印度诗中常见的白色水禽。
cmp.en: haṃsa, often rendered “swan” or “goose,” is the white waterbird beloved of Indian poetry.

verses.en: And as it was thrown, the dwellers of heaven caught it, out of reverence and the wish to worship it; and in heaven the hosts of gods honored it fittingly with celestial offerings.

Now that he had cast off his ornaments and his wives, and had made his head an exile from royal splendor, the steadfast one looked at his fine garment, embroidered with golden geese, and longed for a forest dweller’s robe.

cmp.note: 原文是并列复合词「装饰与妻室」：他舍掉了装饰，也舍掉了妻子。白话读成「除去装饰品——像除去了妻子一样」，把并列误作比喻。
cmp.en: The compound pairs “ornaments and wife”: he has given up both. The plain Chinese reads it as a simile (“took off his ornaments as if leaving a wife”), turning the pair into a comparison.

verses.en: Then a dweller of heaven, pure of heart, who knew his wish, came near in the form of a deer hunter, wearing an ochre robe; and the scion of the Shakya king said to him:
“This auspicious ochre robe, the banner of the seers (rishis), does not go with that murderous bow of yours. So, my friend, if you are not too attached to it, give it to me and take this one.”

cmp.note: 「仙人的旗帜」：赭色衣是出家修行人的标志。这里首次以 ṛṣi（仙人、圣者，英译 seers (rishis)）称修行者。
cmp.en: “The banner of the seers (rishis)”: the ochre robe is the badge of the renunciant.

verses.en: The hunter said, “Giver of what others desire, it is true that with this I win the deer’s trust, then kill them from close by. But if you have need of it, you who are like Indra, here, take it and give me that white one.”

cmp.note: Śakra 即因陀罗（帝释）；猎人以此称呼王子，暗中也是天神对未来佛的敬称。
cmp.en: Shakra is Indra; the hunter, himself a god in disguise, quietly honors the future Buddha with the comparison.

verses.en: Then with the greatest joy he took the forest robe and gave up the fine linen; and the hunter, taking on his heavenly body again, took the white garment and went back to heaven.
The prince and the keeper of the horse were amazed to see him go like that, and at once held the forest robe in still greater reverence.

Then the great-souled one dismissed Chanda, whose face was wet with tears, and wearing the ochre robe, bearing steadfastness and glory, he went toward the hermitage, like the king of stars wrapped in clouds of twilight.

cmp.note: 「被晚霞包裹的星王（月亮）」：赭色衣如同红色晚霞，王子如同明月。古译改为「青绛云围绕日月轮」。
cmp.en: “The king of stars (the moon) wrapped in twilight clouds”: the ochre robe is the red evening cloud, the prince the moon. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version speaks instead of blue and crimson clouds around the sun and moon.

verses.en: When his master, with no longing for the kingdom, went off like that to the ascetics’ grove in a faded robe, the horse keeper threw up his arms, wailed aloud, and fell to the ground.

cmp.note: vivarṇa 意为「褪色的」，也可读作「无种姓的、被逐出种姓的」——王子穿上了失去种姓身份者的衣服，一语双关。
cmp.en: vivarṇa means “faded, discolored,” but can also be read as “without caste”: the prince now wears the dress of one outside the social order, a double meaning.

verses.en: Looking back once more, he wept aloud and threw his arms around the horse Kanthaka; then, without hope, lamenting again and again, he went to the city in body, but not in mind.
Now he fell to brooding, now he lamented, now he stumbled, now he fell; and so, going on in misery under the sway of his devotion, he acted out many things along the road, helpless.

Then Sarvarthasiddha sent away Chanda, weeping, his face wet with tears; with his heart set on the forest and caring for nothing else, outshining the hermitage with his beauty, he entered it like one already perfected.

cmp.note: 双关：王子名为 Sarvārthasiddha（一切义成），进林时「如同成就者（siddha）」——名字与比喻用的是同一个词根。
cmp.en: A pun: the prince’s name, Sarvarthasiddha, means “one who has achieved every aim,” and he enters “like a siddha,” a perfected being; name and simile share the same root.

verses.en: That king’s son, who walked like the king of beasts, came into the hermitage yard, full of deer, as gently as a deer; and though he had left royal fortune behind, by the fortune of his body he drew the eyes of everyone in the hermitage.

cmp.note: 同一个词 lakṣmī 用了两次：先指王家的富贵荣华，再指身上的光彩美貌。
cmp.en: The word lakṣmī is used twice: first for royal fortune and splendor, then for the beauty and radiance of his body.

verses.en: The wheel-bearing ascetics with their wives stood still out of curiosity, yokes still in their hands; they gazed at him, who was like Indra, and did not move on, like draft oxen with heads half bowed.

cmp.note: cakradhara 字面「持轮者」，指某一类苦行者，确切所指不明；白话作「拿着车轭的」修行人，是把 hastasthayugāḥ 的意思也合进去了。
cmp.en: cakradhara, literally “wheel-bearers,” names some class of ascetics whose exact identity is unclear; the plain Chinese folds it into “holding yokes,” the other phrase in the line.

verses.en: And the brahmins who had gone out for firewood came back with fuel sticks, flowers, and kusha grass in their hands; though devoted to austerity and firm of mind, they went to see him and did not go back to their huts.
The peacocks cried out for joy, as if they had seen a dark cloud rising; and the deer, and the ascetics who lived like deer, left their grass and stood facing him, their eyes darting.
Seeing him, the lamp of the Ikshvaku clan, blazing like the rising sun, the cows kept for the fire offering were filled with delight and let their milk flow, though they had already been milked.
“Might he be the eighth of the Vasus? Or one of the two Ashvins, fallen from heaven?” Such were the words the sages called out aloud in their wonder at the sight of him.

cmp.note: 婆薮神（Vasu）共八位，原文问的是「他是不是八婆薮中的第八位」；白话「八位之外的第八位」说法自相矛盾。古译把猜测扩成一长串神名。
cmp.en: The Vasus are eight gods; the question is whether he is “the eighth of the Vasus.” The plain Chinese “an eighth beyond the eight” contradicts itself. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version expands the guesses into a long list of gods.

verses.en: Like a second body of Indra, lord of the gods, or like the radiance of the whole world, moving and unmoving, he lit up the entire forest, as if the sun had come down to it of its own accord.
Then the hermits honored him as was fitting and invited him to stay; and he returned their honor to those keepers of Dharma in a voice like a cloud heavy with rain.
The hermitage was crowded with people doing meritorious works out of desire for heaven; and he, steadfast, desiring liberation, walked through it, observing their many kinds of austerity.

cmp.note: 对照：他们「想要升天」，他「想要解脱」——这一章的主旨就在这两种愿望的差别。
cmp.en: The contrast is pointed: they desire heaven, he desires liberation. The whole chapter turns on the difference between these two aims.

verses.en: Having observed the forms of austerity practiced by the ascetics in that grove, the gentle prince, wishing to know the truth of it, spoke to one of them who was walking along with him:
“This is the first time I have seen a hermitage, and I do not know the rules of practice here. So please tell me what you have resolved to do, and toward what end you are striving.”
Then that twice-born man, whose delight was austerity, explained in order to the bull of the Shakyas, who had the valor of a bull, the different kinds of austerity and their fruits.

cmp.note: dvijāti「再生族」，指受过入教礼的高种姓男子，此处即婆罗门。
cmp.en: dvijāti, “twice-born,” means a man of the upper castes who has undergone initiation; here, a brahmin.

verses.en: “Food not grown in villages, plants that grow in water, leaves, water, fruit and roots: this, according to scripture, is how the sages live. But their ways of austerity differ one from another.

cmp.note: 「非村落之食」即不靠耕种得来的野生食物——苦行者不吃农田出产的东西。
cmp.en: “Food not of the village” means wild food, not from cultivated fields; forest ascetics refused farmed produce.

verses.en: “Some live like birds on gleaned grain; some graze on grass like deer; some live on the forest wind together with the snakes, until they turn into anthills.
“Some earn their living by pounding with stones; some eat grain husked with their own teeth; and some cook for others first, then make their own meal from whatever is left.

“Some, their coils of matted hair wet with water, pour offerings into the fire twice a day with sacred chants; some plunge into the water and live there with the fish, their bodies scratched by turtles.

“By such austerities, built up over long stretches of time, the highest go to heaven, the lesser to the world of men. By a painful road one comes to happiness; for pain, they say, is the root of merit.”

cmp.note: 此处原文作 sukham（乐），字面是「乐是法之根」，与上文不合；依上下文应读作 duḥkham（苦）：「苦是法的根」。白话译成「乐的根是法」，颠倒了主语和属格。
cmp.en: The text as given reads sukham, “happiness is the root of dharma,” which does not fit the argument; the sense requires duḥkham, “pain is the root of dharma (merit),” and this translation follows that. The plain Chinese, “dharma is the root of happiness,” reverses the grammar.

verses.en: When the son of the lord of men had heard these and other words of the ascetic, though he had not yet seen the truth himself, he was not satisfied, and he said quietly to himself:
“Austerity is suffering by its very nature, and takes many forms; its fruit is at best heaven; and all the worlds are subject to change. Great indeed is the toil of these hermitages for so little!

cmp.note: 文字游戏：āśrama（修行林、净修处）一词里就含着 śrama（劳苦）；「修行林的劳苦」是双关。
cmp.en: Wordplay: āśrama, “hermitage,” contains śrama, “toil”; “the toil of the hermitages” is a pun.

verses.en: “Those who give up dear kinsmen and the pleasures of the senses and keep vows for the sake of heaven are parted from their ties, only to go willingly into a still greater bondage.

“Whoever, through the torments of the body called austerity, longs for further existence for the sake of pleasure, without examining the evils of the round of rebirth, seeks suffering by means of suffering.

cmp.note: pravṛtti 字面「流转、继续活动」，指继续投生、在轮回中存在下去，与后文 nivṛtti（止息、出离）相对。
cmp.en: pravṛtti, literally “going on, activity,” means continued existence in the round of rebirth; it is the opposite of nivṛtti, “ceasing, turning away,” which appears later (7.48).

verses.en: “Creatures are always terrified of death, and yet they strive to be born again; but where there is existence, death is certain, and so they sink into the very thing they fear.

“Some take on weariness for gain in this world, others take on toil for heaven; the world of the living, made wretched by hope, seeking happiness and never reaching its goal, falls indeed into misfortune.

“Not that this effort is wholly to be blamed, which leaves the low behind and goes toward something higher; but the wise, with the same labor, should do that work after which nothing remains to be done.

cmp.note: 「做了以后再也无须再做的事」，即彻底解脱，不再轮回；古译作「两舍永无为」。
cmp.en: “That after which there is nothing more to do” means final liberation, with no further rebirth; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version renders it 两舍永无为 (liǎng shě yǒng wúwéi, “giving up both, forever free of action”).

verses.en: “If tormenting the body is dharma here, then the body’s comfort is adharma; and yet by dharma one gains happiness hereafter. So here dharma bears adharma as its fruit!

cmp.note: 此处 dharma 指「功德、正当行为」，adharma 是其反面；王子用苦行者自己的说法推出矛盾。
cmp.en: Here dharma means “merit, right action,” and adharma its opposite; the prince turns the ascetics’ own premise into a contradiction.

verses.en: “Since the body acts and ceases to act under the control of the mind, it is the mind alone that should be tamed; without the mind, the body is no more than a log.
“If merit comes from purity of diet, then deer too have merit, and so do those men cut off from good things, whose fortunes have turned away from them through bad luck.

“If the intention in enduring pain is what causes merit, should not that same intention be applied to pleasure as well? And if intention counts for nothing in pleasure, surely it counts for nothing in pain either.
“In the same way, those who touch water to purify their deeds, believing it to be a holy ford, find in it only a satisfaction of the heart; for water will not wash away evil.

cmp.note: tīrtha 原意「渡口」，引申为河边的圣地、朝圣沐浴之处；下一偈王子把「真正的 tīrtha」说成德行。
cmp.en: tīrtha means a ford, and by extension a holy bathing place of pilgrimage; in the next verse the prince redefines the true tīrtha as virtue itself.

verses.en: “If water is held to be a holy place on earth wherever it has been touched by the virtuous, then I regard virtues alone as the true holy place; water, without a doubt, is only water.”
So he spoke, reasoning in many ways, and the sun went down. Then he entered the forest, calm with austerities, where the trees were darkened by the smoke of oblations.

There the sacred fires had been carried forth and were blazing; it was crowded with seers who had finished their ritual bathing; the shrines of the gods hummed with the sound of murmured prayers; it seemed a workshop of Dharma in full operation.

cmp.note: karmānta 意为「作坊、工场」：林中像一座正在开工的「法之作坊」。白话只说「法事正在进行」，比喻没有译出。
cmp.en: karmānta means a workshop or works: the grove is likened to a “workshop of Dharma” in full swing. The plain Chinese gives only “as if a religious rite were under way,” losing the image.

verses.en: He, who shone like the moon, stayed there for some nights, examining their austerities; and having surveyed it all and come to his judgment on austerity, he left that field of austerity.
Then the hermits followed him, their minds won over by his form and his greatness, as great seers (rishis) follow Dharma when it is departing from a land overrun by the ignoble.
Then he saw those ascetics, with matted hair and fluttering garments of bark and rags; and out of regard for their austerities he stopped and stood at the foot of an auspicious, splendid tree.
The hermitage dwellers came up and stood around that best of men; and the eldest of them, with great respect, spoke these words in a soft and gentle voice:
“When you came, the hermitage seemed full; when you go, it becomes empty indeed. So, my son, you should not leave it, as cherished life does not leave the body of one who longs to live.

cmp.note: 比喻的主语是「寿命」：就像珍爱的生命不离开想活下去的人的身体。白话改成「想活下去的人不会舍弃心爱的身体」，主宾颠倒了。
cmp.en: The subject of the simile is life: as cherished life does not leave the body of one who wants to live. The plain Chinese turns it around (“as one who wants to live does not abandon his beloved body”).

verses.en: “Close by stands the holy mountain Himalaya, frequented by brahmin seers, royal seers and divine seers; by being near it, the austerities of ascetics are multiplied.

cmp.note: 三类仙人：婆罗门出身的梵仙、王族出身的王仙、天界的天仙。
cmp.en: Three kinds of seers: brahmin seers, royal seers (kings who became sages), and divine seers.

verses.en: “All around, too, there are holy fords that serve as stairways to the sky, frequented by men of righteous and self-governed mind, by divine seers and by great seers.
“And from here it is better still to keep to the north alone, for the sake of advancing in Dharma; a wise man should not take even one step toward the south.

cmp.note: 北方与喜马拉雅、诸神相连，被视为吉祥；南方则与死神阎摩相连，被视为不祥。
cmp.en: The north, home of the Himalaya and the gods, was considered auspicious; the south, the direction of Yama, god of death, inauspicious.

verses.en: “Or have you seen in this ascetics’ grove someone who neglects the rites, or has fallen through mixing his duties, or is impure, so that you do not wish to stay? Tell us, so that your stay may be to your liking.

cmp.note: 「因混乱法规而堕落」，大概指违背种姓或生活阶段规矩的人；古译把这一偈改成苦行者自责并愿意让位。
cmp.en: “Fallen through confusion of dharma” probably means one who has broken the rules of caste or stage of life. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version recasts the verse as the hermits offering to leave so he can stay.

verses.en: “For these men want you as a companion in austerity, you who are like a treasure-store of austerity; living together with you, who are equal to Indra, would bring prosperity, as it did for Brihaspati (teacher of the gods).”
When the chief of the ascetics had spoken thus among the ascetics, the chief of the wise, who had vowed to destroy existence, told them what was in his heart:

cmp.note: bhava「有、存在」，在佛教里指轮回中不断的生存；「灭有」即终结再生。
cmp.en: bhava, “becoming, existence,” in Buddhist usage means continued existence in the round of rebirth; to “destroy existence” is to end rebirth.

verses.en: “You sages, upright of heart and keepers of Dharma, who are so fond of guests that you treat them like your own kin: such feelings toward me have given me the greatest joy and made me honor you.
“These affectionate words, which go to the heart, have, in a word, bathed me through and through; and my delight in Dharma, I who am a newcomer to it, now stirs more strongly than ever.
“You who act like this, who are a refuge, who have shown me such marked favor: the thought that I must leave you and go pains me too, just as it pained me to leave my kinsmen.
“But this Dharma of yours aims at heaven, while my longing is never to be born again. The reason I do not wish to stay in this forest is that the way of ceasing is different from the way of going on.

cmp.note: pravṛtti（流转、投入世间）与 nivṛtti（止息、出离）是印度宗教的一对基本概念：前者求更好的来生，后者求彻底停止轮回。
cmp.en: pravṛtti (going on, engagement) and nivṛtti (ceasing, withdrawal) are a basic pair in Indian religion: the first seeks a better rebirth, the second an end to rebirth altogether.

verses.en: “So it is not discontent, nor any wrong done by others, that makes me wander on from this forest; for all of you abide in a Dharma true to the ages of old, and are like the great seers.”
Hearing the prince’s words, gracious and full of meaning, finely turned, forceful and dignified, the ascetics held him in especially high regard.
But one brahmin there, who slept on ashes, tall, with a topknot, wearing a garment of bark, with reddish-brown eyes and a long thin nose, a water pot in one hand, spoke these words:
“Wise one, noble indeed is your resolve, since though young you have seen the evil of birth. For one who weighs heaven against final release and sets his mind on release, he truly exists.

cmp.note: apavarga 指最终解脱；「此人方为存在」即真正活得有价值、才算一个人。
cmp.en: apavarga is final release; “he truly exists” means he alone lives a life worth the name.

verses.en: “Men full of passion hope to reach heaven by sacrifices, austerities and all kinds of vows; but men of true mettle fight passion as an enemy and seek to win liberation.
“If this is your settled purpose, go quickly to the Vindhya country. There lives the sage Arada, who has gained insight into the final good.

cmp.note: 阿罗蓝（Arāḍa Kālāma），后来第十二章中王子的第一位老师；古译作「阿罗蓝」。
cmp.en: Arada (Arada Kalama) becomes the prince’s first teacher in Chapter 12; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version calls him 阿罗蓝 (Āluólán).

verses.en: “From him you will hear the path to truth, and if it pleases you, you will follow it. But as far as I can see, this mind of yours will move on, shaking off even his views.
“This face of yours, with its high, clear-cut nose, long wide eyes, red lower lip, sharp white teeth and thin red tongue, will drink up the whole ocean of what can be known.

cmp.note: 「可知之海」，即一切应知之事；古译作「悉饮尔炎水」，意象不同。
cmp.en: “The ocean of the knowable,” all that there is to know; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has a different image, of drinking up the flaming water.

verses.en: “That unfathomable depth of yours, your radiance and the marks on your body, will win you the rank of teacher on earth, one that even the seers of the former age did not attain.”
“Excellent,” said the king’s son, and with thanks to the company of seers he went away; and the hermits, having taken their leave of him with due courtesy, went back into the ascetics’ grove.
When his master had gone off to the forest like that, free of all attachment, the groom was sick at heart. On the road he struggled to master his grief, and still his tears would not stop.
The road he had covered in a single night with that horse, at his master’s command, he now travelled in eight days, brooding on his master’s absence.

And the horse Kanthaka, for all his strength, went on listlessly, worn down in spirit, his fire gone. He still wore his trappings just as before, yet without his master he seemed to have lost all his splendour.

Again and again he turned back to face the ascetics’ grove and neighed long and piteously. Though he was hungry on the road, he no longer welcomed grass or water as he once had, and would not take them.

So, step by step, the two of them drew near the city named after Kapila, now bereft of that great soul whose whole self was given to the good of the world. It seemed empty, like a sky without the sun.
His pleasure garden, too, was graced with waters full of white lotuses and adorned with trees in flower, as lovely as a wild wood; yet with the townsfolk robbed of their joy, it no longer shone.

Then, among people wandering aimlessly, downcast, their faces dull and their eyes blinded by tears, the two of them slowly entered the city, as if they themselves were fading out, and the city looked like one that has just bathed after a funeral.

cmp.note: nirvāyamāṇa 字面是「正在熄灭、渐渐消失」,这里按此译作二者仿佛将要熄灭;白话中文译作「被拦着似的」,依据不明。apasnāta 指办完丧事后洗身的人,城像刚为死者沐浴过。
cmp.en: nirvāyamāṇa literally means “being extinguished, fading out”; the plain Chinese has 被拦着似的 (bèi lánzhe shìde, “as if held back”), which is hard to justify. apasnāta is someone who has bathed after a death in the family: the whole city looks as if it has just come from a funeral.

verses.en: When the townsfolk saw the two of them coming with drooping bodies, returning without the bull of the Shakya clan, they wept in the street, as people once wept when the chariot of Dasharatha’s son came back without him.

cmp.note: 暗用《罗摩衍那》:罗摩流放入林,车夫须曼陀罗(Sumantra)驾着空车回到阿逾陀,满城哭泣。车匿空马而还正是同一场面。
cmp.en: An allusion to the Ramayana: when Rama went into exile, his charioteer Sumantra drove back to Ayodhya with the chariot empty, and the whole city wept. Chandaka returning with the riderless horse is the same scene.

verses.en: Then, angry and in tears, people followed behind Chandaka on the road, saying, “Where is the king’s son, the joy of the city and the kingdom? You have stolen him away!”
He answered those loyal people, “I did not abandon the king’s son. It was he who sent me away, weeping, in the empty forest, and sent away his householder’s clothes along with me.”

When they heard what he said, they were convinced that it was a very hard thing he had done. The tears fell from their eyes and they let them fall; and they reproached their own hearts, as things born of the fruit of past deeds. (The second half of this verse is obscure.)

cmp.note: 这半句文字可疑,字面像是「他们放下了落下的水,不是眼里生的」,各家读法不一。这里取大意:眼泪落下,任其流淌。
cmp.en: This half-line is doubtful; taken literally it seems to say “they let fall the falling water, not born of the eyes,” and readings differ. The translation gives only the general sense: they let their tears fall.

verses.en: Then they said, “Let us go into that forest this very day, where he has gone with the stride of a king of elephants. Without him we have no wish to live, just as embodied beings cannot live once their senses depart.”
“Without him this city is a forest, and with him that forest is a city. Without him our city has lost its beauty, as heaven did when Indra, lord of the Maruts, was away slaying Vritra.”
“The prince has come back!” the women thought, and crowded to the rows of windows; but when they saw the horse with an empty back, they shut the windows again and wailed.

The king, meanwhile, had taken a vow of consecration to win back his son. Worn out in mind by the vow and by grief, he was murmuring prayers in the temple and performing one rite after another as his heart desired.
Then Chandaka, his eyes brimming with tears, leading the horse and following behind it, entered the royal palace stricken with grief, as if his master had been carried off by an enemy in battle.
And Kanthaka, as he went into the king’s palace, gazing about with eyes running with tears, cried out in a loud voice, as though telling the people of his sorrow.
Then the birds that lived within the palace, and the well-tended horses tethered nearby, echoed that horse’s cry, thinking the king’s son was coming.
And the people near the king’s inner apartments, deceived by a rush of joy, thought, “Since the horse Kanthaka is neighing like this, surely the prince is coming in.”

Then the women, who had been faint with grief, in an excess of joy and with eyes restless to see the prince, came hurrying out of their rooms in hope, like flickering lightning out of an autumn cloud.

Their hair hung loose, their clothes were soiled, their faces bare of collyrium and their eyes blinded by tears. Without their grooming the women did not shine, like stars in the sky reddened at the end of night.

Their feet were not reddened with dye and wore no anklets; their faces had no earrings, their necks were bare and plain; their hips, full by nature, wore no girdles; and their breasts, without the strings of their necklaces, looked as if they had been robbed.
When those lovely women saw Chandaka and the horse alone, without their master, their eyes filled with tears and their faces fell, and they wept like cows in the forest abandoned by their bull.
Then Gautami, the king’s chief queen, tender as a buffalo cow that has lost her calf, threw up her arms and fell to the ground in tears, like a golden plantain tree with trembling leaves.

cmp.note: 双关:mahiṣī 既是「正宫王后」,又是「母水牛」。王后像丢了小牛的母水牛,一个词两用。白话中文作「母牛」,丢了「王后」这层字面呼应。
cmp.en: A pun: mahiṣī means both “chief queen” and “buffalo cow,” so the queen is a mahiṣī like a mahiṣī that has lost her calf. The plain Chinese 母牛 (mǔniú, “cow”) keeps the image but not the wordplay.

verses.en: Other women, their radiance gone, shoulders and arms hanging slack, as if senseless with despair, did not cry out, did not shed tears, did not breathe, did not move; they stood there as if painted.

Others, losing all composure and faint with grief for their lord, let the streams from their eyes run down from their faces onto their breasts, no longer anointed with sandal, as a mountain wets its rocks with its springs.

And with their faces beaten by the water of their eyes, the royal palace looked then like a pond at the coming of the rains, its red lotuses beaten by the rain from the clouds and dripping with water.

The lovely women beat their breasts with their lotus-like hands, the fingers round and full and closely set, unadorned, the veins hidden, like creepers tossed by the wind striking themselves with their own shoots.

And those women, their breasts, full and rising together, set shaking by the blows of their hands, looked like rivers whose pairs of chakravaka birds (ruddy geese, emblems of faithful love) are rocked by lotuses swaying in the forest wind.
As they bruised their breasts with their hands, so they bruised their hands with their breasts; heedless of pity, the frail women made fingertips and breasts torment each other.
Then Yashodhara spoke, her eyes reddened with anger, her voice choked and hoarse with despair, her bosom heaving with sighs, her face streaming with the tears of deep grief:

cmp.note: 诗人连用三个 -dharā 结尾的词押韵:payodharā(胸脯)、aśrudharā(含泪的)、yaśodharā(名字本义「持有名声的」)。英文无法保留,只能说明。
cmp.en: The poet chimes three words ending in -dharā: payodharā (“bosom”), aśrudharā (“bearing tears”) and Yaśodharā, whose name means “bearer of fame.” English cannot keep the jingle.

verses.en: “Chandaka, where has he gone, the one my heart longs for, leaving me helpless, asleep in the night? You and Kanthaka have come back, but three went out together, and my heart trembles.”
“Cruel man, you have done me an ignoble, heartless deed, the deed of an enemy. Why do you stand here weeping today? Hold back your tears and be glad; your tears do not match what you have done.”
“With you as his helper, so dear, so obedient, so well-meaning, so good, so efficient, my noble husband has gone, never to return. Rejoice, then; congratulations, your labour has borne fruit!”

cmp.note: diṣṭyā 是道喜的套语(「可喜可贺」),这里是反话,耶输陀罗在讥讽车匿。
cmp.en: diṣṭyā is the formula for congratulation (“what luck!”); here it is bitter irony aimed at Chandaka.

verses.en: “Better for a man a clever enemy than a foolish friend with no sense of what is fitting. You, a witless so-called friend, have brought great ruin on this family.”

“Pity these women, their ornaments cast off, their eyes red and clouded with endless tears. Though their husband is still alive, steady as the Himalaya and the earth, they have lost their beauty like widows.”

“And these rows of palaces, their dovecote eaves flung out like arms, the long cooing of the doves never ceasing, seem to weep bitterly along with the women of the inner rooms, now that they are deprived of him.”
“This horse Kanthaka too must surely wish this household every kind of harm, for he has carried off from here everything I had, like a jewel thief in the night while people slept.”
“He can bear even the arrows that strike him in battle, let alone whips. How could he have gone off for fear of the whip, taking with him our fortune and my heart together?”
“Today this vile creature neighs loudly, as if to fill the king’s palace; but when he was carrying away my beloved, then the wretched horse was dumb.”
“If he had neighed and woken the household, or made a noise with his hooves on the ground, or even made a sound with his jaws, I would not be suffering like this.”
When Chandaka heard the lady’s words, full of lament, the syllables knotted with tears, he lowered his face, tears welling, joined his palms, and slowly gave this answer:

cmp.note: devī 是对王族女子的尊称,这里指王子的妻子耶输陀罗,不是国王的王后。白话中文作「王后」,容易误会成瞿昙弥。
cmp.en: devī is an honorific for a royal lady; here it is Yashodhara, the prince’s wife, not the king’s queen. The plain Chinese 王后 (wánghòu, “queen”) could make readers think of Gautami.

verses.en: “My lady, you should not blame Kanthaka, nor should you be angry with me. Understand that we two are wholly without fault. That god among men, my lady, went away as a god goes.”
“I knew the king’s command, yet as if forced by some gods, I quickly brought him this horse, and followed him on the road without any weariness.”

“And this fine horse, as he went, did not touch the ground with the tips of his hooves, as if they were held up in between; and his mouth was held shut, as though by fate, so that he neither champed his jaws nor neighed.”
“When the king’s son went out, the gate opened of its own accord, and the darkness of night was torn apart as if by the sun. Take this, too, as the working of fate.”

cmp.note: 写本此处作 tapo(苦行),与后两颂的叠句 tato 'pi(「由此也」)不合,当是抄误,按 tato 译。
cmp.en: The manuscript reads tapo (“austerity”) here, which does not fit the refrain tato 'pi (“from this too”) of the next two verses; it is probably a copying error and is translated as tato.

verses.en: “Though thousands of people in the palace and the city were on watch by the king’s order, at that moment not one of them woke; sleep had carried them off. Take this, too, as the working of fate.”

“And at that very moment a dweller in heaven gave him a garment fit for living in the forest, and the diadem he tossed into the sky was caught and carried off. Take this, too, as the working of fate.”
“So, queen among women, you should not count his going as a fault of us two. It was not my will, nor this horse’s. He went with the gods as his escort.”

When the women heard of that great soul’s marvellous departure, attended by so many gods, they were filled with wonder, as if their grief had vanished; but at the thought of his going forth into homelessness they were seized with a fever of the heart.
Then Gautami, her eyes swimming with despair, grieving like an osprey that has lost its young, cast off all self-control and wailed aloud; she fainted, and then, her face wet with tears, she spoke:
“His hair, waving in great curls, soft, black, lovely, each hair growing from its own root, rising thick and high, fit to be wound about a king’s crown, has been thrown down on the ground.”

cmp.note: 「每根头发各自从一个毛孔生出」是大人物的相好之一,瞿昙弥列举的都是王子身上的吉相。
cmp.en: “Each hair growing from its own root” is one of the bodily marks of a great man; Gautami is listing the auspicious signs on the prince’s body.

verses.en: “Long-armed, with the stride of the lion, king of beasts, with the eyes of a great bull, shining bright as gold, broad-chested, with a voice like a drum or a thundercloud: does such a man deserve to live in a hermitage?”
“Surely this earth is unworthy of so noble and peerless a lord, and so he has gone. For a king of such virtue is born only through the merit and good fortune of his people.”
“His feet, soft, the toes spread with fine webbing, the ankles hidden, tender as lotus flowers, a wheel marked at the centre of each sole: how will they walk on the hard ground of the forest?”
“That strong body, used to beds and couches on the upper terraces of the palace, honoured with costly clothes, aloe wood and sandal: how will it fare in the forest, in cold and heat and rain?”
“Proud of his family, his courage, his strength, his radiance, his learning, his fortune and his youth, used to giving and never to asking: how will he go begging alms from others?”
“He slept on a spotless golden bed and was woken at night by the sound of music. Alas, how will my son, bound by his vows, sleep today on the bare earth, with only a strip of cloth between?”
Hearing this pitiful lament, the women threw their arms around one another and shed water from their eyes, like creepers shaken by the wind letting honey fall from their flowers.
Then Yashodhara fell to the ground like a female chakravaka bird parted from her mate, and in her distress she lamented slowly, again and again, in a voice choked with sobs:

“If he wants to practise Dharma and has cast me off, his partner in Dharma, leaving me without a protector, what Dharma can he have, when he wants to enjoy austerity without the partner of his Dharma?”

cmp.note: sahadharmacāriṇī 是「妻子」的正式说法,字面「一同奉行法的女伴」。耶输陀罗抓住这个词反问:他要修法,怎能撇下与他「同修法」的人?一词之中的双关是全颂的锋芒。
cmp.en: sahadharmacāriṇī is the formal word for “wife,” literally “she who practises dharma together with him.” Yashodhara turns it against him: how can he seek Dharma by leaving the very person whose title is “partner in Dharma”?

verses.en: “Surely he has never heard of the kings of old, his forefathers, Mahasudarsha and the rest, who went to the forests together with their wives, since he wants to practise Dharma without me.”

“Or else he does not see that at sacrifices, consecrated by the rites of the Veda, husband and wife are consecrated together, and together they wish to enjoy its fruit in the next world. That is why he has grown stingy with his Dharma toward me.”

“Surely this lover of Dharma knows that my heart was always picking jealous lovers’ quarrels with him, and so, at ease and unafraid, he has left me, the angry one, and wants to win the apsarases in great Indra’s heaven.”
“But this is what I keep wondering: what beauty, what charms do the women there possess, that for their sake he practises austerities in the forest, leaving behind royal fortune and my devotion too?”
“I have no craving for the joys of heaven; for a person of self-mastery those are not hard to win. My one wish is this: that my beloved should never leave me, here or in the world beyond.”
“Even if I am not fortunate enough to look on my husband’s face, with its long eyes and pure smile, does poor unlucky Rahula, too, not deserve to roll about now and then on his father’s lap?”
“Ah, how cruel, how very hard is the heart of that high-minded man, for all his tender beauty, that he can abandon such a little son, babbling sweetly, who would delight even an enemy!”

“My heart too must be very hard, made of stone or even of iron, since it does not break now that my husband, used to comfort, has gone into the forest stripped of his royal fortune, like a man with no one to protect him.”
So the lady, faint with grief for her husband, wept and brooded and lamented over and over. Steady by nature though she was, and virtuous, in her sorrow she forgot her composure and felt no shame.
When they saw Yashodhara lying on the ground, overcome with grief and lament, the women cried out, their tearful faces like great lotuses beaten by the rain.

The king, having finished his prayers and performed the fire offering and the rites of blessing, came out of the temple. Struck by the people’s cries of pain, he shook like an elephant at a clap of thunder.

cmp.note: 写本此词不通,大概原作「被那悲苦的哭声」(tena ārtaraveṇa),按此译。
cmp.en: The manuscript word does not make sense; it was probably “by that cry of pain” (tena ārtaraveṇa), and is translated so.

verses.en: When he saw Chandaka and Kanthaka both, and heard of his son’s firm resolve, the lord of the earth fell, struck down by grief, like Indra’s banner when the festival is over.
Then for a while he was dazed with grief for his son. Held up by men of his own rank, he sat on the ground, gazed at the horse with eyes full of tears, and lamented:

“Kanthaka, you did me many kindnesses in battle, but now you have done me a great unkindness. For my dear son, who loves virtue, beloved as he is, you have carried off to the forest as if he were not loved at all.”
“So today either take me to where he is, or go quickly and bring him back again. Without him I have no life left, like a man gravely ill without good medicine.”

“When Death carried off the son who spat gold, it was a hard thing indeed that Sanjaya did not die. But now that my son, who delights in Dharma, has gone, I long to be rid of myself, like a man who has lost all self-control.”

cmp.note: 典出《摩诃婆罗多》:国王 Sṛñjaya(此处写作 Saṃjaya)得一子,其排泄物皆是黄金,后被杀,国王悲痛而未死。昙无谶译本作「珊阇梵志,为子死杀身」,说他为儿子自杀,与梵文「没有死」正相反。
cmp.en: An allusion to the Mahabharata: King Srinjaya (spelled Sanjaya here) had a son whose very spittle and waste were gold; the boy was killed, and the king grieved but lived. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says the opposite, that the brahmin 珊阇 (Shānshé) killed himself for his son: 为子死杀身 (wèi zǐ sǐ shā shēn, “died, killing himself for his son”).

cmp.note: mumukṣu 通常是「求解脱者」,这里字面是「想舍弃自身」(想死)。诗人用了一个宗教词来写一个父亲的绝望,讽意在其中:儿子求解脱,父亲只想解脱于生命。
cmp.en: mumukṣu usually means “one who seeks liberation”; here it literally means “wanting to let go of myself,” that is, wanting to die. The irony is pointed: the son seeks liberation, the father seeks only release from life.

verses.en: “Even the mind of Manu, the mighty lord of creatures, son of Vivasvat the sun, who founded the ten kshatriya lines and knew both the higher and the lower, would surely be shaken if he lost a good and beloved son.”
“I envy the wise son of King Aja, the king who was Indra’s friend: when his son went to the forest, he went to heaven, and did not drag out a wretched life shedding useless tears.”

cmp.note: 「阿阇王之子」就是十车王(Daśaratha):罗摩被放逐入林,十车王悲恸而死。白话中文照字面译,没点明;昙无谶译本则说成阿阇王本人「爱子游山林,感思而命终」,把父子弄混了。
cmp.en: “The son of King Aja” is Dasharatha, who died of grief when Rama was exiled to the forest. The plain Chinese renders it literally without naming him; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version makes King Aja himself the one who died, mixing up father and son.

verses.en: “Good friend, tell me where that hermitage lies to which you carried off the one who should pour my handful of funeral water. For my life-breaths, longing to set out on the road of the dead, are thirsting for him.”

cmp.note: jalāñjali 是「一捧水」,指儿子为亡父献上的祭水。国王把儿子称作「我的那捧水」:没有儿子,死后就没人供水。昙无谶译本据此发挥成饿鬼渴死的长段。
cmp.en: jalāñjali is “a handful of water,” the funeral offering a son pours for his dead father. The king calls his son “my handful of water”: without him, no one will make the offering. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version expands this into a long passage about dying of thirst and becoming a hungry ghost.

verses.en: Thus the king, in the pain of parting from his son, abandoned the steadiness, firm as the earth, that was born in him, and like Dasharatha in the grip of grief for Rama, he lamented at length, almost out of his senses.
Then his counsellor, endowed with learning, discipline and virtue, and the aged family priest spoke to him in measured and fitting words, neither distraught in face nor yet unmoved:

cmp.note: pariptamukha 写本有误,大概原作 paritaptamukha(「满面焦灼」)。白话中文作「没有板着脸」,这里译作「神色不慌乱」,两种读法都不确定。
cmp.en: pariptamukha is corrupt, probably for paritaptamukha (“with burning, distressed faces”). The plain Chinese reads 没有板着脸 (méiyǒu bǎnzhe liǎn, “not stern-faced”); this translation reads “not distraught in face.” Neither is certain.

verses.en: “Best of men, let go of grief and take hold of your courage. Steadfast as you are, you should not shed tears like a man with no fortitude. Many kings on earth have cast off royal fortune like a crushed garland and gone to the forests.”

“Besides, this disposition of his was destined. Remember what the seer Asita said long ago: neither in heaven nor in the kingdom of a wheel-turning emperor could he be made to stay happily even for a moment.”
“But if, best of kings, an effort must be made, tell us quickly, and we two will go there at once. Let there be a contest of every kind there between us and your son, and his fate in all its forms.”

cmp.note: vidhi 在本章叠句「天意的安排」(daivo vidhiḥ)里就是「命运、天定」,这里也当指「种种天命」。白话中文作「他的种种心意」,恐怕不对。
cmp.en: vidhi is the word used in this chapter’s refrain daivo vidhiḥ, “the working of fate,” and here too it most likely means fate in its various forms. The plain Chinese 他的种种心意 (tā de zhǒngzhǒng xīnyì, “his various intentions”) is probably mistaken.

verses.en: So the king commanded the two of them, “Then go quickly, straight from here. For my heart finds no peace, like a forest bird’s that longs for its young.”

“Very well,” they said, and at the king’s command the minister and the family priest set out for that forest. And the king, thinking “It is done,” turned with his daughters-in-law and his wives to whatever else remained to be done.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Search for the Prince (Kumārānveṣaṇa)

verses.en: Then the counselor and the family priest, lashed by the king with the goad of his tears, set out for that forest with all their strength, quick with loyal affection, like good horses pricked by the spur.

Worn out by the journey, they came in good time to the hermitage, with a following that suited their rank. There they laid aside the pomp of royalty and, in modest bearing, entered the dwelling of Bhargava.

cmp.note: dhiṣṇya 原指祭火的位置、祭坛，引申为住处。用这个词说跋伽婆的「住所」，暗示那是一个以祭火为中心的苦行者道场，正好呼应上一章苦行林里拜火的仙人。白话「住所」和英文 dwelling 都只取了引申义。
cmp.en: Dhiṣṇya first means the place of a sacred fire, an altar, and by extension a dwelling. Using it for Bhargava’s “dwelling” hints at an ascetic camp built around the sacrificial fire, echoing the fire-tending seers of the previous chapters. The plain Chinese 住所 (zhùsuǒ, “residence”) and the English “dwelling” keep only the extended sense.

verses.en: They paid due honor to that brahmin, and he honored them in return as was fitting. When they had taken their seats and Bhargava too was seated, they cut short the courtesies and spoke of their errand:
“Sir, know that we serve a king of pure vigor and pure, far-reaching fame, born in the line of Ikshvaku: one of us keeps his sacred learning, the other his counsels of state.”

“He is like Indra, and his son, like Jayanta (Indra’s son), wishing to cross over the fear of old age and death, has come here, so we hear. For his sake we two have come. Let your reverence know this.”

He said to them, “Yes, that long-armed prince did come here, and he was no fool. Judging that our way of life only turns one back into the round of rebirth, he left, seeking liberation, and went toward Arada.”

cmp.note: āvartaka 是「使人转回来的」，就是让人一再回到生死轮回。苦行仙人自己转述王子对他们的评语，口气很坦然。白话「会让人一再轮回」准确；古译「随顺生死法」意思相同，用的是佛教现成说法。
cmp.en: Āvartaka means “that which makes one turn back,” that is, back into the cycle of birth and death. The ascetic reports the prince’s verdict on his own group quite calmly. The plain Chinese is accurate; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version renders it 随顺生死法 (suíshùn shēngsǐ fǎ, “a teaching that goes along with birth and death”), the same idea in stock Buddhist wording.

verses.en: Having learned the truth from him, they took leave of the brahmin at once. Tired as they were, their devotion to the king made them seem untired, and they hurried on in the direction he had gone.
As they went on, they saw him: without any adornment, yet blazing with the beauty of his body, seated by the road at the foot of a tree, like the sun that has passed behind a bank of cloud.

Then the family priest, together with the keeper of counsel, left his carriage and went up to him, as the sage Vasishtha, son of Urvashi, went with Vamadeva, longing to see Rama when he lived in the forest.
They honored him as he deserved, as Shukra and Angiras honor great Indra in heaven; and he honored them as they deserved, as great Indra in heaven honors Shukra and Angiras.

cmp.note: Śukra 是阿修罗的祭司，Aṅgiras（这里指其后裔、天神的祭司毗诃波提）是诸天的祭司。两位祭司一起礼敬因陀罗，对应这里的家师和大臣。整首诗前后两行字面几乎相同、只换了主宾，是作者有意的回文式对称。古译把 Śukra 音译作「儵迦罗」，把这种对称拆成两句叙述。
cmp.en: Śukra is the priest of the anti-gods and Aṅgiras (here standing for his line, the priests of the gods) the priest of the gods; together they mirror the priest and the minister. The two halves of the verse repeat almost word for word with subject and object swapped, a deliberate mirror. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version transcribes Śukra as 儵迦罗 (Shūjiāluó) and breaks the mirror into two plain statements.

verses.en: Given leave, the two sat down on either side of him, the banner of the Shakya clan; and close beside him they shone like the twin stars of Punarvasu (a lunar mansion) in conjunction with the moon.
The family priest addressed the king’s son, who sat glowing at the foot of the tree, as Brihaspati spoke to Jayanta, son of Shakra (Indra), seated in heaven beneath the coral tree (parijata):
“Prince, with the arrow of grief for you lodged deep in his heart, the king fell senseless to the ground for a moment. Then, with tears raining from his eyes, he said this to you. Listen:

‘I know your resolve toward the Dharma, and I am sure this goal will one day be yours. But because you have gone to the forest before the proper time, I am burning in a fire of grief as fierce as fire itself.’

‘So come, you who love the Dharma: for my sake, and for the Dharma’s own sake, give up this resolve. For this flood of grief, swelling high, beats against me as a river’s flood beats against its bank.’
‘What wind, sun, fire and the great thunderbolt do to clouds, water, dry brush and mountains, scattering, drying, burning and splitting them, grief does to us.’
‘So for now enjoy lordship over the earth, and go to the forest at the time the scriptures prescribe. Have some regard for me, your unwanted kinsman; for compassion toward all beings is the Dharma.’

cmp.note: aniṣṭa-bandhu 字面是「不受欢迎的亲人」，可以理解为国王的自嘲：你既然不要我这个亲人，也请顾念我。也有人读作「被不幸（aniṣṭa）缠住的亲人」。白话「不受欢迎的亲人」取前一种，英文同。
cmp.en: Aniṣṭa-bandhu literally means “an unwelcome kinsman,” which reads as the king’s rueful self-description: you no longer want me as kin, but still spare me a thought. It can also be taken as “a kinsman bound up in misfortune.” The plain Chinese 不受欢迎的亲人 (bù shòu huānyíng de qīnrén, “an unwelcome relative”) takes the first sense, as does the English.

verses.en: ‘And this Dharma is not won only in the forest; even in the city success is sure for those who strive. Understanding and effort are what count here; the forest and the ascetic’s badge are the marks of the timid.’

cmp.note: 国王说林居和出家标志是「胆小者的记号」，话说得很重。古译把这层意思扩成两句：「剃发服染衣，自放山薮间，此则怀畏怖」，意思一致而更直白。
cmp.en: The king says forest life and the ascetic’s badge are “the marks of the timid,” a harsh charge. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version expands it into two lines, 剃发服染衣，自放山薮间，此则怀畏怖 (“shaving the head, wearing dyed robes, abandoning oneself to the wilds: this is to harbor fear”), the same point put more bluntly.

verses.en: ‘Kings wearing crowns, with necklaces slung over their shoulders and arms clasped in bracelets, rolling in the lap of Lakshmi (goddess of fortune), have won the Dharma of liberation while living as householders.’
‘Bali and Vajrabahu, the two younger brothers of Dhruva; Vaibhraja, Ashadha and Antideva; Janaka, king of Videha; Shalvadruma; and kings like Senajit:’

cmp.note: rājñaḥ 是复数宾格，senajitaḥ 可能也是复数，意思更像「以舍那耆为代表的诸王」或「舍那耆等王」。白话「舍那耆的两位国王」把复数理解成「两位」，没有根据。这一串古王名单写本也有讹误，古译所列的名字与梵本差异很大。
cmp.en: Rājñaḥ is accusative plural, and senajitaḥ probably is too, so the sense is “kings such as Senajit.” The plain Chinese 舍那耆的两位国王 (“the two kings of Senajit”) turns the plural into “two,” which the text does not support. This list of ancient kings is also corrupt in the manuscripts, and the names in Dharmakshema’s Chinese version differ widely from the Sanskrit.

verses.en: ‘Know that these were householder kings, yet trained in the practice that leads to the highest good. So enjoy both at once: mastery over the mind and the glory of kingship.’
‘For I long to hold you tight when you have been consecrated, still wet from the anointing water, to gaze on you beneath the royal parasol, and then, in that same joy, to enter the forest myself.’
“So the lord of the earth spoke to you, in words whose syllables were knotted with tears. Having heard them, you ought for his sake to answer his love with love.
“The Shakya king is sinking in a fathomless ocean of sorrow whose waters spring from you. So rescue him, helpless and without support, as a boat rescues a man drowning in the sea.
“You have heard what Bhishma, born of Ganga’s womb, did to please his father, and Rama, and Rama of the line of Bhargava. You too should do what your father wishes.

“Think of the queen who reared you, who has not yet gone to the quarter where Agastya dwells (the south, the realm of death): she weeps piteously without end, like a loving cow that has lost her calf.

“Your wife is like a female goose parted from her mate, like a cow elephant left alone in the forest by the bull. Though her husband lives, she grieves as one who has none. You should save her by letting her see you.

“Your only son is a little child who does not deserve to suffer, yet he carries a pain hidden inside him. Free Rahula from his grief for his kin, as the full moon is freed from the grip of Rahu (the demon who swallows the moon).

cmp.note: Rāhula 与 Rāhu 同音相关，诗人借此作比：把罗睺罗从悲伤中救出，就像把满月从罗睺的吞食中救出。中文「罗睺罗」与「罗睺」也正好保留了这个音的联系，英文只能靠并列的两个名字让读者看出。
cmp.en: Rāhula and Rāhu echo each other, and the poet builds the simile on it: free Rahula from grief as the full moon is freed from Rahu’s eclipse. The Chinese 罗睺罗 (Luóhóuluó) and 罗睺 (Luóhóu) happen to keep the sound link; in English the reader has to notice it from the two names side by side.

verses.en: “The palace and the whole city are burning in a fire of grief, fueled by your absence, with sighs for its smoke and darkness for its flame. They long for the water of seeing you.
The Bodhisattva, perfect in his inner strength, heard the family priest’s words. He reflected for a moment, and then, knowing what virtue is, he gave this modest and courteous answer:

cmp.note: bodhi-sattva 与 paripūrṇa-sattva 押同一个 sattva：「觉悟之有情」与「心力圆满」，是一个文字游戏。白话「心志圆满的菩萨」意思对，但双关丢了。
cmp.en: Bodhi-sattva and paripūrṇa-sattva both end in sattva, “a being” in the first and “inner strength” in the second: a play on words. The plain Chinese 心志圆满的菩萨 (“the Bodhisattva of complete resolve”) gets the meaning but loses the pun.

verses.en: “I understand the feeling fathers have for a son, and especially the king’s feeling for me. And yet, though I know it, I am leaving my family because I have no other way, afraid as I am of sickness, old age and death.

“Who would not want to see his own dear ones, if parting from what is dear did not come in the end? But since parting comes even after long being together, I am leaving my father, beloved though he is.
“As for the grief you say the king feels on my account, it gives me no pleasure: that in these meetings, which are like a dream, people should torment themselves over a parting that is bound to come.
“Let your mind come to this firm conclusion, seeing how varied is the way the world goes: neither son nor kinsman is the cause of this pain. This pain has ignorance as its cause.
“As for travelers who meet on the road, parting comes at its fixed time; so it is for all creatures. What wise person would give way to grief when separated from people who were called his kin?

“A man leaves his kin in another world and comes here; having taken in kin here too, he goes off again; having gone there, he moves on somewhere else. Among people who are always leaving like this, what room is there for attachment?

cmp.note: pra-labh 常义是「骗取、欺哄」，也可解作「获得」。白话取「骗得了亲人」，语气尖刻；按上下文（离开彼处亲人—在此得亲人—又离去），译作「得到、结下」也通，英文取较中性的 taken in，两种意思都留一点。古译「暂亲复乖离」只说暂时成为亲人。
cmp.en: Pra-labh usually means “to deceive, take in,” but can also mean “to obtain.” The plain Chinese 骗得了亲人 (piàn dé le qīnrén, “cheated his way into kin”) takes the sharp sense; the flow of the verse (leave kin there, gain kin here, leave again) also allows simply “acquiring.” The English “taken in” keeps a little of both. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version, 暂亲复乖离 (“briefly kin, then parted”), says only that they are kin for a while.

verses.en: “And since from the womb onward death is at work in every stage of life to kill us, why did his honor, who loves his son, say that my going to the forest is untimely?

“There is a wrong time for taking up the pleasures of the senses, and likewise a set time for the pursuit of wealth. But Time drags the world away at all times; for the highest good, which carries one out, there is no fixed time.

cmp.note: 同一个 kāla 在一首偈里用了好几次：「不是时候」「时候」「时间（即死神）」「一切时候」。王子把国王的「不是时候」接过来，翻成「时间（死）无时不在拖人走」，这是一组字面游戏。白话把第三个 kāla 直接写成「死亡」，意思准确，但词的重复看不出来。古译「一切时死故，除死法无时」处理得很简洁。
cmp.en: The single word kāla appears again and again in this verse: “wrong time,” “set time,” “Time” (that is, Death), “all times.” The prince takes the king’s word “untimely” and turns it into “Time drags everyone off at every moment.” The plain Chinese renders the third kāla straight as 死亡 (sǐwáng, “death”), which is accurate but hides the repetition. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version puts it tersely: 一切时死故，除死法无时 (“since death comes at all times, the teaching that removes death has no set time”).

verses.en: “As for the king wishing to hand his kingdom over to me, that too is generous and worthy of a father. But it is not right for me to accept it, any more than a sick man should, out of greed, take food that is bad for him.
“How could a wise man rightly take up kingship, the very home of delusion? In it are anxiety, intoxication and toil, and harm to right conduct through wrongs done to others.
“A kingdom is delightful, yet it is a home of disaster: like a golden mansion on fire, like the finest food laced with poison, like a lotus pond teeming with crocodiles.

“So kingship is neither happiness nor right conduct. That is why kings of old, when disgust arose in them, left their kingdoms in the fullness of age, when suffering could not be avoided, and went to the forest.
“Better to eat grass in the forest, clasping supreme contentment to oneself like a jewel, than to live alongside the evils that come so easily with royal fortune, unseen, like black snakes.
“It is praiseworthy for kings to leave their kingdoms and enter the forest out of longing for the Dharma. But it is not fitting for one who has broken his vow to abandon the forest and go back home.

“What man of spirit, born of a good family, having entered the forest out of longing for the Dharma, would throw off the ochre robe and, all shame cast aside, go to live in a city, even the city of Indra?
“A man who, from greed or delusion or fear, would take up again food he had vomited, is the kind who, from greed or delusion or fear, would take up again the pleasures he had renounced.

“Like a man who has somehow escaped a burning house and then goes back into that same house is one who, having renounced the household life and seen its faults, would in his delusion long to take it up again.

“As for the tradition that kings won liberation while living as householders, that is not so. How far apart are the way of liberation, whose heart is calm, and the way of kings, whose heart is the rod of punishment!

cmp.note: śama「寂静、平息」和 daṇḍa「刑杖、惩罚」两相对照，各配一个 pradhāna（以……为主）。daṇḍa 在政治论里就是国家强制力本身。白话「以刑杖为主的为王之道」保留了字面；英文用 the rod of punishment 同样保留了这个具体的形象。
cmp.en: Śama, “calm, quieting,” is set against daṇḍa, “the rod, punishment,” each paired with pradhāna, “having as its chief part.” In Indian political theory daṇḍa is the coercive power of the state itself.
