The plain Chinese 以刑杖为主 (“based on the rod”) keeps the literal image, and so does the English “the rod of punishment.”

verses.en: “If a king delights in calm, his rule grows slack; if his mind is on ruling, his calm is wrecked. Calm and harshness do not go together, any more than the coolness of water and the heat of fire.

“So those lords of the earth either made a firm decision, gave up their kingdoms and won calm, or else, while keeping the royal state, because they had their senses under control, took a state that is not final for liberation.

“But let us grant that they had real calm while they ruled. I did not come to the forest in a spirit of indecision. I have cut the snare called home and kin, I am free, and I have no wish to go back in.
When the king’s son had given this answer, worthy of his self-knowledge and his virtue, free of craving, well reasoned and forceful, the keeper of counsel replied in his turn:
“This resolve of yours to follow the Dharma is not wrong; but it is not timely. To hand over your aging father to grief cannot be right conduct, for one like you who loves the Dharma.

“Surely your understanding is not very subtle, or else you are not skilled in matters of right conduct, wealth and pleasure, since for the sake of an unseen reward you scorn what is before your eyes and go away.
“Some say there is rebirth; others firmly declare there is not. Since this matter is so uncertain, it is right to enjoy the royal fortune that lies ready to hand.
“If there is any further existence, we will enjoy ourselves there according to the birth we get. And if there is no existence beyond this, then this world is liberated without any effort.

cmp.note: 大臣的口气带着狡黠：如果死后什么都没有，那人人死了就算「解脱」了，何必费力。这是在挖苦求解脱的人。白话「不必费力就已经解脱了」把这层讽刺译出来了。
cmp.en: The minister’s tone is sly: if nothing comes after death, then everyone is “liberated” simply by dying, so why strive? It is a jab at seekers of liberation. The plain Chinese 不必费力就已经解脱了 (“already liberated without effort”) captures the irony, as does the English.

verses.en: “Some say there is a world beyond, yet they do not describe a means to liberation; they say that just as heat belongs to fire and wetness to water, so continued existence is simply nature.
“Some explain that good and evil, existence and non-existence, all come from inherent nature (svabhava); and since all this happens by its own nature, effort is useless.
“That the senses each work in a fixed way, that objects are pleasant or unpleasant, that we are joined with old age and pain: what effort has any part in that? Is it not simply inherent nature?
“Fire is quenched by water, and fires make water dry up; yet the elements, distinct as they are, come together into one in the body and hold up the world.
“That the form of a child in the womb develops with hands, feet, belly, back and head, and that the self is joined with it: those who know this doctrine call that the work of inherent nature.
“Who makes the thorn sharp, or gives beasts and birds their many varied forms? All this comes about by inherent nature. There is no acting at will here; how then can there be effort?
“Others say creation comes from the Lord (Ishvara); then what is the use of a person’s effort? The very cause that sets the world going is surely also the cause that brings it to rest.
“Some say that the arising of existence and the ending of existence are caused by the self alone. Arising, they say, comes without effort, but liberation, they declare, is reached by effort.

“A man is born together with three debts: to the ancestors, paid off with offspring; to the seers (rishis), with the Vedas; to the gods, with sacrifices. Whoever is freed from these, they say, has freedom indeed.

cmp.note: mokṣa 一词两用：先指「免除（债务）」，再指宗教意义上的「解脱」。还清三债的人才「有解脱」，等于说「从债里解脱才是解脱」。大臣用的是婆罗门正统的「三债」说。白话「还清这三种债的人才有解脱」把第一个 mokṣa 意译成「还清」，双关就没有了；英文用 freed ... freedom 勉强保留。
cmp.en: Mokṣa is used twice in two senses: first “release” from the debts, then “liberation” in the religious sense. Whoever has release from the three debts has liberation, as the orthodox brahmin doctrine of the three debts holds. The plain Chinese 还清这三种债的人才有解脱 (huánqīng zhè sān zhǒng zhài de rén cái yǒu jiětuō, “only one who has paid off these three debts has liberation”) renders the first mokṣa as 还清 (huánqīng, “paid off”), so the pun is lost; the English “freed … freedom” keeps a trace of it.

verses.en: “So those who know these things say liberation comes to one who strives by following this ordered sequence of rules. Those who seek liberation by forcing their way, however hard they strive, only wear themselves out.
“So, gentle one, if you are devoted to liberation, follow in due order the rule just described. In this way you will reach your goal, and the king’s anguish will come to an end.

“And as for the thought that came to you that it would be wrong to go back home from the ascetics’ groves, do not worry about that either, my son. Men of old went back from the forests to their own homes.

“King Ambarisha, though he lived in an ascetics’ grove, went back to his city surrounded by his people. And Rama came back from the ascetics’ grove and protected the earth when wicked men had ravaged it.

“So too the king of the Shalvas, named Druma, came back from the forest to his city with his sons; and Antideva, son of Sankriti, after he had become a brahmin seer, received royal power from the sage Vasishtha.

“Men like these, shining with righteousness and fame, left the forests and returned to their palaces. So there is no fault in going home from the ascetics’ grove, if it is for the sake of the Dharma.”

Then, having heard the words of the minister, the king’s eye, words that were pleasant and meant for his good, the king’s son, standing firm in his resolve, spoke words that were neither too few nor too many, neither muddled nor halting nor hurried:

“As for this doubt whether there is or is not a life to come, I will not settle it on the strength of another’s words. I will learn the truth through austerity and calm, and grasp for myself what is certain here.
“It is not right for me to take up a view born of doubt, unclear and contradicting itself. What wise man would walk by another’s faith, like a blind man in the dark led by a blind guide?

“And yet, though I have not seen the truth, when good and evil are in doubt my mind leans toward the good. For one whose heart is good, even fruitless toil is better; for one whose heart is base, there is no happiness even in the truth.

“Seeing that this scriptural tradition is unsettled, know that what the trustworthy have said is sound. And know that trustworthiness means being rid of faults; for one rid of faults will not speak falsely.

cmp.note: āpta「可信的人、权威」是印度认识论里的术语，「可信者之言」（āpta-vacana）是一种正当的知识来源。王子在这里给 āpta 下了定义：断尽过失的人。这为后来佛陀以「断尽过失者」为权威埋下伏笔。白话「可信的人」意思对，术语色彩淡了。
cmp.en: Āpta, “a trustworthy authority,” is a technical term in Indian theory of knowledge: the word of the trustworthy (āpta-vacana) counts as a valid source of knowledge. The prince defines it here as one who has shed all faults, quietly preparing for the Buddha’s own authority. The plain Chinese 可信的人 (kěxìn de rén, “a trustworthy person”) is right in meaning but loses the technical color.

verses.en: “As for Rama and the others you held up to me as examples of going home: they are no standard. Men who broke their vows are no authority for deciding what is right.

“So the sun may fall to earth, and Himalaya, king of mountains, may lose its firmness; but I will not go back home as an ordinary worldly man, without having seen the truth and with my senses turned toward their objects.

“I would rather walk into a blazing fire than enter my home with my purpose unaccomplished.” So he vowed, with lofty resolve, and he rose as he wished and went on his way, free of any sense of ‘mine.’

cmp.note: garvita 一般是「骄傲」，带贬义；用在菩萨身上，应理解为「凛然、意气坚定」。nirmama「无我所」，即不把任何东西当成「我的」，是佛教修行用语。白话「骄傲地」「毫无牵挂」都照字面，前者容易让读者误会成傲慢。英文译作 with lofty resolve，取的是「意气坚定」这层意思。
cmp.en: Garvita usually means “proud,” often negatively; applied to the Bodhisattva it is better read as “with lofty resolve.” Nirmama, “without ‘mine’,” not treating anything as one’s own, is a Buddhist practice term. The plain Chinese 骄傲地 (jiāo’ào de, “arrogantly, proudly”) is literal and could suggest arrogance. The English “with lofty resolve” takes the sense of firm determination.

verses.en: Then the counselor and the brahmin, both in tears, realizing that his resolve could not be shaken, followed him a while with downcast faces and heavy hearts, and then, having no choice, slowly made their way back to the city.

Out of love for him and loyalty to the king, they went back, then stopped, looking back again and again. They could neither look at him on the road, unassailable and blazing with his own light like the sun, nor bring themselves to leave him.

To learn where he would go, he whose goal was the highest, they set trusty spies to follow him in secret. Then, wondering, “How shall we go and face the king, who longs for his dear son?” they somehow made their way back.

The king’s darling son, broad and deep of chest, left the two men in charge of the sacred offerings and the counsels of state, crossed the Ganges with its tossing waves, and came to Rajagriha, city of splendid houses.

cmp.note: Rājagṛha 意为「王舍」，诗人在前面配了 śrīmad-gṛha「富丽之舍」，两个 gṛha 相呼应。中文「王舍城」正好保留了「舍」字，英文只能音译 Rajagriha，再用 city of splendid houses 补出那个呼应。
cmp.en: Rājagṛha means “royal house,” and the poet sets śrīmad-gṛha, “splendid houses,” beside it, so the two gṛha echo. The Chinese 王舍城 (Wángshè chéng, “city of the king’s house”) happens to keep the word “house”; English must transliterate Rajagriha and add “city of splendid houses” to keep the echo.

verses.en: He entered the city marked by five hills, well guarded and adorned by its mountains, sustained and purified by its auspicious hot springs, calm as the Self-Existent (Brahma) entering the vault of heaven.

Seeing his depth and his power, and his body blazing beyond all other men, the people there were struck with wonder, as at the sight of Shiva, whose vow is to stand firm as a post and whose banner bears the bull.

cmp.note: Sthāṇu「柱子、树桩」是湿婆的名号之一，指他苦行时一动不动如柱。sthāṇu-vrata 既可指「守柱誓（静立苦行）的人」，又直接点出湿婆。白话「守着『柱子之誓』」照字面译，读者未必知道这正是湿婆的名号。
cmp.en: Sthāṇu, “post, stump,” is a title of Shiva, who stands motionless as a post in his austerities. Sthāṇu-vrata thus means “one whose vow is to stand like a post” and at the same time names Shiva. The plain Chinese 守着「柱子之誓」 (“keeping the ‘vow of the post’”) is literal, and a reader may not see that it is Shiva’s own title.

verses.en: Seeing him, whoever was going the other way stopped; whoever stood in the road followed him; whoever was hurrying slowed to a steady pace; and whoever was sitting sprang up.
Some honored him with joined palms; some reverently bowed their heads to him; some greeted him with affectionate words. No one passed him by without paying him respect.
Those in gaudy clothes were ashamed when they saw him; those chattering in the road fell silent. As if in the very presence of the Dharma in bodily form, no one had a wrongful thought.
Even the men and women on the royal highway who were busy with other things gazed with deep reverence at this godlike son of a king among men, and their eyes could not have enough of him.
His brows, his forehead, his mouth or his eyes, his body, his hands, his feet or his gait: whatever part of him anyone looked at, there that person’s eyes were held fast.

Seeing him with the tuft of hair between his brows, his long eyes, his shining body, his hands marked with a lovely web, dressed as a mendicant though fit to rule the earth, the Fortune of Rajagriha herself was shaken.

cmp.note: ūrṇā（眉间白毫）和手上的网纹（jāla）都是佛经所说「大人三十二相」中的两相，诗人借此暗示他是将成佛的「大人」。白话「白毫」「网纹」沿用了佛教译名，中文读者容易认出；英文 tuft of hair 和 web 只能照字面，相好的背景要靠读者自知。
cmp.en: The tuft of hair between the brows (ūrṇā) and the web on the hands (jāla) are two of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man in Buddhist texts; the poet uses them to hint that he is a buddha-to-be. The plain Chinese uses the established Buddhist terms 白毫 (báiháo, “white tuft”) and 网纹 (wǎngwén, “web pattern”), which Chinese readers will recognize; the English “tuft of hair” and “web” can only be literal.

verses.en: Then Shrenya (King Bimbisara), lord of the realm of Magadha, saw from his outer palace the great crowd of people and asked the reason. A man told him:

“The brahmins said he would attain either the highest knowledge or the sovereignty of the earth. That is he, the son of the lord of the Shakyas, who has gone forth as a wandering mendicant, and the people are gazing at him.”
When the king had heard this, his mind was deeply stirred, and he said to that same man, “Find out where he is going.” “Very well,” said the man, and followed him.
With steady eyes, looking only a yoke’s length ahead, silent, walking slowly and with restraint, that best of mendicants went on his begging round, holding his limbs and his restless mind in check.
Taking whatever alms came his way, he went to a secluded spring on the mountain. There he ate it in the proper manner, and then climbed Mount Pandava.

On that mountain, wrapped in groves of lodhra trees, its thickets filled with the cries of peacocks, that sun among men shone in his ochre robe like the young sun above the eastern mountain of sunrise.
The king’s servant saw him there and told King Shrenya. When the king heard it, he set out for the place out of deep respect, with only a small retinue.
Equal in valor to the Pandavas, tall in stature as a mountain, wearing his crown, moving with a lion’s gait, that lion among men climbed Pandava, best of mountains, like a lion with tossing mane.

cmp.note: Pāṇḍava 一词两用：山名「般荼婆山」，又指《摩诃婆罗多》里的般度五子。「勇力堪比般度族的国王登上般荼婆山」，加上「如山的身躯登上最好的山」「人中之狮像狮子一样」，整首偈都是同词重叠。白话把意思译全了，重叠的趣味只能靠英文并列的同一个词稍稍保留。
cmp.en: Pāṇḍava is used twice: the name of the mountain, and the five sons of Pandu in the Mahabharata. “He whose valor equals the Pandavas climbed Pandava,” together with “mountain-sized body climbing the best of mountains” and “lion among men like a lion,” makes the whole verse a chain of echoes. The plain Chinese gets the full meaning; the English keeps a little of the play by repeating the same name.

verses.en: Then he saw the Bodhisattva up above, like the mountain’s own peak, his senses at peace, sitting cross-legged and shining, like the moon rising from a bank of cloud.
The lord of men, full of wonder and humility, approached him, who sat there in beauty and calm as though the Dharma had taken form, as Shakra (Indra) approaches the Self-Existent (Brahma).

He came up to him in the proper manner, to him who was foremost among those who know what is proper, and asked whether the elements of his body were in balance. He in turn, with equally fitting courtesy, asked after the king’s peace of mind and freedom from illness.

cmp.note: dhātu-sāmya 是印度医学用语：身体诸要素（风、胆、痰等）保持平衡，即健康。这是古印度见面时的标准问候。白话「身体是否安和」意思到了，医学色彩没了；英文 the elements of his body were in balance 保留了原来的说法。
cmp.en: Dhātu-sāmya is a term of Indian medicine: the balance of the body’s elements (wind, bile, phlegm), that is, good health; it was a standard greeting. The plain Chinese 身体是否安和 (“whether his body was at ease”) gives the sense but drops the medical color; the English keeps the original image.

verses.en: Then the king sat down on a clean slab of rock, dark as an elephant’s ear. Seated close by with his leave, and wishing to know his mind, he spoke these words:

“I have a deep friendship with your family, handed down through the generations and well tested. Since you are of my own age, I feel the wish to speak to you; so listen to these words spoken out of affection.
“Your family is great, with the Sun as its first ancestor; your youth is fresh, and your body shines. Why has your mind turned, against the natural order, to delight in begging and not in ruling?
“Your limbs deserve red sandalwood paste, not the touch of an ochre robe. This hand is fit to protect the people, not to eat food given by others.

“So, gentle one, if out of love for your father you do not wish to take your ancestral kingdom by force, and you have no mind to wait patiently for it in due course, then take half of my realm and enjoy it, at once.

“In this way there will be no harm done to your own kin, and in the course of time royal fortune will come to you peacefully. So do me this kindness; for the prosperity of the good grows by keeping company with the good.
“But if, out of pride in your family, you cannot now bring yourself to trust me, then plunge with your arrows into the enemy’s battle lines, with me as your ally, and seek to conquer your foes.

“So choose one of these two courses, and pursue right conduct, wealth and pleasure as is proper. For those who, swayed by passion, upset these three aims of life come to ruin in this world and after death.

“Pleasure that crushes wealth and right conduct, wealth that overrides right conduct and pleasure, and right conduct that puts an end to pleasure and wealth: these must be given up, if the whole goal is what you want.

cmp.note: 国王讲的是婆罗门传统的「人生三目标」（trivarga）：dharma（正当、义务）、artha（财利、事功）、kāma（欲乐）。他主张三者平衡，正好和王子要追求的第四个目标 mokṣa（解脱）对立。白话用「正法、利益、欲乐」，「正法」一词带佛教色彩，容易和佛陀的 Dharma 混；英文在这里用 right conduct, wealth, pleasure，避开大写的 Dharma。
cmp.en: The king is invoking the brahmin scheme of the three aims of life (trivarga): dharma (right conduct, duty), artha (wealth, worldly success) and kāma (pleasure). He urges a balance of the three, which stands against the fourth aim the prince seeks, mokṣa (liberation). The plain Chinese uses 正法 (zhèngfǎ, “the true Dharma”) for dharma, a Buddhist-colored word easily confused with the Buddha’s Dharma; the English uses “right conduct, wealth, pleasure” here to avoid the capitalized Dharma.

verses.en: “So, by pursuing the three aims, make this handsome form of yours bear fruit. For they say that to attain right conduct, wealth and pleasure in full is to attain the full purpose of human life.
“You should not let these two brawny arms go to waste, made to draw the bow. Like Mandhatri’s, they are able to conquer even the three worlds, let alone this earth.
“I say this truly out of affection, not out of love of power, nor from arrogance. For seeing you in this mendicant’s garb, I am filled with pity, and tears have come to my eyes.

“So, you who long for the begging life, while old age has not yet come to overpower your beauty, so worthy of your line, enjoy pleasures. When the time comes, you who love the Dharma, you will practice the Dharma.

“An old man can certainly attain the Dharma, but old age has no access to the enjoyment of pleasures. That is why they say pleasures belong to the young, wealth to the middle-aged, and the Dharma to the old.
“For in this world of the living, youth is the enemy of right conduct and wealth. However carefully it is guarded it is hard to hold, because pleasures carry it off along their own road.
“The old are thoughtful, steady, set on stability. With little effort they become calm, simply because there is nowhere else to go, and out of shame.
“So when people have passed through youth, fickle, ruled by the senses, heedless, impatient, short-sighted and full of tricks, they breathe again, as if they had crossed a wilderness.

cmp.note: chala 是「诡计、欺骗、借口」。bahu-chala 说青春「诡计多端」，会骗人、也会自欺。白话「充满了诱惑」把重点移到了外来的引诱上，与原意略有出入。
cmp.en: Chala means “trick, deceit, pretext”; bahu-chala calls youth “full of tricks,” deceiving others and itself. The plain Chinese 充满了诱惑 (chōngmǎn le yòuhuò, “full of temptations”) shifts the focus to outside lures, slightly off from the Sanskrit.

verses.en: “So let this first stage of life, unsteady, fickle and careless, pass away for now. For the early years are a target for Kama’s arrows and cannot be guarded against the senses.

“Or, if your only wish is for the Dharma, then offer sacrifice, for that is the dharma of your family. By sacrifices even Indra, lord of the Maruts, mounted the back of his elephant and rose to the vault of heaven.

cmp.note: 这里有一个只差一个音的文字游戏：nāga-pṛṣṭha「象背」（因陀罗的坐骑爱罗婆多）与 nāka-pṛṣṭha「天穹之顶」。因陀罗靠祭祀骑上象背、登上天顶。白话只译了「登上了天界的顶峰」，漏掉了「象背」半句。英文两半都译出。
cmp.en: There is a one-sound pun here: nāga-pṛṣṭha, “the back of the elephant” (Airavata, Indra’s mount), and nāka-pṛṣṭha, “the vault of heaven.” Through sacrifice Indra mounted the elephant’s back and reached heaven’s vault. The plain Chinese gives only 登上了天界的顶峰 (“climbed to the summit of heaven”) and drops the elephant half; the English translates both.

verses.en: “For royal seers, their arms clasped by golden bracelets, their bright crowns blazing with lamps of jewels, reached by their sacrifices the very same state that great seers reached by their toil.”
So the lord of Magadha spoke, shining as he spoke rightly, like Indra, splitter of Vala. But hearing it, the king’s son did not waver, like Mount Kailasa with its many-colored peaks.

So the lord of Magadha spoke, with a friend’s face, words that ran against the prince’s purpose. But the son of Shuddhodana, steady and unshaken, pure with the purity of his family, gave him this reply:

“It is no wonder that you should act like this—you, born into the great house of the Haryankas (Shrenya’s royal line), you who love your friends, you whose conduct is pure. That you should behave so toward a friend is only natural.

cmp.note: Haryaṅka 是频婆娑罗所属的王族名，字面是「狮子（家族）」；古译音写作「诃梨名族胄」。英文保留族名并加一句注。
cmp.en: Haryanka is the royal line of Bimbisara; the name literally suggests “lion.” Dharmakshema’s Chinese version transliterates it as 诃梨 (hēlí). The English keeps the name with a brief gloss.

verses.en: “Among the base, a friendship handed down in the family does not last, just as fortune does not stay with the faint-hearted. But good men take the affection their forefathers formed and make it grow, through a chain of kindnesses, from one generation to the next.

cmp.note: śrī 既是「财运、福运」，也是吉祥天女（Lakṣmī）的名字；「好运不留在胆怯者身边」暗含女神弃人而去的形象。英文译作 fortune，中文译作「财运」，都只取了一层。
cmp.en: Śrī is both “fortune, prosperity” and the goddess of fortune (Lakshmi); the image is of the goddess deserting the faint-hearted. Both “fortune” and the Chinese 财运 (cáiyùn, “luck with wealth”) keep only one layer.

verses.en: “Those people in the world who make their friends’ cause their own when things go hard—those, I judge in my mind, are friends indeed. For who would not be a friend to a man who is doing well and prospering?

“In the same way, those in the world who gain wealth and put it to work for their friends and for righteousness—their riches have yielded their true worth, and when at last they are lost, they leave no regret behind.
“This resolve of yours concerning me, O king, comes surely from friendship and from nobility. So here I will reason with you in friendship too; I have no other answer to give.

“I have understood the terror of old age and death, and longing for release I have taken up this way of life. I left behind my loved ones, their faces wet with tears—how much sooner, then, the pleasures that are the causes of evil!
“I do not fear poisonous snakes so much, nor thunderbolts falling from the sky, nor fire driven on by the wind, as I fear the objects of the senses.

cmp.note: viṣaya 指色、声、香、味、触这些感官对象，也泛指由它们而来的享受；古译直接说「五欲境」。英文用 objects of the senses，后文视语境也译作 sensual pleasures。
cmp.en: Viṣaya means the objects of the senses (sights, sounds, smells, tastes, touches) and, by extension, the enjoyments they bring. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says outright 五欲境 (wǔyù jìng, “the realm of the five desires”). The English uses “objects of the senses” here and “sensual pleasures” elsewhere as the context requires.

verses.en: “Pleasures are fleeting; they are thieves that steal the wealth of good deeds; they are hollow, like a conjurer’s illusion in the world. Even when they are only hoped for they bewilder people’s minds—how much more when they are lodged within!

“Those whom desire has overpowered find no peace even in the third heaven, let alone in the world of mortals. One who thirsts is never sated by pleasures, just as fire, with the wind for its friend, is never sated by fuel.

“There is no calamity in the world equal to pleasures, yet in their delusion people cling to them above all. Knowing this truth, what wise man, afraid of calamity, would go looking for calamity himself?

“Even when they have won the whole earth, whose mouth is the sea, men long to conquer the far shore of the great ocean. The world is no more sated by pleasures than the ocean is by the waters that pour into it.
“Though heaven rained a shower of gold for him, though he conquered all four continents and even won half of Indra’s throne, Mandhatri still was not sated with the objects of sense.

cmp.note: 曼陀多（Māndhātṛ）是古代传说中的转轮王，古译作「曼陀转轮王」。英文按常见拼法写作 Mandhatri。
cmp.en: Mandhatri (Māndhātṛ) is a legendary universal monarch; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version calls him 曼陀转轮王 (Màntuó zhuǎnlún wáng, “Mandhata the wheel-turning king”).

verses.en: “Nahusha ruled the kingdom of the gods in heaven when Indra of the hundred sacrifices had vanished for fear of Vritra (a dragon-demon). In his pride he even made the great seers (rishis) carry him; and still unsated with pleasures, he fell.

cmp.note: 梵文只说「堕落了」；古译补出传说的结局：那护沙被仙人咒成大蛇（「即堕蠎蛇中」）。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says only “he fell.” Dharmakshema’s Chinese version supplies the end of the legend—Nahusha was cursed by the seers into a python: 即堕蠎蛇中 (jí duò mǎngshé zhōng, “at once he fell among the pythons”).

verses.en: “And King Aida (Pururavas, son of Ila) entered the third heaven and brought the goddess Urvashi under his sway; then, out of greed, he tried to seize the seers’ gold, and still unsated with the objects of sense, he went to his ruin.

“From Bali sovereignty passed to great Indra, from great Indra to Nahusha, and from Nahusha back again to Indra. Whether in heaven or on earth, who would put his trust in these objects of sense, tossed about as they are by the tides of fortune?

“Even sages dressed in bark, living on roots, fruit and water, wearing matted locks as long as snakes, with no other business in life, have been broken by them. Who would go looking for these enemies called ‘pleasures’?

“Ugrayudha, ‘He of the Fierce Weapon,’ though he bore a fierce weapon indeed, met his death at Bhishma’s hands because of them. Even to think of them brings misfortune and death to the virtuous—how much more to those who keep no vows!

cmp.note: 人名 Ugrāyudha 字面是「持猛器者」，诗人紧接着说他「手握猛器」，是对名字的文字游戏，英文用括注把双关显出来。古译换成了另一个故事：千臂王被罗摩仙人所杀。
cmp.en: The name Ugrāyudha means “he of the fierce weapon,” and the poet plays on it at once: “though he held a fierce weapon.” The English shows the pun with a gloss. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version substitutes a different legend: 千臂大力王 (qiān bì dàlì wáng, “the mighty thousand-armed king”) slain by the seer Rama.

verses.en: “Seeing how slight is the taste in the objects of sense, how they only tighten our bonds and never satisfy, how good men condemn them and sin follows them for certain—who would swallow this poison called ‘pleasure’?

“When they hear of the suffering of people bent on pleasure, worn down by ploughing and other toil, and see the ease of those who have no craving for pleasures, the self-possessed should be ready to give pleasures up.

“For one who lusts after pleasure, success in pleasure should be known as disaster: once his desires are fulfilled he grows drunk; drunk, he does what he should not and leaves undone what he should, and so, wounded, he goes down to an evil rebirth.
“Won with effort and guarded with care, they deceive us and go away again. What self-possessed, wise man could delight in pleasures that are like borrowed goods?

“Men seek them and seize them and are filled with thirst, and when they cannot let them go they come to suffering. Pleasures in this world are like a torch of burning straw—what self-possessed man could delight in them?

cmp.note: 这一行从这里起连用十一颂（11.23–33）作叠句，每颂换一个比喻。英文每次都用同一句 what self-possessed man could delight in them? 保留这种反复。
cmp.en: From here this line returns as a refrain through eleven verses (11.23–33), each with a new simile. The English repeats the same question each time—“what self-possessed man could delight in them?”—to keep the litany.

verses.en: “Men without self-control, bitten by them in the heart, go to destruction and find no peace. Pleasures are like an angry, venomous snake—what self-possessed man could delight in them?
“Even after feeding on them men are never satisfied, like starving dogs gnawing a bone. Pleasures are like a skeleton of old, dry bones—what self-possessed man could delight in them?

“Because they must be shared with kings, thieves, floods and fire, they bring suffering. Pleasures are like a scrap of meat tossed out for the birds to fight over—what self-possessed man could delight in them?

“Those who dwell among them meet disaster on every side, from their enemies and from their own kin as well. Pleasures are like a house where murderers lurk—what self-possessed man could delight in them?
“On mountains, in forests, on rivers and on the sea, men leap after them and come to grief. Pleasures are like fruit at the very top of a tree—what self-possessed man could delight in them?
“Won by fierce and many kinds of striving, in a moment they are gone. Pleasures are like the enjoyments of a dream—what self-possessed man could delight in them?
“Even when men have earned them, increased them and guarded them, they find no peace. Pleasures are like a pit of glowing coals—what self-possessed man could delight in them?
“For their sake the Kurus perished, and the Vrishnis and Andhakas, the Mekhalas and the Dandakas. Pleasures are like a butcher’s chopping block—what self-possessed man could delight in them?
“For their sake the two demons Sunda and Upasunda, swept into enmity with each other, destroyed each other. Pleasures tear friendships apart—what self-possessed man could delight in them?

cmp.note: 孙陀与优孙陀是一对阿修罗兄弟，传说为争夺天女提洛多玛（Tilottamā）而自相残杀；梵文只点到「为了它们」，古译补出「同生相爱念」，强调原本兄弟情深。
cmp.en: Sunda and Upasunda are demon brothers who, in the legend, killed each other fighting over the nymph Tilottama. The Sanskrit only says “for their sake”; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version adds 同生相爱念 (tóngshēng xiāng àiniàn, “born together, they loved each other”) to sharpen the contrast.

verses.en: “For their sake people here cast themselves into water and fire and to flesh-eating beasts. Pleasures are like hostile rivals, bringers of ill—what self-possessed man could delight in them?

cmp.note: sapatna 本义是「共夫的妻妾、情敌」，引申为「仇敌」；英文 hostile rivals 想兼顾这两层。古译本此颂缺。
cmp.en: Sapatna originally means “co-wife, rival,” and so “enemy”; “hostile rivals” tries to keep both senses. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has no counterpart to this verse.

verses.en: “For pleasure’s sake the ignorant man does wretched things and suffers death, chains and the like. For pleasure’s sake the world of the living, pitiful in its hopes, poor wretch, comes to weariness and death.

cmp.note: tapasvin 通常指「苦行者」，这里却是它的另一义「可怜的人」。中文白话本译作「可怜兮兮的众生」是对的，不要读成修苦行。
cmp.en: Tapasvin usually means “ascetic,” but here it has its other sense, “poor wretch.” The plain Chinese rightly gives 可怜兮兮 (kělián xīxī, “pitiful”); it should not be read as ascetic practice.

verses.en: “Deer are lured to their death by song; moths fly into the fire for the sake of its bright form; the fish, greedy for bait, swallows the iron hook. So the objects of sense bear fruit in calamity.
“If anyone thinks that pleasures are enjoyments—when you reckon them up, none of them is an enjoyment at all. Clothes and the other goods of the world should be understood as remedies for pain.

cmp.note: bhoga 既是「享受、受用」，也是「受用之物、财物」。这一段（11.36–41）整个论证就建在这个词上：衣食住行只是「对治」，不是 bhoga。古译用「自在」来对应，意思偏到了「自由自主」。
cmp.en: Bhoga means both “enjoyment” and “things enjoyed, possessions.” The whole argument of 11.36–41 turns on this word: food, clothing and shelter are only remedies, not bhoga. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version renders it 自在 (zìzài, “free, at ease”), which shifts the sense toward freedom.

verses.en: “Water is wanted to quench thirst, and food in just the same way to put an end to hunger; a house to keep off wind, sun and rain; clothing to cover one’s loins and keep out the cold.
“A bed likewise is for overcoming drowsiness; a carriage for putting an end to the weariness of the road; a seat for relief from standing; a bath to give cleanliness, health and strength.
“So for living beings the objects of sense are means of remedying pain, not enjoyments. What wise man, busy with a remedy, would claim, ‘I am enjoying pleasures’?
“Only one who, burning with a bilious fever, decided that a cooling treatment was an enjoyment would, while busy remedying pain, give pleasures the name of enjoyment.
“And because pleasures are never constant, for this reason too I do not think of them as enjoyments. The very things that bring us happiness turn round and bring us pain.
“Heavy garments and fragrant aloe wood are a comfort in the cold but a discomfort in the heat; moonbeams and sandalwood are a comfort in the heat but a pain in the cold.

cmp.note: gurūṇi（厚重的）和 agurūṇi（沉香，字面又可读作「不重的」）只差一个字母，是马鸣常用的文字游戏；中文和英文都只能分别译出两样东西。
cmp.en: Gurūṇi (“heavy”) and agurūṇi (“aloe wood,” which also looks like “not heavy”) differ by one letter—a typical bit of Ashvaghosha’s wordplay. Neither English nor Chinese can carry the jingle, only the two objects.

verses.en: “Since the pairs of opposites—gain and loss and the rest—cling to everyone in the world, for this reason too there is no one on earth who is wholly happy, and no one who is wholly wretched.
“Seeing how happiness and sorrow are mixed together, I hold kingship and slavery to be the same. A king is not always laughing, nor is a slave always in torment.
“If it is said that a king has more—the power to command—that is exactly why a king has great sorrows. For a king is like a carrying pole: he wears himself out for the sake of the world.
“In a kingdom that is quick to desert him and full of enemies, a king who puts his trust in others comes to ruin; yet if he trusts no one, what happiness can there be for a king who lives in fear?

cmp.note: 两个词都修饰「王国」：一个「容易背弃（国王）」、「敌人众多」的国家。中文白话本把 tyāgin 读成「敌人肯施恩收买」，恐怕不对。
cmp.en: Both words describe the kingdom: one that is “apt to desert” its king and “full of enemies.” The plain Chinese reads tyāgin as the enemies being “willing to buy people with favors,” which seems mistaken.

verses.en: “And when he has conquered the whole earth, still only one city serves him to live in, and in it only one palace can he use. Is not kingship, then, mere toil for the sake of others?
“Even a king wears only one pair of garments, and eats only enough food to keep off hunger; he has only one bed and only one seat. All his other splendors serve only to make a king proud.

“If contentment is the fruit that is sought in all this, I have contentment even without a kingdom. And when a man in this world is content, are not all splendors alike, with nothing to choose between them?
“So I am not to be lured toward pleasures. I have set out on the safe and blessed road. But remember our friendship, and say to me again and again, ‘Keep your vow!’
“I have not entered the forest out of resentment, nor because enemy arrows struck the crown from my head, nor out of longing for some greater reward. That is why I do not accept these words of yours.

“Only a man who let go of an angry, biting snake and then made up his mind to seize it again, or threw away a blazing torch of straw that burns by its very nature and picked it up again, would give up pleasures and then go back to them.

“Only a man with sight who envied the blind, a free man who envied the bound, a rich man who envied the destitute, a sound mind that envied a madman, would envy one whose whole self is given to the objects of sense.

“The man who lives on alms is not to be pitied: he is accomplished, set on crossing beyond the fear of old age and death; his is the highest happiness of peace here, and for him the sufferings of the world beyond are shut away.
“It is the man overcome by craving, even while he lives in great wealth, who deserves pity: he does not gain the happiness of peace here, and in the world beyond he is seized by sufferings.
“For you to speak like this befits your character, your conduct and your family; and for me to hold to my vow befits my character, my conduct and my family.

cmp.note: 上下两行用完全相同的结尾，把「您该这样说」和「我该这样守」并排对照。英文照样重复，不换说法。
cmp.en: Both halves end with the identical phrase, setting “it suits you to say this” beside “it suits me to keep my vow.” The English repeats the phrase word for word rather than varying it.

verses.en: “I have been pierced by the arrow of the round of rebirth, and I have come out seeking to win peace. I would not want a kingdom free from all affliction even in the third heaven—how much less one among men!

“As for what you told me, O king—that the full pursuit of the three aims (duty, wealth and pleasure) is the highest goal of man—my view is that it is simply a calamity, for the three aims perish and never satisfy.

cmp.note: trivarga「三事」指 dharma（法、本分）、artha（利、财富）、kāma（欲、享乐）三种世俗人生目标；这里的 dharma 是社会本分，不是佛法，所以英文译作 duty。
cmp.en: Trivarga, “the triad,” means dharma (duty), artha (wealth) and kāma (pleasure), the three worldly aims of life. Dharma here is social duty, not the Buddha’s teaching, so the English says “duty.” The plain Chinese gives 法、利、欲 (fǎ, lì, yù).

verses.en: “But the state in which there is no old age, no fear, no sickness, no birth, no death and no anxiety, where action does not come round again and again—that alone I count the highest goal of man.
“And you said, ‘Wait for old age; youth is bound to change.’ But that is not certain. We see that old age too can be fickle, and youth can be steadfast.

cmp.note: 梵文是说老年也可能浮躁、青年也可能坚定。古译换了论证：老人体力衰弱、做不了事，不如年轻时意志坚决。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says old age can be unsteady and youth steadfast. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version argues differently: the old are too weak to accomplish anything, so it is better to act while young and resolute—我见年耆者，力劣无所堪 (wǒ jiàn niánqí zhě, lì liè wú suǒ kān, “I see the aged too feeble to bear anything”).

verses.en: “And since Death, skilled at his own work, drags off the helpless world at every age, how can a wise man who seeks peace wait for old age, when the hour of destruction is so uncertain?

“When Death stands ready like a cruel hunter, with old age for his weapon and diseases for the arrows he scatters, striking down the creatures like deer that shelter in the forest of fortune—what hope can there be of reaching a great age?
“Therefore young or old, or even a child, one should act with haste here, so that a righteous, self-disciplined man may take up activity as he wishes, or else withdraw from it altogether.

“And you said, ‘For the sake of duty, perform sacrifice as befits your family; it brings the fruits you desire.’ Homage to sacrifices! I do not want a happiness that is sought by causing another’s pain.

cmp.note: 「向祭祀致敬！」是客气的拒绝，意思是「祭祀我就免了」。中文白话本加了「敬而远之」点明语气，英文照字面保留这句带讽刺的敬语。
cmp.en: “Homage to sacrifices!” is a polite dismissal—roughly “sacrifices, no thank you.” The plain Chinese adds 敬而远之 (jìng ér yuǎn zhī, “respect it and keep one’s distance”) to make the tone clear; the English keeps the ironic salute as it stands.

verses.en: “To kill a helpless creature out of desire for a reward is not fitting for a good man whose nature is compassion—not even if the fruit of the sacrifice were eternal. How much less, then, when it is bound to perish!

“Even if there were no other way to righteousness—not by vows, not by moral conduct, not by calming the mind—still one should never take part in a sacrifice in which the reward is said to come from slaughter.
“Even here in this life, happiness that comes from harming others is unwelcome to a wise man who has pity—how much more in another existence, which cannot be seen!

“Nor am I to be lured into acting for the sake of rewards, O king; my mind takes no delight in any state of existence. For all activity, wherever it goes, is unstable, like creepers beaten by the rain from a cloud.
“I have come here wishing to see the sage Arada, who teaches liberation, and I leave this very day. May all go well with you, O king. Forgive my words, harsh because they hold to the truth.

“Protect, as Indra protects heaven; protect always, like the sun, by your virtues; protect what is good here; protect the earth; protect your life; with the help of noble men protect your good sons; protect your fortunes, O king; and protect your own righteousness.

cmp.note: 这一颂把动词 ava（守护）重复了八次，还嵌在 avendravat、avāyuḥ 等字里形成谐音，是宫廷诗的技巧。英文用八次 protect 来保留这种叠用。
cmp.en: This verse repeats the verb ava (“protect”) eight times, even tucking it into the sounds of neighboring words (avendravat, avāyuḥ)—a court-poetry display. The English repeats “protect” eight times to keep the effect.

verses.en: “As a bird flies on through the thing born of the thing born of the banner of the enemy of snow—through rain, born of cloud, born of smoke, the banner of fire—and keeps its body free, so may you go on through the slaying of the enemy of the destroyer of the enemy of the enemy of snow, and set your mind free.” (This is a deliberate riddle-verse; the second half’s key is uncertain.)

cmp.note: 这是一颂谜语诗：「雪之敌」是火，火的「旗」是烟，烟生云，云生雨——鸟在雨中飞而身不沾湿。下半颂的连环称谓（雪之敌之敌之毁灭者之敌）解法不定。古译把谜底解成「杀重怨」、「饮雨不雨身」，并劝太子降伏烦恼。
cmp.en: A riddle verse: “the enemy of snow” is fire, fire’s “banner” is smoke, smoke gives rise to cloud, cloud to rain—the bird flies through rain without its body being soaked. The chained epithet in the second half has no agreed solution. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version reads it as a call to slay the inner foe: 杀重怨 (shā zhòng yuàn, “slay the grave enemy”) and 饮雨不雨身 (yǐn yǔ bù yǔ shēn, “drinking the rain yet not wetted by it”).

verses.en: The king, palms joined, and longing now stirring in him, said, “May you gain what you desire without hindrance. And when in time you have accomplished what you set out to do, show your favor to me as well.”

He gave the king his firm promise—“So be it”—and then went on to the hermitage of Vaishvantara. The king watched him wander away, marveling, and himself went back to Girivraja, the city ringed by hills.

cmp.note: Girivraja「山围之城」是王舍城（Rājagṛha）的古名。英文保留原名并加释义。
cmp.en: Girivraja, “enclosure of hills,” is the old name of Rajagriha. The English keeps the name and glosses it.

verses.en: Then that moon of the Ikshvakus came to the hermitage of Arada, the sage who dwelt in calm, and seemed to fill it with his radiant form.
As soon as the man of the Kalama clan caught sight of him from far off, he called out loudly, “Welcome!” and the prince went up to him.
The two asked each other, as custom requires, whether all was well in body, and then sat down in a clean place on two pure wooden seats.

cmp.note: 字面是「体内诸要素（体液）平衡」，即印度医学所说的健康；白话译作「身体是否安好」是意译，古译只作「相问安吉」。
cmp.en: Literally “the balance of the bodily elements (humours)”, the Indian medical idea of health; the plain Chinese renders the sense, “whether the body is well”, and Dharmakshema’s Chinese version simply has 相问安吉 (xiāngwèn ānjí, “asked after each other’s welfare”).

verses.en: When the king’s son was seated, that best of sages spoke to him, his eyes wide with reverence, as if he would drink him in.
“I know, gentle friend, how you left your home, cutting the noose of love the way a proud elephant snaps its tether.
“Your mind is steady and wise in every way, for you have come here after casting off royal fortune as one would a creeper bearing poisoned fruit.
“It is no wonder when kings grown old go off to the forest, handing their fortune to their children like a garland worn and left over.
“What I find wonderful is that you, in the freshness of youth, standing right in the pasture of the senses, have come here without even tasting your fortune.
“So you are a worthy vessel to receive this highest teaching. Board the raft of knowledge and cross the ocean of sorrow quickly.

cmp.note: 这里的 dharma 指阿罗蓝自己的学说，英文作 teaching，不写成大写的 Dharma（佛法）。
cmp.en: Here dharma is Arada’s own doctrine, so the English has “teaching”, not the capitalized Dharma reserved for the Buddha’s saving truth.

verses.en: “Although a teacher usually expounds his doctrine only in time, once the student is well known to him, I need not test you: you are deep, and your resolve is firm.”
When that bull among men had taken in Arada’s words, he was deeply pleased, and he answered him:
“Though you are free of passion, you show me such great kindness that, though I have not reached my goal, I feel at this moment as if I had.
“For I look on the sight of you as one who longs to see looks on a lamp, one who wants to travel on a guide, and one who wants to cross on a boat.
“So, if you think it proper to tell, please tell me how this person can be set free from old age, death and sickness.”
Moved by the prince’s greatness of spirit alone, Arada then set out briefly the settled conclusions of his doctrine.
“Hear, best of listeners, this established view of ours: how the round of rebirth (samsara) comes about, and how it ceases.
“Primal nature and its transformations, birth, death and old age — all this together is called ‘a being’ (sattva). Understand this, you whose being is firm.

cmp.note: sattva 这里不是三德里的「喜德」，而是「存在者、有情」；下半句又用 sthirasattva（心志坚定者）作双关，同一个词换了一种意思。
cmp.en: Sattva here is not the guna of that name but “a being, a living entity”; the vocative sthirasattva, “you of firm being (= steadfast mind)”, plays on the same word in another sense.

verses.en: “Of these, you who know primal nature, know that primal nature (prakriti, the source from which all evolves) consists of the five elements, the sense of ‘I’ (ahamkara), intellect (buddhi), and the Unmanifest.

cmp.note: 数论里 prakṛti 是一切从中演化出来的根本质料；这里阿罗蓝列出的「本性」共八项，与古典数论把二十五谛中前八项称为「本变」的说法一致。英文用 primal nature，首次附注 prakriti。
cmp.en: In Samkhya, prakriti is the root matter from which everything evolves; Arada counts eight items as prakriti, matching the classical scheme in which these eight are ‘generative’. English has “primal nature”, glossed once as prakriti.

verses.en: “Know that the transformations (vikara, what evolves out of primal nature) are the objects of the senses and the senses themselves, hands and feet, the organ of speech, the organs of excretion and generation, and the mind (manas).
“Because it knows this field, the conscious one is called the Knower of the Field (kshetrajna); and those who reflect on the self call the Knower of the Field the self (atman).

cmp.note: 「知田者」：「田」(kṣetra) 指由本性与变化构成的身心，「知田者」是认知它的意识主体，即数论的「神我」。英文译作 the Knower of the Field。
cmp.en: “Knower of the Field”: the field (kshetra) is the body-and-mind made of primal nature and its transformations, and its knower is the conscious subject, Samkhya’s purusha; the English keeps the image as “the Knower of the Field”.

verses.en: “Tradition holds that Kapila (founder of this school), together with his disciples, is here called ‘the awakened’, while Prajapati with his sons is here called ‘the unawakened’.
“Whatever is born, grows old, is afflicted and dies should be known as the Manifest; the Unmanifest is to be known by its opposite.
“Ignorance, karma and craving are to be known as the causes of the round of rebirth. A creature who stands in this triad does not pass beyond that state of being.
“It works through wrong perception, the sense of ‘I’, confusion, conflation, failure to discriminate, wrong means, attachment and falling in.
“Of these, wrong perception goes the wrong way about things: it does what should be done otherwise, and thinks what should be thought otherwise.
“‘I speak, I know, I go, I stand’ — this, you who are free of ego, is how the sense of ‘I’ operates here.
“And one who sees things that are not mixed together as a single thing, like a lump of clay — that, you who are free of confusion, is here called confusion.
“‘What I am, that is this mind, this intellect and this action; and whatever this whole group is, that is I’ — thinking so is conflation.
“And one who sees no distinction between the awakened and the unawakened, or among the forms of primal nature — that, you who know distinctions, is known as failure to discriminate.
“Bowing in homage, crying vashat at the sacrifice, sprinkling and pouring water and the like — these, you who know the right means, the wise declare to be wrong means.

cmp.note: vaṣaṭ 是吠陀祭祀中投供物入火时的呼声；阿罗蓝把礼拜、祭祀、洒水等宗教仪式都归为「错误的方法」。
cmp.en: Vashat is the cry uttered as an offering is thrown into the Vedic fire; Arada classes bowing, sacrifice and ritual sprinkling alike as “wrong means”.

verses.en: “That by which the dull-witted cling to the objects of sense through mind, speech, intellect and action — that, you who are free of clinging, is known as attachment.
“The sorrow a man brings on himself by thinking, ‘This is mine, I belong to this’ — know that as falling in, for by it he is thrown down into the round of rebirth.
“So the wise man holds that ignorance has five joints: Darkness, Delusion, Great Delusion, and the two kinds of Gloom.

cmp.note: 这五项是数论所说的「五种无明」，名称与《数论颂》传统一致。tamas 在这里是无明的一种（懒惰），不是三德之一的「暗德」，英文用 Darkness 以免混淆。
cmp.en: These five are Samkhya’s “fivefold ignorance”, named as in the classical tradition. Tamas here is one form of ignorance (sloth), not the guna of the same name, so the English uses “Darkness” to keep them apart.

verses.en: “Of these, know that sloth is Darkness, and birth and death are Delusion; and Great Delusion, you who are free of delusion, should be understood as desire.
“Because even great beings are utterly deluded by it, mighty-armed one, it is known as Great Delusion.
“Anger, you who are without anger, they call Gloom; and despair, you who never despair, they call Blind Gloom.
“Bound up with this five-jointed ignorance, the fool is poured out into birth after birth in the round of rebirth, where sorrow is the greater part.
“Coming to think, ‘I am the one who sees, hears and thinks; I am both the effect and the instrument’, he keeps turning in the round of rebirth.

cmp.note: kārya-karaṇa 在数论里常指「身体及诸根」或「所作与能作之具」；白话作「我是果也是因」，把 karaṇa（工具、器官）说成「因」，略有偏差。
cmp.en: In Samkhya kārya-karaṇa usually means the body with its organs, “what is produced and the instruments of action”; the plain Chinese turns karaṇa (instrument, organ) into “cause”, which shifts the sense slightly.

verses.en: “By these causes, wise one, the stream of births flows on here. You should understand that where the cause is absent, the effect is absent too.
“Then the one of right understanding who longs for liberation (moksha) should know the four: the awakened and the unawakened, the Manifest and the Unmanifest.
“For when the Knower of the Field has truly understood these four, it leaves behind the coming and going of rebirth and reaches the imperishable state.
“For this purpose brahmins in the world, who teach the supreme brahman, live the holy life of chastity here and lead other brahmins to live it.
When the king’s son heard these words of the sage, he asked him about the means, and about the final state itself:
“How is this holy life to be lived, for how long, and where? And where does this teaching end? Please explain it to me.”
So Arada, following his doctrine, explained that same teaching to him briefly and clearly in another way:
“First a man leaves his home and takes up the mendicant’s marks; he adopts a discipline rich in good conduct and lives by it.
“Holding to the highest contentment, taking whatever comes from wherever it comes, he lives in solitude, untouched by the pairs of opposites, learned in the scriptures and accomplished.
“Then, seeing the danger in passion and the highest good in dispassion, he reins in the whole troop of the senses and strives for calm of mind.

cmp.note: grāma 本义「村落」，在复合词里常只是「一群、全部」；白话「收摄六根这一群村落」过于字面。原文也没有说「六」根。
cmp.en: Grāma literally means “village”, but in compounds it often just means “the whole group”; the plain Chinese “this flock of villages of the six senses” is over-literal, and the Sanskrit does not say “six”.

verses.en: “Next, set apart from sense desires and from ill will and the like, he reaches the first meditation (dhyana), born of detachment and still accompanied by reasoning.
“Having won the bliss of that meditation and pondering it again and again, the foolish man is carried away by the gain of a joy he has never known before.
“By a calm of this kind, which spurns desire and hatred, he reaches the world of Brahma, but is cheated by his own contentment.
“The wise man, however, knowing that reasonings stir up the mind, reaches a meditation free of them, filled with rapture and bliss.
“He who is carried away by that rapture and sees nothing higher reaches a shining place among the Radiant gods (Abhasvaras).

cmp.note: bhāsvara（光明的）与 ābhāsvara（光音天）同根，诗人有意叠用；中文「光音天」是佛教的传统译名。
cmp.en: Bhāsvara (“shining”) and Ābhāsvara (the Radiant gods) share a root, a deliberate echo; Chinese Buddhism names these gods 光音天 (Guāngyīn tiān, “heaven of light and sound”).

verses.en: “But he who separates his mind from that rapture and bliss reaches the third meditation, blissful but without rapture.
“He who sinks into that bliss and makes no effort toward anything higher attains a bliss equal to that of the All-Lovely gods (Shubhakritsnas).
“He who reaches such bliss yet does not delight in it, but stays even-minded, reaches the fourth meditation, beyond both pleasure and pain.
“At this point some, thinking much of themselves, conclude that this is liberation, because pleasure and pain have been given up and the mind has ceased to act.
“But those who examine with great wisdom say that the fruit of this meditation equals that of the Great-Fruit gods (Brihatphalas), and lasts a great length of time.

cmp.note: 一句里连用三个 bṛhat（广、大）：广果天、长时、大智，是诗人的文字游戏。
cmp.en: Three compounds with bṛhat (“great”) in one verse: the Great-Fruit gods, a great time, great wisdom, an intentional word-play.

verses.en: “Rising from that concentration (samadhi) and seeing the faults of embodied beings, the wise man climbs on toward knowledge, to put an end to the body.
“Then, giving up that meditation and resolved upon something higher, the wise man turns away from form itself, as before he turned away from sense desires.
“First he imagines the openings that are in this body, and then he fixes his mind on empty space even within solid substances.
“Another wise man, drawing in the self that had spread out into space, sees that same self as without end, and so reaches a higher state.
“Yet another, skilled in the inner self, turns the self back by means of the self and, seeing that nothing exists, is said to have reached Nothingness.
“Then, like a reed stalk drawn out of its munja sheath, like a bird flying from its cage, the Knower of the Field escapes from the body and is called liberated.

cmp.note: 从蒙阇草的叶鞘里抽出芦芯，是《奥义书》里比喻「把自我从身体中分离出来」的经典意象。
cmp.en: Drawing the reed stalk out of the muñja grass sheath is a classic Upanishadic image for separating the self from the body.

verses.en: “This is that supreme brahman, without marks, constant and imperishable, which the wise who know reality call liberation.
“So I have shown you both the means and liberation. If you have understood it and it pleases you, take it up as it should be practised.
“Jaigishavya, Janaka, and Parashara the elder reached this path and were freed, and so were others who sought liberation.”
He took in those words and weighed them; and, strengthened by the causes laid down in earlier lives, he gave his answer:
“I have heard this subtle knowledge, each stage more auspicious than the last. But because the Knower of the Field is not given up, I understand that it is not final.
“For even when the Knower of the Field is freed from the transformations and primal nature, I think it still has the nature of something that gives birth, the nature of a seed.

cmp.note: 这里王子把数论用来描述「本性」的术语（能生、种子性）反过来套在「知田者」身上：只要还有一个自我，它就是能再生的种子。
cmp.en: The prince turns Samkhya’s own language for primal nature (“productive”, “seed-natured”) back on the Knower of the Field: as long as a self remains, it is a seed that can sprout again.

verses.en: “Even if the purified self is imagined to be released, it will become unreleased again when the conditions are present once more.
“Just as a seed does not sprout without the right season, soil and water, but sprouts when those conditions are there, so I hold it is with the self.
“You suppose that liberation comes from abandoning karma, ignorance and craving; but as long as a self exists, there is no complete abandonment of them.
“By giving up these three again and again, one does reach a higher state; but wherever the self remains, there these three remain in subtle form.
“It is because the faults have grown subtle, the mind has stopped acting and life has grown long that you imagine this to be liberation.
“And as for this giving up of the sense of ‘I’ that you suppose — as long as a self exists, there is no giving up the sense of ‘I’.
“Nor is this self free of qualities (guna), since it is not free of number and the rest; and where there is no freedom from qualities, there can be no talk of its liberation.

cmp.note: guṇa 在这里是一般意义的「属性」（如数目），而不专指数论三德；英文用 qualities 并首次附注 guna。
cmp.en: Guna here means “quality” in the general sense (number, for instance), not specifically the three Samkhya gunas; the English uses “qualities”, glossed once as guna.

verses.en: “For there is no separating the thing that has qualities from its qualities: fire is never found apart from its form and heat.
“There can be no embodied one before the body, nor a possessor of qualities before the qualities; so, though free at the start, the embodied self is bound again.
“Again, the bodiless Knower of the Field must either know or not know. If it knows, it has something to know; and while there is something to know, it is not free.
“If instead you settle that it does not know, what use is this self you imagine? Even without a self, lack of knowing is plain enough — in a log or a wall.
“Since each further step of renunciation is held to be of greater merit, I believe that the whole of the goal is reached only by renouncing everything.”
So, having come to know Arada’s teaching, he was not satisfied; seeing that it was incomplete, he went away from there.
Then, eager to hear something higher, he went to the hermitage of Udraka; but because Udraka too clung to a self, he did not accept his view either.
For the sage Udraka, seeing the fault both in perception and in non-perception, had reached beyond Nothingness a state whose nature is neither non-perception nor perception.

cmp.note: 即佛教所说的「非想非非想处」；saṃjñā 是「想、认知」，英文译作 perception。
cmp.en: This is the state Buddhists call “neither perception nor non-perception”, 非想非非想处 (fēixiǎng fēifēixiǎng chù); saṃjñā means “perception, ideation”.

verses.en: And because its object is subtle, higher than both perception and non-perception — neither without perception nor with it — he had set his heart on going there.
And because the intellect rests right there and does not move elsewhere, subtle and dulled, there is in that state neither non-perception nor perception.
But because living beings, even after reaching that state, come back again, the Bodhisattva, seeking what lies beyond, left Udraka.
Leaving his hermitage, set firmly on seeking the highest good, he went to the hermitage of the royal seer Gaya, a place known as “the City”.
Then on the pure bank of the Nairanjana river the sage, pure in his striving, who delighted in dwelling alone, made his home.
There he saw five mendicant monks who had come before him, proud in their mastery of the five senses, given to austerity and keeping their vows.
Seeing him there, those monks, longing for liberation, came to wait on him, as the objects of the senses wait on a lord who has won wealth and health by his merit.
He was honoured by these disciples, who bowed low, followed him out of good discipline and stayed at his command, as the restless senses obey the mind.
Thinking, “This may be the way to put an end to death and birth,” he then took up hard austerities by fasting.
For six years, seeking peace, he practised many kinds of fasting that other men could hardly endure, and wasted his body away.
At mealtimes he lived on a single jujube, a single sesame seed, a single grain of rice, longing to reach the far shore of the round of rebirth, whose far shore lies beyond reach — and so he held out.

cmp.note: 一句里连用 pāra（彼岸）四次：「想到达那彼岸无从到达的轮回的彼岸，他撑过来了」，最后的 apārayat（撑住、做到）也由 pāra 派生。中文和英文都只能略存其意。
cmp.en: The line rings on pāra (“far shore”) four times: longing for the far shore of a samsara whose far shore is out of reach, he “carried through” (apārayat, from the same root). Neither Chinese nor English can keep the full echo.

verses.en: Whatever loss his body suffered through that austerity was made up for again in the growth of his inner radiance.
Lean as he was, his glory and splendour were not lean, and he gladdened the eyes of others as the moon at the start of autumn’s bright fortnight gladdens the night-lotuses.
Only skin and bone remained, his fat, flesh and blood all spent; yet though wasted, his depth was not wasted, and he shone like the ocean.
Then the sage, his body plainly tormented to no purpose by harsh austerity, fearing further existence and longing for buddhahood, reflected in this way:

cmp.note: buddhi（念头、心思）与 buddhatva（成佛）同根并列，是诗人常用的谐音。
cmp.en: Buddhi (“thought, resolve”) and buddhatva (“buddhahood”) stand side by side, a sound-play on the same root that the poet likes.

verses.en: “This practice does not lead to dispassion, nor to Awakening, nor to liberation. The method I found that time at the foot of the rose-apple tree — that was the sure one.

cmp.note: 指他少年时在阎浮树下自然入定的经历（第五章）。
cmp.en: This refers to his boyhood meditation under the rose-apple tree (jambu), told in Chapter 5.

verses.en: “But that cannot be reached by someone who is weak.” Taking this to heart, he thought further about how to build up the strength of his body:
“How can one worn out by hunger, thirst and fatigue, his mind unsettled by exhaustion, reach the fruit that the mind must reach, while he is not at ease?
“Ease is properly won by keeping the senses constantly satisfied; when the senses are satisfied, the mind is at rest.

cmp.note: 原文是「由于持续满足诸根而得安宁」，白话加了「只有」，把语气说得比原文更绝对。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit says ease comes “from the constant satisfying of the senses”; the plain Chinese adds 只有 (zhǐyǒu, “only”), making it more absolute than the original.

verses.en: “In a mind at rest and clear, concentration arises; in a mind joined with concentration, the practice of meditation goes forward.
“When meditation goes forward, the states are gained by which one reaches that hard-won, peaceful, ageless, supreme, deathless state.
“So food is the root of this method.” Having settled this, the steadfast one, of boundless mind, made up his mind to take food.
Having bathed, he came up slowly from the bank of the Nairanjana, thin as he was, and the trees on the bank lent him a hand with the tips of their branches bent low in devotion.
Then Nandabala, daughter of the chief of the cowherds, urged on by the gods, came there, her heart brimming with joy.
Her arms gleamed with white conch-shell bracelets, and she wore a dark-blue woollen cloth, like the Yamuna, best of rivers, its blue waters garlanded with foam.
Her joy grown greater through faith, her lotus eyes opening wide, she bowed her head to him and had him accept a dish of milk-rice.
By eating it he made her birth bear its fruit, and he himself, all six senses satisfied, became able to win Awakening.
His body now fully filled out, and his fame growing with it, the sage alone bore the loveliness of the moon and the steadiness of the ocean together.
Thinking he had turned back, the five monks left him, as the five elements leave the wise self once it is freed.
Then, with resolve as his only companion, determined to win Awakening, he went to the foot of an ashvattha tree (a sacred fig, the bodhi tree), where the ground was spread with grass.
Then Kala, best of serpents (nagas), woken by his matchless footfall as he strode like a king of elephants, knew that the great sage had made up his mind to Awakening, and sang his praise:
“Since the earth, pressed by your feet, O sage, seems to rumble again and again, and since your splendour shines like the sun, surely today you will enjoy the fruit you desire.
“Since flocks of blue jays wheel in the sky, circling you to the right in reverence, lotus-eyed one, and since gentle breezes blow through the sky, today you will surely become a Buddha.”

cmp.note: 「右绕」：以右侧朝向被敬者绕行，是印度表示敬意的礼节；鸟群右绕被视为吉兆。
cmp.en: Pradakshina is circling with one’s right side toward the honoured person, the Indian gesture of reverence; birds doing so are an auspicious omen.

verses.en: Praised by the foremost of serpents, he took clean grass from a grass-cutter and, having made his vow, sat down for Awakening at the foot of the great pure tree.
Then he took up the supreme cross-legged posture, unshakeable, coiled like the body of a sleeping serpent: “I will not break this posture on the earth until I have done what I must do.”

cmp.note: 字面是「我不打破这个坐姿」，白话作「决不离开这个座位」，意思相近，但原文强调的是坐姿本身不散。
cmp.en: Literally “I will not break this posture”; the plain Chinese has “I will not leave this seat”, close in sense, though the Sanskrit stresses holding the posture itself unbroken.

verses.en: Then the dwellers of heaven felt joy beyond compare; no herds of beasts cried out, no birds called, and the forest trees, though struck by the wind, made no sound, when the Blessed One took his seat, his mind made firm.
When the great seer, sprung from a line of royal seers, had sat down there, vowing to win liberation, the world rejoiced; but Mara, the enemy of the true Dharma, trembled.

He whom the world calls Kamadeva, the god of love, bearer of bright weapons and of arrows made of flowers — that same lord of the workings of desire is the one they name Mara, the enemy of liberation.

cmp.note: 马鸣在这里把印度教的爱神（Kāmadeva，花箭之神）和佛教的魔罗等同起来：迷人的爱欲之神，就是阻挡解脱的死魔。英文直接写成同一个人物的两个名字。古译只说「五欲自在王……故名为波旬」，没有提爱神。
cmp.en: Ashvaghosha deliberately identifies the Hindu love-god Kamadeva, with his flower arrows, with the Buddhist Mara: the charming god of desire is the same figure as the death-dealing obstacle to liberation. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version keeps only 五欲自在王 (wǔyù zìzài wáng, "sovereign of the five desires") and calls him 波旬 (Bōxún, Papiyan), dropping the love-god.

verses.en: His three sons, Confusion, Elation and Pride, and his three daughters, Discontent, Delight and Thirst, asked him why his mind was troubled, and he spoke these words to sons and daughters alike.

cmp.note: 梵本是三子（Vibhrama 迷乱、Harṣa 欢喜、Darpa 骄傲）加三女（Arati 不乐、Prīti 快意、Tṛṣ 渴爱）。古译只写三个女儿，名字也不同（欲染、能悦人、可爱乐），三个儿子没有出现。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit gives Mara three sons (Vibhrama, Harsha, Darpa: Confusion, Elation, Pride) and three daughters (Arati, Priti, Trish: Discontent, Delight, Thirst). Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has only three daughters, with different names — 欲染 (yùrǎn, "stained by desire"), 能悦人 (néng yuè rén, "able to please"), 可爱乐 (kě àilè, "lovable") — and leaves out the sons.

verses.en: “That sage over there, wearing the armor of resolve, has drawn back the arrow of insight on the bow of courage, and sits there bent on conquering my realms. That is why my mind is downcast.”

“For if he gets the better of me and goes on to proclaim to the world the path to final release, then this realm of mine will stand empty today, like the kingdom of the Videhan king who fell from right conduct.”

cmp.note: 这里暗指一个传说：毗提诃（Videha）的一位国王因行为失德而亡国。古译把典故换成泛泛的「譬如人犯戒，其身则空虚」。
cmp.en: An allusion to a legend of a king of Videha who lost his kingdom by falling from right conduct. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version replaces the allusion with a general image: 譬如人犯戒，其身则空虚 ("as when a man breaks the precepts, he himself becomes empty").

verses.en: “So while he has not yet gained the eye of wisdom, while he still stays within my range, I will go and break his vow, as a swollen river in flood breaks through a dam.”

Then he who unsettles the minds of creatures took up his bow made of flowers and the five arrows that bewilder the world, and went with his children to the root of the ashvattha tree (the sacred fig under which the Bodhisattva sat).
There sat the sage, calm upon his seat, longing to cross to the far shore of the ocean of existence. Mara rested his left hand on the tip of his bow, and toying with an arrow he said:

“Get up, you kshatriya, you who fear death! Follow your own duty and give up this law of liberation. Bring the world to order with arrows and with sacrifices, and from this world win the realm of Indra.”

cmp.note: 魔罗玩弄 dharma 一词：svadharma 是武士阶层「自己的本分」，mokṣadharma 是「求解脱的法」。英文分别译成 your own duty 和 this law of liberation，两个词在原文里是同一个字。
cmp.en: Mara plays on the word dharma: svadharma is a warrior’s ‘own duty’, mokshadharma the ‘law (or path) of liberation’. The English has to split them into “your own duty” and “this law of liberation”, though the Sanskrit uses one word for both.

verses.en: “This is the glorious road to set out on, the one traveled by the kings of the most ancient times. For a man born into a great family of royal seers, to take up a beggar’s life is nothing to be proud of.”
“But if you will not get up today, then stay firm, you resolute one, and do not let go of your vow — for the arrow I hold ready here is the very one I loosed at Shurpaka, the enemy of fish.”

cmp.note: Śūrpaka「鱼的敌人」大概是传说中的一个渔夫，被爱欲之箭射中而爱上公主；典故今已不详。白话把它当作人名照录，古译则略去。
cmp.en: Shurpaka, “the enemy of fish”, is probably a fisherman of legend who was struck by love’s arrow and fell for a princess; the story is now obscure. The plain Chinese keeps it as a name; Dharmakshema’s Chinese version leaves it out.

verses.en: “Touched by it, even Aida (Pururavas, son of Ila), the Moon’s grandson, lost his wits, and Shantanu too lost all self-control. What hope, then, for anyone weaker, now that the age has run down?”

“So get up quickly and come to your senses! For this arrow stands ready, flicking out its tongue like a snake — the arrow I do not waste on those already slaves to their beloved and in love with pleasure, just as I do not waste it on the chakravaka birds.”

cmp.note: 这半句难解。较顺的读法是：这支箭用不着射向那些早已被情人支配、贪恋欢爱的人，就像用不着射向成对恩爱的赤麻鸭（cakravāka）——它是专门留给难对付的人的。白话译成「舍不得射它们」，意思接近但语气不同。
cmp.en: A difficult line. The likeliest sense is that this arrow is not wasted on people already ruled by their lovers, any more than on the devoted chakravaka birds (a pair of ruddy geese, emblem of faithful love) — it is kept for hard cases like the Bodhisattva. The plain Chinese renders it as 舍不得射 (shěbude shè, "cannot bear to shoot"), close in sense but different in tone.

verses.en: Even when he was spoken to like this, the Shakya sage paid no heed and did not even shift from his seat. Then Mara loosed the arrow at him, putting his daughters and sons in front.
But even when that arrow had been let fly, he gave it no heed and did not waver from his steadiness. Seeing him like this, Mara lost heart, and caught up in his thoughts he said slowly:

“Struck by this arrow, even the god Shambhu (Shiva) was shaken with love for the daughter of the king of mountains. Yet this man does not even notice it. Can he have no heart at all? Or is this not the same arrow?”
“So he is not one for the flower arrow, nor for arousal, nor for sending in Rati, goddess of pleasure. What he needs is to be frightened, threatened and beaten by hosts of savage creatures.”
Then Mara called his army to mind, wanting to break the Shakya sage’s calm; and his followers, in bodies of every kind, crowded round with spears, trees, javelins, maces and swords in their hands.

Some had the faces of boars, fish, horses, donkeys and camels, some the heads of tigers, bears, lions and elephants; some were one-eyed, some many-faced, some three-headed; some had hanging bellies and some had spotted bellies.

Some had neither knees nor thighs, some had knees like water-pots; some were armed with fangs, some with claws; some had faces like skulls, some many bodies, some faces broken in half, some enormous mouths.

Some were ash-red and spattered with drops of blood, carrying skull-topped staffs, their hair tawny or smoke-gray; they wore drooping garlands and had ears that hung down like an elephant’s; some were dressed in hides and some went naked.

Some had faces half white, some bodies half green; some were copper-red, some smoke-gray, some tawny, some black; some wore snakes slung over their arms like shawls, and some had girdles crowded with jangling bells.
Some were as tall as palm trees and gripped spears; some were no bigger than children, but hideous with fangs; some had rams’ faces and birds’ eyes, some cats’ faces on human bodies.

Some had wild, loose hair, some topknots, some heads half-shaved; some wore red clothes, some had their turbans in a tangle; some faces grinned and some scowled; some sapped a man’s strength, and some stole away his mind.

cmp.note: manohara 字面是「夺心的」，平常却是「迷人、可爱」的意思；与 tejohara「夺人精气的」并列，形成双关：既可怕又迷人。白话译「摄人心魄」保留了一半。
cmp.en: Manohara literally means ‘mind-stealing’ but in ordinary use means ‘charming, lovely’; set beside tejohara, ‘strength-stealing’, it makes a pun — these creatures are both frightening and alluring. The plain Chinese 摄人心魄 (shè rén xīnpò, "seizing the soul") keeps only one side.

verses.en: Some leapt wildly about as they went, others sprang on top of one another; some played in the sky, and some ran along the tops of the trees.
One danced, whirling a trident; one thundered as he dragged a mace along; one bellowed for joy like a bull; one blazed with fire that shot from the hairs of his body.
Such were the hosts of creatures that stood round the root of the bodhi tree on every side, eager to seize him and eager to kill him, waiting only for their master’s order.
Seeing that hour of battle between Mara and the bull of the Shakyas, in the first watch of the night, the sky lost its brightness, the earth shook, and the quarters of the world blazed and roared.
The wind blew wildly from every side in unleashed fury; the stars did not shine and the moon gave no light; night spread a deeper darkness, and all the oceans heaved.
The nagas who bear up the earth, devoted to the Dharma, could not endure this hindrance to the great sage; they rolled their eyes in anger at Mara, hissed, and opened their jaws wide.

cmp.note: mahībhṛt「托大地者」通常指山；这里也可读作「群山和龙」两个主语。白话和本译都把它当作龙的称号（托着大地的龙），因为后面的翻眼、呼气、张口都是蛇龙的动作。
cmp.en: Mahibhrit, ‘earth-bearer’, usually means a mountain, so the line could also be read as ‘the mountains and the nagas’. Like the plain Chinese, this translation takes it as an epithet of the nagas (serpent beings who hold up the earth), since rolling eyes, hissing and gaping are serpent actions.

verses.en: But the divine seers of the Pure Abodes (the highest heavens), intent only on the triumph of the true Dharma, felt pity for Mara in their hearts; being free of passion, they felt no anger.
Seeing the root of the bodhi tree overrun by that murderous army of Mara, the beings in the sky whose hearts were set on the Dharma and who longed for the world’s liberation cried out, “Alas!”
But the great seer, seeing Mara’s army standing there to wreck his work for the Dharma, was not shaken and did not change at all, like a lion seated among cattle.
Then Mara ordered his surging army of creatures to frighten him; and that army, each using its own powers, set out to break his steadfastness.
Some, with many lolling tongues, sharp-pointed fangs, eyes like round yellow discs, gaping mouths and ears stiff as stakes, stood there doing their best to terrify him.
Faced with these creatures standing there, dreadful in form and dreadful in temper, the great seer felt neither fear nor alarm, as if they were small children playing rough games.
Then one, his eyes rolling with rage, raised his mace against him; and his arm froze where it was, mace and all, as Indra’s arm once froze with the thunderbolt in it.
Some lifted rocks and trees but could not manage to hurl them at the sage; they toppled over, trees, rocks and all, like spurs of the Vindhya mountains shattered by the thunderbolt.
Others leapt up into the sky and flung rocks, trees and axes; these stayed hanging in the sky and did not fall, like the many-colored trailing edges of evening clouds.
Another hurled down on him a blazing heap of chaff as big as a mountain peak; the moment it was let go, while still in the air, it burst into a hundred pieces by his power.
One, blazing like the newly risen sun, let loose from the sky a great rain of live coals, like Meru on fire at the end of an eon, shedding the crumbled dust of its golden caves.
But that rain of sparking coals, as it scattered over the foot of the bodhi tree, turned into a shower of red lotus petals, because the best of seers was dwelling in loving-kindness.

cmp.note: maitrī-vihāra 是「安住于慈」，一种禅修状态，不只是心地好。炭火变成莲花，是这种禅定的力量所致。古译改成「雷震雨大雹，化成五色花」，原因没有交代。
cmp.en: Maitri-vihara, ‘dwelling in loving-kindness’, is a meditative state, not just a kindly mood; it is this state that turns the coals into lotus petals. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version has thunder and hail turning into 五色花 (wǔsè huā, "five-colored flowers") and gives no cause.

verses.en: Though such torments of body and mind, burning and searing, rained down on him one after another, the Shakya sage did not stir from his seat, but held his resolve close, as one embraces a kinsman.
Others spewed snakes from their mouths, as if from hollow, rotting trees; but near him the snakes, as though bound by a spell, did not hiss, did not crawl, did not move.
Others became great rain clouds, with lightning and the fierce crash of thunderbolts, and let fall a rain of stones on that tree; but it became a lovely rain of flowers.
Another set an arrow to his bow; it blazed up right there and never flew, like the anger of a powerless man who cannot swallow an insult, smoldering away inside himself.

The five arrows loosed by another stood still in the air and did not fall on the sage — like the five senses of a man who weighs things carefully and fears the round of rebirth, which do not settle on their objects.

cmp.note: 爱神（即魔罗）的「五支箭」在这里与人的「五根（五种感官）」对照：箭射不到牟尼，正如审慎者的感官不会扑向感官对象。白话译出了这层对照。
cmp.en: The ‘five arrows’ of the love-god (Mara) are matched against the ‘five senses’ (indriya): the arrows cannot reach the sage, just as a careful person’s senses do not rush out to their objects. The plain Chinese keeps the parallel.

verses.en: Another, in a fury, rushed at the great seer with a mace, meaning to kill him; but he failed in his aim and fell helpless, as the world falls into faults that bring ruin.

A woman named Meghakali, holding a skull-bowl in her hand, meant, it is said, to bewilder the great seer’s mind; but she wandered about there aimlessly and could not keep still, like the mind of a fickle man among the scriptures.

cmp.note: 梵本只说是「一个女人，名叫云时黑（Meghakālī）」，似是凶相的女鬼神。古译说她是魔王的姊妹「弥伽迦利」，并以淫惑扰乱菩萨，加入了色诱的意味。
cmp.en: The Sanskrit simply says “a woman, Meghakali” (‘black as a storm cloud’), apparently a fierce female spirit. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version makes her Mara’s sister 弥伽迦利 (Míjiājiālì) and has her try to seduce the Bodhisattva (婬惑 (yínhuò, “lustful enticement”)), adding an erotic note.

verses.en: One fixed his blazing eye on him, longing to burn him up with the fire of his gaze, as a venomous snake does; yet he could not see the seer sitting right there, just as a man ruled by desire cannot see the good when it is pointed out to him.
