Another, heaving up a heavy rock, wore himself out in vain, his efforts all thwarted — like a man who hopes to win the highest good, the Dharma that is reached through knowledge and meditation, by tiring out the body.

cmp.note: 「靠折磨身体」——暗讽苦行。菩萨此前已放弃六年苦行（第12章），这里借比喻再次表明：解脱靠智慧与禅定，不靠苦身。
cmp.en: ‘By tiring out the body’ is a jab at extreme asceticism: the Bodhisattva has just given up his years of self-mortification (Chapter 12), and the simile restates that liberation comes through knowledge and meditation, not bodily hardship.

verses.en: Others, shaped like hyenas and lions, let out great roars, so that living things everywhere cowered, thinking the sky was splitting apart under the stroke of the thunderbolt.
Deer and elephants, crying out in distress, fled and hid; and that night, as though it were day, birds flew about from every direction, screeching in alarm.
But though all creatures shook at such roaring, the sage was not frightened and did not shrink, any more than Garuda, king of birds, at the cawing of crows.
And the less the sage feared those terrifying hosts of followers, the more Mara, the enemy of those who uphold the Dharma, sank down in grief and rage.
Then some being of high rank, whose form could not be seen, standing in the sky itself, saw Mara bent on harming the seer and angry without any cause for enmity, and spoke to him in a loud voice:
“Mara, you should not wear yourself out for nothing. Give up your violent nature and go home in peace. He cannot be shaken by you, any more than Meru, the great mountain, by the wind.”
“Fire might lose its heat, water its wetness, earth its firmness; but he, who has gathered merit by his deeds through many eons, will never let go of his resolve.”

“With such resolve as his, such valor and radiance and compassion for living beings, he will not rise until he has reached the truth, just as the thousand-rayed sun does not rise without destroying the darkness.”
“Rub firewood and you get fire; dig the earth and you find water. For the persistent nothing is out of reach: everything done with the right method succeeds.”
“He pities the world, suffering from the diseases of passion and the rest; he is the great physician, toiling to find the medicine of knowledge. He does not deserve to be hindered.”
“When the world has been carried off down many wrong roads, he labors to find the right one. Such a guide should not be harassed — no more than a good guide when the caravan has lost its way.”
“When beings are lost in a great darkness, he is a lamp of knowledge being kindled. It is not right to put out the noble one’s light, like a lamp just lit in the dark.”

cmp.note: nirvāpayati「吹灭」与 nirvāṇa（涅槃，本义「熄灭」）同根。魔罗想「吹灭」的，正是将要带人走向涅槃的那盏灯——一个反讽。
cmp.en: Nirvapayati, ‘to blow out, extinguish’, comes from the same root as nirvana (literally ‘going out, extinction’). Mara wants to ‘blow out’ the very lamp that will lead others to nirvana — an irony the English can only hint at.

verses.en: “He saw the world sunk in the great flood of the round of rebirth, unable to find the far shore, and set out to carry it across. What decent person could think of doing him harm?”

“Patience is its rootlets, steadfastness its deep-sunk root, good conduct its flowers, mindfulness and understanding its branches: this tree of knowledge, which gives the fruit of Dharma, is still growing, and it must not be torn up.”
“His purpose is to set free a people whose minds are bound fast by the strong nooses of delusion. He is toiling to free the world from its bonds; it is not fitting for you to want to kill him.”
“For all the deeds he has done for the sake of Awakening, today is the appointed time of ripening; and he is seated on this spot just as the sages before him were seated.”
“For this is the navel of the earth, endowed in full with the highest power; there is no other place on the ground that could bear the force of his concentration.”
“So do not grieve; find peace. Do not let your greatness make you proud, Mara. Fortune is fickle and cannot be trusted. Why are you so pleased with yourself when your footing is unsteady?”
When he had heard those words and seen how unshaken the great sage was, Mara went away dejected, his efforts broken, together with the arrows with which he wounds the hearts of the world.
His army, its glee gone and its labors made useless, threw away its rocks, its chaff and its trees and fled in all directions, like an enemy’s army whose leader has been killed by the foe.

When the flower-bannered god had been beaten and fled with his followers, and the great seer had won, free of darkness and free of dust, the sky shone with its moon like a smiling young woman, and a fragrant rain of flowers fell, heavy with dew.

cmp.note: 「胜过黑暗、离开尘垢」：tamas（黑暗、愚痴）与 rajas（尘土、激情）既是自然景象，又是心性术语。魔军散去时天空也变得无暗无尘，一语双关。
cmp.en: ‘Free of darkness and free of dust’: tamas (darkness, dullness) and rajas (dust, passion) are both images of the night sky and terms for mental states. As Mara’s army scatters, the sky too is cleared of dark and dust — a double meaning.

verses.en: Then, having conquered Mara’s army by steadfastness and calm, he who was skilled in meditation sat in meditation, longing to know the highest truth.

cmp.note: paramārtha 是「最高的意义 / 究竟真实」，后来成为佛教「胜义谛」的术语。古译作「第一义」，白话作「最高的真实」，英文作 the highest truth。
cmp.en: Paramartha, ‘the highest meaning, ultimate reality’, later became the technical term for ultimate truth in Buddhist philosophy. Dharmakshema’s Chinese version renders it 第一义 (dìyī yì, "the first meaning"); the English uses “the highest truth”.

verses.en: Having gained supreme mastery in every method of meditation, in the first watch of the night he called to mind the long chain of his former births.
“There I was so-and-so by name; passing away from there, I came here” — in this way he remembered thousands of births, as if he were living through them again.
When he had remembered birth and death in each of those many existences, he whose very nature was compassion felt compassion for living beings.
“Here a creature leaves its own people behind, and elsewhere it takes up its business all over again. Truly this world has no protector, and it goes round and round like a wheel.”
As he remembered in this way, with his mind held steady, he reached a firm conviction: the round of rebirth is as empty of substance as the core of a plantain stalk.

cmp.note: 芭蕉（kadalī）的茎一层层剥开，中间没有硬心，是印度佛教常用的「无实」之喻。白话、古译都作「芭蕉」；英文用 plantain stalk。
cmp.en: The plantain or banana stem (kadali) peels away layer by layer with no hard core inside — a stock Indian image for something without substance. Both Chinese versions use 芭蕉 (bājiāo, "plantain").

verses.en: When the second watch came, he whose valor had no second, the best of all who have eyes, gained the supreme divine eye.

cmp.note: 文字游戏：dvitīya「第二」更，advitīya「无第二」的勇猛。英文以 second watch / had no second 保留。白话译「勇猛无双」意思对，但失去了与「第二更」的呼应。
cmp.en: A play on words: in the ‘second’ (dvitiya) watch, the one whose valor was ‘without a second’ (advitiya). The English keeps it with “second watch” / “had no second”; the plain Chinese 勇猛无双 (yǒngměng wúshuāng, "peerless in valor") is correct but loses the echo.

verses.en: Then, with that divine and perfectly pure eye, he saw the whole world, as one sees things in a spotless mirror.
As he watched beings of low deeds and of lofty deeds passing away and being reborn, his compassion grew deeper still.
“These creatures, whose deeds were evil, go to a bad destiny; these others, whose deeds were good, find their place in heaven.”
“These, born into a hell that is terrifying and utterly cruel, are tormented by sufferings of many kinds. How pitiful!”
“Some are made to drink molten iron, boiling and the color of fire; others, screaming, are hoisted onto a red-hot iron pillar.”
“Some are cooked like dough, head downward, in iron cauldrons; some are pitifully burned on heaps of glowing coals.”
“Some are devoured by savage dogs with sharp iron teeth; some by fierce crows with iron beaks, as if they too were made of iron.”
“Some, worn out by the burning and longing for cool shade, walk into the dark-blue Forest of Sword-Leaves as if they were being led there in chains.”
“Some, with their arms bound, are split like logs with axes; yet even in such pain they do not perish, for their own deeds keep the life in them.”
“The deed that was done with the thought ‘this will bring pleasure’, to keep pain away — this is its fruit: nothing but pain, endured against their will.”
“These who did evil for the sake of pleasure and are now in such agony — does that taste they once enjoyed give them even the slightest happiness now?”
“The foul deed that foul-hearted people did while laughing is suffered, with wailing, when its time has ripened.”
“If evildoers could see the fruit of their deeds like this, they would vomit hot blood, as if struck in a vital spot.”
“These others, poor wretches, because of the varied deeds that spring from the restlessness of the mind, have been born among the many kinds of animals.”

cmp.note: tapasvin 本义「苦行者」，口语里也指「可怜的人」。这里是后一义，但字面上带着反讽：它们受的苦比苦行者还多。白话作「可怜的生灵」，正确。
cmp.en: Tapasvin literally means ‘one who practices austerity’, but in ordinary speech it also means ‘poor wretch’. The second sense is meant here, with an ironic shadow of the first. The plain Chinese 可怜的生灵 (kělián de shēnglíng, "pitiable creatures") is right.

verses.en: “There they are pitifully slaughtered for their flesh, skin, hair or tusks, out of enmity, or even just for sport, while their own kin look on.”
“Born as oxen and horses, they are driven on helplessly even when they have no strength left, tormented by hunger, thirst and weariness, their bodies torn by the goad.”
“Born as elephants, they are driven by creatures weaker than themselves, strong as they are, their heads tormented by the hook, kicked with feet and heels.”
“Though there are other sufferings too, the special suffering here comes from their enmity toward one another and from being in the power of others.”

“Creatures of the air are harried by creatures of the air, those of the water by those that live in the water, those of the land by those that dwell on land — they prey on one another whenever they meet.”
“And these, their minds overcome by meanness, have been reborn in the lightless world of the departed, where they pitifully eat the fruit of their deeds.”

cmp.note: pitṛloka 字面是「祖灵界」，在佛教语境里就是饿鬼（preta）所在之处。古译直接作「饿鬼趣」；白话保留字面「祖灵界」，读者可能不知道指的是饿鬼。
cmp.en: Pitriloka literally means ‘world of the fathers (ancestors)’; in a Buddhist setting it is the realm of hungry ghosts (preta). Dharmakshema’s Chinese version says so directly, 饿鬼趣 (èguǐ qù, "realm of hungry ghosts"); the plain Chinese keeps the literal 祖灵界 (zǔlíng jiè), which may not tell readers what is meant.

verses.en: “With mouths like the eye of a needle and bellies like mountains, these wretched ones are racked by the pains of hunger and thirst.”
“Their hopes betrayed, held fast by their own deeds, they cannot manage to eat even the filth that others have thrown away.”
“If people knew that meanness bears such fruit, they would give freely in every way — even the limbs of their own bodies, as King Shibi did (he gave his own flesh to save a dove).”

“These other creatures, born among humans, come to suffering in a filthy pool, like a hell, that is called the womb.” (The surviving Sanskrit breaks off here; the rest of the poem is known only from the Chinese and Tibetan translations.)
